samples.human_continuation: According to the results, voters for Sarkozy's UMP make love on average 6.7 times a month, slightly less often than supporters of his main challenger, the Socialist Party's Francois Hollande, on 7.6. samples.prefix: TOP 5 SPENDING TOP 5 SPENDING WASHINGTON  Tuesday's midterm elections — and the record-shattering amounts outside groups spent to oust Democratic incumbents — are just a warm-up to the 2012 presidential race, analysts and experts say. Conservative groups outspent liberal groups by a more than 2-to-1 ratio heading into an Election Day that brought the biggest Republican sweep in the House of Representatives in decades and sliced into the Democratic majority in the Senate.
samples.human_continuation: "The Democrats brought a bat, and the Republicans brought a grenade," said Dave Levinthal of the Center for Responsive Politics, which tracks campaign money. "If you think spending is out of control by outside groups, it likely will blow your mind in the presidential election." President Obama has repeatedly lambasted conservative groups for their role in the midterm elections and criticized the Supreme Court's decision in January that opened the floodgates to unlimited corporate and union spending on election ads. Conservative spending has topped $187 million this year, up from $19.6 million in 2006, the last midterm election, the center's data show. The leader of one of the leading GOP organizations said on Wednesday that it plans to play a big role in 2012.
samples.ai_continuation_chat: Dave Levinthal, president of the Center for Responsive Politics, warns that the financial deluge seen this November is merely a precursor to an unprecedented spending war in 2012. With the Supreme Court’s Citizens United ruling removing caps on independent expenditures, conservative groups are poised to mobilize even greater resources than their liberal counterparts. Analysts predict that outside spending will far exceed the record levels established during these midterms, fundamentally altering the political landscape. President Obama faces a daunting challenge as the GOP leverages this newfound financial firepower to target his re-election bid. The sheer volume of money flooding into the race suggests that 2012 will be defined not just by policy debates, but by an unprecedented scale of independent advocacy that could overwhelm traditional campaign structures.
samples.ai_continuation_free: The sheer volume of cash poured into the midterms, much of it flowing through Super PACs and other independent expenditure committees, has fundamentally altered the landscape of American politics. Experts note that while the 2012 presidential election is still months away, the infrastructure built by these outside groups is already in place and ready to scale up. Conservative organizations, emboldened by their financial dominance and the electoral gains, are preparing to spend even more heavily to challenge President Obama’s re-election bid. Meanwhile, liberal groups are scrambling to close the funding gap, recognizing that the traditional party-based fundraising model is no longer sufficient to compete with the new era of unlimited independent spending. As the political dust settles from Tuesday’s results, both sides are already turning their attention to the next big battle, where the war chests are expected to swell to unprecedented levels.

samples.prefix: MISSISSAUGA, Ontario — The Maine Red Claws, used a balanced attack and solid defense to shut down Raptors 905 Saturday afternoon, 100-91. Damion Lee led the Red Claws with 22 points, and Marcus Georges-Hunt finished near another triple-double with 19 points, 10 rebounds and 4 assists. Demetrius Jackson, on assignment from the Boston Celtics, added 19 points, 8 rebounds and 7 assists in the win.
samples.human_continuation: Arthur Edwards led the bench with 11 points, while Coron Williams contributed 10 points in his first start of the season. The Red Claws (5-2) carried Lee to a hot offensive start. Scoring both inside and outside, Lee was able to score 10 of his points in the 1st quarter, including eight straight to give the Claws the lead. With Lee and Georges-Hunt leading the charge, Edwards and Jason Calliste added three’s off the banch, and Maine rolled out to a 31-18 lead after one. Edwards opened the 2nd quarter with a three-point play, putting Maine up 38-23. Raptors 905 (3-1) would go on a 11-0 run, thanks in large part to Will Sheehey, who drained back-to-back three-pointers. The 905 took a 44-42 lead. Williams snapped a 49-49 tie with a pair of free throws, and. Panoske’s three late in the 2nd gave Maine a 59-50 lead at the break.
samples.ai_continuation_chat: The first half saw the Red Claws establish an early rhythm, with Jackson orchestrating the offense and finding open shooters. Georges-Hunt attacked the rim relentlessly, drawing fouls and converting from the line. Arthur Edwards provided a spark off the bench, knocking down a pair of three-pointers to stretch the lead to 12 midway through the second quarter. Coron Williams answered for Raptors 905, hitting a contested jumper and a corner three to keep the deficit manageable. Will Sheehey added physical drives and a putback dunk, while Jason Calliste contributed crafty finishes in transition. However, Panoske’s interior presence for the Red Claws disrupted Raptors 905’s pick-and-roll game, forcing tough mid-range attempts. By halftime, Maine held a 54-43 advantage, thanks to 54% shooting and 10 assists on 18 made field goals.
samples.ai_continuation_free:
Maine shot 47 percent from the floor and forced 19 turnovers, turning them into 25 points on the other end. The Red Claws also controlled the glass, outrebounding Raptors 905 46-38. Georges-Hunt was especially active on both ends, drawing charges and crashing the boards from the wing. Jackson provided steady leadership in the backcourt, running the offense efficiently and knocking down timely shots when the Raptors looked to make a run.

For Raptors 905, Kennedy Meeks recorded a double-double with 18 points and 12 rebounds, and Kaza Keane added 15 points off the bench. However, the home team struggled to find consistent offense, shooting just 39 percent from the field and 30 percent from three-point range. Turnovers plagued them throughout, particularly in the third quarter when Maine stretched a six-point halftime lead to as many as 17.

The win improved Maine’s record to 16-13, while Raptors 905 fell to 15-14. The two teams will meet again Monday afternoon in Mississauga to close out their weekend series.

samples.prefix: Plants can’t run away from a threat but they can stand their ground. “They are very good at avoiding getting eaten,” said Linda Walling of the University of California , Riverside. “It’s an unusual situation where insects can overcome those defenses.” At the smallest nip to its leaves, specialized cells on the plant’s surface release chemicals to irritate the predator or sticky goo to entrap it.
samples.human_continuation: Genes in the plant’s DNA are activated to wage systemwide chemical warfare, the plant’s version of an immune response . We need terpenes, alkaloids, phenolics — let’s move. Photo “I’m amazed at how fast some of these things happen,” said Consuelo M. De Moraes of Pennsylvania State University . De Moraes and her colleagues did labeling experiments to clock a plant’s systemic response time and found that, in less than 20 minutes from the moment the caterpillar had begun feeding on its leaves, the plant had plucked carbon from the air and forged defensive compounds from scratch. Just because we humans can’t hear them doesn’t mean plants don’t howl. Some of the compounds that plants generate in response to insect mastication — their feedback, you might say — are volatile chemicals that serve as cries for help.
samples.ai_continuation_chat: If the attack persists, the plant mounts a systemic defense, sending signals from the wounded leaf to distant tissues. Within minutes, genes switch on to produce toxic alkaloids, bitter phenolics, or other deterrent compounds throughout the plant. “It’s not just a local response,” Walling explained. “The whole plant prepares for battle.” Meanwhile, the plant releases a bouquet of volatile chemicals—terpenes and other airborne signals—that can attract predatory wasps or parasitic flies to come and attack the herbivores. “These volatiles are like a cry for help,” said Consuelo M. De Moraes of ETH Zurich. Some volatiles even warn neighboring plants of the impending threat, allowing them to prime their own defenses. This sophisticated, multi-layered arsenal helps plants survive in a world full of hungry insects.
samples.ai_continuation_free: Some plants even send out airborne signals to warn their neighbors. When a lima bean leaf is chewed by spider mites, it releases a blend of volatile compounds that drift through the air. Nearby lima bean plants detect these chemicals and begin fortifying their own leaves with defensive toxins before the mites ever arrive. “It’s like a silent scream,” Walling explained. “The plant under attack is telling its neighbors, ‘Brace yourselves.’” Other species take a more direct approach. The tomato plant, for example, produces alkaloids that make its leaves taste bitter and cause digestive distress in hungry caterpillars. If the assault continues, it can ramp up production of proteinase inhibitors, which block the insect’s ability to digest the plant tissue, effectively starving the attacker. These defenses are costly to maintain, so plants only deploy them when a real threat is detected—saving energy for growth and reproduction when no predator is in sight.

content_constraint.topic: Plants activate rapid systemic chemical defenses and volatile signals in response to insect attack.
content_constraint.content_direction: Describes the speed and mechanism of plant systemic immune response, including de novo synthesis of defensive compounds and release of volatile signals as distress calls.
content_constraint.scope: Covers the activation of genetic defenses, rapid carbon fixation for compound production, and the role of volatiles as communication signals, ending with the analogy of plants 'howling'.

samples.prefix: Abstract Early warning signals of the coronary heart disease (CHD) risk of sugar (sucrose) emerged in the 1950s. We examined Sugar Research Foundation (SRF) internal documents, historical reports, and statements relevant to early debates about the dietary causes of CHD and assembled findings chronologically into a narrative case study.
samples.human_continuation: The SRF sponsored its first CHD research project in 1965, a literature review published in the New England Journal of Medicine, which singled out fat and cholesterol as the dietary causes of CHD and downplayed evidence that sucrose consumption was also a risk factor. The SRF set the review’s objective, contributed articles for inclusion, and received drafts. The SRF’s funding and role was not disclosed. Together with other recent analyses of sugar industry documents, our findings suggest the industry sponsored a research program in the 1960s and 1970s that successfully cast doubt about the hazards of sucrose while promoting fat as the dietary culprit in CHD. Policymaking committees should consider giving less weight to food industry–funded studies and include mechanistic and animal studies as well as studies appraising the effect of added sugars on multiple CHD biomarkers and disease development.
samples.ai_continuation_chat: By the early 1960s, the SRF recognized that mounting evidence linking sugar consumption to elevated triglycerides and insulin response posed a direct threat to the industry's commercial interests. In 1964, the SRF's board approved a research budget specifically aimed at countering this narrative. The following year, the foundation secretly commissioned a literature review from prominent Harvard nutritionists, paying them the equivalent of roughly $50,000 today. The review, published in the *New England Journal of Medicine* in 1967, systematically dismissed studies implicating sucrose in CHD development while aggressively foregrounding data that indicted dietary fat and cholesterol. The authors did not disclose SRF's funding or editorial input. This strategic manipulation helped shape U.S. nutritional policy for decades, diverting attention from sugar's metabolic consequences and entrenching the low-fat paradigm that dominated public health guidance until the early 2000s.
samples.ai_continuation_free: By the mid-20th century, coronary heart disease had become a leading cause of death in industrialized nations, spurring intense scientific debate over its dietary origins. Two primary hypotheses emerged: one implicated dietary fat and cholesterol, while the other pointed to sugar as a key driver. In 1954, the Sugar Research Foundation, an industry group funded by sugar producers, began funding research that would shape public understanding. Internal documents reveal that the SRF strategically sponsored studies that downplayed sugar's role and highlighted fat as the culprit. For instance, in 1967, the SRF paid three Harvard researchers $6,500 (equivalent to roughly $50,000 today) to publish a review article in the New England Journal of Medicine that minimized evidence linking sugar to CHD and criticized the sugar hypothesis. The article, which became highly influential, helped steer dietary guidelines and medical advice toward fat reduction for decades.

content_constraint.topic: The Sugar Research Foundation's undisclosed sponsorship of a 1965 literature review that downplayed sucrose's role in coronary heart disease and promoted fat as the main dietary cause.
content_constraint.content_direction: Reveals how the SRF manipulated a scientific review to shift blame from sugar to fat, and argues that industry-funded studies should be given less weight in policy decisions.
content_constraint.scope: Covers the SRF's 1965 sponsored review and its impact, then extends to broader implications for food industry research and policy recommendations.

samples.prefix: Three people you may have heard of—writer John Gruber, developer Brent Simmons, and designer Dave Wiskus—have joined forces to create Q Branch, an app development company whose first product is a $5 iPhone app called Vesper. The app, released Thursday, aims to help “collect your thoughts.” Yes, it’s Yet Another iPhone Notes App.
samples.human_continuation: But it’s one that’s meticulously and tastefully designed—not surprising, coming from the principals of Q Branch. I’ve spent the past few weeks beta-testing the app, and in advance of the release I also talked to Gruber, Simmons, and Wiskus (all of whom have written for Macworld in the past) about what went into building it. A notebook in your iPhone There’s no shortage of notebook and reminder apps on iOS. I’ve used many of them, including Apple’s own Notes, Evernote, and a vast collection of text editors. And yet none of them has stuck for any length of time. The Q Branch group has had the same experience. Vesper's full list view. “I’d been waiting for [a note-taking app] I liked and wanted to use,” Simmons said. “That one just hadn’t appeared.
samples.ai_continuation_chat: But do not let that dismissive label fool you. Vesper is not merely another clone in a crowded field; it is a meticulously crafted tool that understands the nuances of iOS design. The trio recognized a glaring gap in the market: while many apps exist, few prioritize the tactile joy of writing with the same reverence as reading. Vesper fills this void with an interface so intuitive it feels less like software and more like an extension of the mind itself. The creators’ motivation stems from a genuine desire to provide a superior experience, one that respects the user’s time and attention. By focusing on simplicity and elegance, they have produced something rare in the modern app ecosystem. It is a testament to what happens when passion meets precision, proving that even in saturated markets, there is always room for excellence if you care enough about the details.
samples.ai_continuation_free: But Vesper distinguishes itself through a minimalist design philosophy and a focus on capturing fleeting ideas with minimal friction. The trio behind Q Branch has long been vocal about their disdain for cluttered interfaces and overly complex workflows, and Vesper reflects that ethos by stripping away the bells and whistles that typically plague note-taking applications. Instead of offering rich text formatting, attachments, or cloud sync options right out of the gate, the app prioritizes speed and simplicity, allowing users to jot down thoughts as quickly as they occur. This approach aligns with the broader trend in the indie app scene toward tools that respect the user’s attention rather than demanding it. By charging a modest upfront fee, Gruber, Simmons, and Wiskus are also making a statement about sustainable software development, moving away from the free-to-use, ad-supported models that dominate the App Store.

samples.prefix: For the bread, see croutons In Quebec cuisine, cretons (sometimes gorton or corton, especially among New Englanders of French-Canadian origin) is a forcemeat-style pork spread containing onions and spices. Due to its fatty texture and taste, it resembles French rillettes. Cretons are usually served on toast as part of a traditional Quebec breakfast.
samples.human_continuation: It is not to be confused with "fromage de tête" (tête fromagée in Quebec) or head cheese. Recipes [ edit ] Recipes vary, but traditional preparation involves covering 1–3 lbs of ground pork shoulder in milk or water in a large pot, then seasoning with onions and a mix of spices. The blend of spices varies from recipe to recipe, but nearly all include ground cloves. Other spices often used include cinnamon, allspice, ginger, nutmeg, and bay leaf. Some recipes include minced garlic. Basics The mixture is simmered gently over low heat, and stirred often to prevent scorching until all the liquid is cooked off and the mixture is thick. It is then allowed to cool, then stirred again to incorporate all the rendered fat, and transferred to a large, clean container or individual containers, covered tightly, and refrigerated for several hours or overnight until firm.
samples.ai_continuation_chat: The traditional recipe calls for ground pork shoulder combined with finely diced onions, milk, salt, pepper, and ground cloves. The mixture is slowly cooked over low heat, stirring frequently, until the pork becomes tender and the liquid reduces to create a spreadable consistency. Unlike head cheese (tête fromagée), which is made from the actual meat of a pig's head set in aspic, cretons contain no aspic and are not pressed into a loaf form. Head cheese is typically sliced and served cold as a terrine, while cretons remain soft and spreadable. This distinction is important: cretons are essentially a seasoned pork spread rather than the head meat preparation that gives head cheese its name. The slow cooking process breaks down the pork shoulder fibers, creating the characteristic smooth texture that spreads easily on toast.
samples.ai_continuation_free: creton is often compared to other pork-based spreads like pâté or head cheese, though it has a distinctively smoother consistency due to the high proportion of fat used in its preparation. The dish traces its roots to French-Canadian culinary traditions, particularly from the Normandy and Brittany regions of France, where similar pork preparations have been made for centuries. Traditional homemade cretons are prepared by slowly cooking pork shoulder or belly with onions, salt, pepper, and often warm spices such as cinnamon, cloves, or allspice. The mixture is cooked until the meat is tender enough to be easily shredded, then combined with the rendered fat to create a spreadable consistency. Once cooked, it is typically pressed into molds or loaf pans and allowed to cool and set, resulting in a firm yet spreadable product that can be sliced or spread as desired. In Quebec, cretons can be found in most grocery stores, both in the deli section and packaged in cans or rectangular blocks.

samples.prefix: Two of the three investigations into the actions of Salt Lake City Police officers Detective Jeff Payne and Lt. James Tracy following Payne’s arrest of University of Utah Health nurse Alex Wubbels have finished. The first — the police department’s internal affairs investigation — concluded that Tracy violated five departmental policies.
samples.human_continuation: It found that he acted with conduct unbecoming of an officer. Other rules broken include behaving with courtesy in public contacts, a policy favoring misdemeanor citations over arrests ”whenever possible,” the code of ethics and a standards of conduct policy. It also found that Payne violated all five of those same policies, plus an additional policy which required him to report his use of physical force while arresting Wubbels — which he did not do. Of Payne’s actions, the department wrote, “You demonstrated extremely poor professional judgment (especially for an officer with 27 years of experience), which calls into question your ability to effectively serve the public and the Department in a manner that inspires the requisite trust, respect, and confidence.” To both employees, letters said, “disciplinary action, which may include termination of your employment, is being considered in response to actions on your part which appear to be a violation of policy and/or expectations related to the performance of your job duties.” Payne’s lawyer, Greg Skordas, responded to the internal investigation’s results.
samples.ai_continuation_chat:
The findings, released in a detailed report, indicate that Lt. Tracy failed to properly supervise Detective Payne, neglected to de-escalate the situation, and did not intervene when Payne’s conduct escalated beyond protocol. The department also found that Tracy made misleading statements during the subsequent review process. Detective Payne, who physically arrested Wubbels for refusing to draw blood from an unconscious patient without a warrant, was found to have violated six policies, including excessive force and conduct unbecoming an officer.

The internal affairs report highlighted that Payne ignored clear instructions from hospital staff and Wubbels herself, who cited the hospital’s policy requiring a warrant or patient consent. The investigation noted that Payne’s actions were not only contrary to law but also undermined public trust in the department. As a result, both officers face disciplinary action, though specifics remain pending a final review by the police chief.

Greg Skordas, Wubbels’ attorney, commented that the findings validate her courageous stand and underscore the need for systemic reform. He emphasized that the violations were clear and that accountability is long overdue. The second investigation, by the Utah Medical Board, is still ongoing, and a third federal probe into potential civil rights violations continues.

samples.prefix: Researchers at the University of Maryland, College Park have printed transparent transistors on transparent paper. The finished device is flexible, up to 84% transparent, and in theory this could be the first step towards green, paper-based electronics. As we’ve covered before, printing computer circuits isn’t overly difficult — you just need to find the right conductive and semiconductive inks (which can be tricky), and then print them out on a suitable substrate until you have a transistor.
samples.human_continuation: Because these ink-based printed circuits are very thin, though, the smoothness of the substrate is very important. When you’re dealing with layers of ink that are a few nanometers thick, any blemish on the substrate is enough to disrupt the flow of electrons and break the circuit. In the case of regular old paper, bumps and blemishes are usually measured in micrometers — far too irregular to print circuitry on. Not to be deterred, the researchers at the University of Maryland used nanopaper — paper created from wood pulp that’s been specially treated with enzymes and mechanically beaten. Nanopaper has a much more regular structure than normal paper, and is stronger (and transparent) as a result. More importantly, though, nanopaper is smooth to within just a few nanometers. “It’s as flat as plastic,” says Liangbing Hu, one of the researchers who worked on the project.
samples.ai_continuation_chat: However, standard paper presents a significant hurdle due to its inherent surface irregularities. These microscopic peaks and valleys are far too large for nanometer-thick printed circuits, which require an exceptionally smooth foundation to function correctly. If the substrate is too rough, the delicate electronic structures break or fail to form proper connections, rendering the device useless. To overcome this limitation, the team led by Liangbing Hu turned to nanopaper, a material engineered specifically to provide the necessary smoothness while retaining the environmental benefits of cellulose. By processing wood pulp with enzymes, they created a dense, uniform sheet that eliminates the rough texture of conventional paper. This innovative substrate allows the ink-based circuits to adhere properly and operate efficiently, bridging the gap between traditional printing methods and high-performance, flexible electronics.
samples.ai_continuation_free: The breakthrough here lies in the substrate itself. Instead of using traditional silicon wafers or even standard flexible plastics, the team utilized a specially engineered paper that maintains its structural integrity while allowing light to pass through. By layering conductive inks made from silver nanowires and semiconductive materials onto this transparent base, they created a functional thin-film transistor that bends without breaking. This flexibility is crucial for applications where rigid electronics would fail, such as wearable health monitors or interactive packaging. If scaled up, this technology could revolutionize how we think about disposable electronics, offering an eco-friendly alternative to the plastic-heavy devices that currently dominate the market, potentially reducing electronic waste while opening new avenues for augmented reality interfaces that blend seamlessly into our physical environment.

content_constraint.content_direction: It argues that standard paper is too rough for nanometer-scale electronics and details how nanopaper's smoothness and strength make it a viable alternative.
content_constraint.scope: The text covers the technical constraints of substrate smoothness, the composition of nanopaper, and its physical advantages over regular paper, stopping after a quote from researcher Liangbing Hu.

samples.prefix: There is no shortage of things to protest when it comes to this small Middle Eastern country. From the raging war next door, to its repercussions, to the rampant corruption, human rights abuses, the disappearance of elections, rising unemployment, emigration, crippled institutions, and pollution -the grounds are endless.
samples.human_continuation: However, when one looks at Lebanon, protests are virtually non-existent on a large scale at least, not since the 2015 garbage-fueled summer demonstrations -which were an exception to the rule- died out. At every turn of events we witness as those directly impacted take to the streets in small numbers. It is a rarity to see any significant form of consequential solidarity on the advent of crises. Take the kidnapped Lebanese soldiers debacle and the resurfaced waste management disaster for instance. The only protests that occurred related to these issues were those organized by a handful of citizens even though the repercussions of said crises are wide-reaching. In a bid to better understand what has been repeatedly described as a self-induced state of perpetual sleep, I revisited some studies pertaining to cognitive behavior in high stress environments.
samples.ai_continuation_chat:
Yet mass mobilization remains elusive. The last significant wave of demonstrations occurred in the summer of 2015, sparked by a waste management disaster that left garbage piling up in Beirut's streets. That movement, though powerful in its initial burst, eventually dissipated. More recently, the kidnapping of Lebanese soldiers by ISIS-linked militants drew public attention but failed to ignite sustained public anger or demands for systemic change.

Psychologists studying collective action in high-stress environments offer some explanation. Research on cognitive behavior suggests that when people are constantly bombarded with crises, they can develop a form of learned helplessness—a psychological state where individuals believe their actions cannot change their circumstances. In Lebanon, where multiple emergencies coexist simultaneously, the very pervasiveness of problems may paradoxically paralyze the population rather than mobilize it.
samples.ai_continuation_free: Yet somehow, the protests that do erupt tend to be sporadic and short-lived, fizzling out before they can build any real momentum. Part of this fatigue stems from a population that has been ground down by decades of political mismanagement, but there's also a more practical reason: survival has become the primary concern for most Lebanese. The economic collapse has meant that simply putting food on the table and affording basic utilities takes up most people's energy and attention. The middle class has been decimated, with savings wiped out and salaries worth a fraction of their former value. The currency has lost over 90% of its value against the dollar, and the official exchange rate remains artificially maintained at a fraction of what it trades for on the black market. Imports – which Lebanon depends on for nearly everything from food to medicine to fuel – have become prohibitively expensive.

samples.prefix: One of the strangest sentences in American law comes from Justice Lewis F. Powell, Jr. “Under the First Amendment,” he wrote, in 1974, “there is no such thing as a false idea.” That is not a decree that the world brims with truth. He meant that we rely on the marketplace of ideas, rather than on judges and juries, to sort out truth from falsehood—and to continually check our understanding of the truth.
samples.human_continuation: The Justice was restating the central tenet embraced in New York Times v. Sullivan, in 1964, the Supreme Court’s most important decision about freedom of speech and of the press. The Court extended the scope of the First Amendment to libel law and held that, even if a citizen stated or a newspaper published criticism about a public official that was incorrect, that mistake could be punished as libel only if the critic knew or suspected that the criticism was false. In 1967, the Court applied this rule to public figures as well. The premise of the marketplace applies broadly, not just to libel law. The First Amendment protects a lot of harmful speech, including much that is incendiary, offensive, and untrue. That protection covers President Trump, even if he does not believe the torrent of falsehoods he has uttered.
samples.ai_continuation_chat: This principle reached its zenith in the landmark case New York Times v. Sullivan, where the Supreme Court established that public officials must prove actual malice to win libel suits. The ruling recognized that robust debate about public affairs requires breathing space, even if that space occasionally accommodates erroneous statements. Without such protection, critics would self-censor out of fear of costly litigation, chilling the very discourse democracy depends upon. This legal framework extends to all public figures, including President Trump, who, by virtue of his prominence and influence, must endure harsher criticism and factual inaccuracies than private citizens. The Court’s logic remains consistent: the remedy for false speech is not censorship, but more speech, allowing the marketplace of ideas to ultimately correct the record through open and uninhibited discussion.
samples.ai_continuation_free: This principle underscores a profound skepticism toward government authority to determine what is true or false in matters of public discourse. Powell recognized that truth is not a static commodity to be discovered and declared by an elite few, but a dynamic process that emerges from the clash of opposing viewpoints. By protecting even erroneous ideas, the law ensures that the community retains the agency to challenge, debate, and ultimately refine its collective understanding. If the state were permitted to suppress falsehoods, it would inevitably gain the power to define truth itself, a danger that the First Amendment was designed to prevent. Thus, the protection of false ideas is not an endorsement of error, but a safeguard for the liberty necessary to find the truth.

content_constraint.content_direction: It traces the evolution of libel standards from public officials to public figures and argues that the First Amendment broadly protects harmful and untrue speech.

Hodges was celebrated loudly as a victory for supporters of gay “marriage” Friday, and yet, the way the case was decided, using a new interpretation of the 14th Amendment’s due process clause, may have opened the floodgates for gun rights reform. I argued Friday morning that the Obergefell decision validated concealed carry reciprocity nationwide.
samples.human_continuation: By using the Constitution in such a manner, the Court argues that the Due Process Clause extends “certain personal choices central to individual dignity and autonomy” accepted in a majority of states across the state lines of a handful of states that still banned the practice. The vast majority of states are “shall issue” on the matter of issuing concealed carry permits, and enjoy reciprocity with a large number of other states. My North Carolina concealed carry permit, for example, was recognized yesterday as being valid in 36 states, which just so happened to be the number of states in which gay marriage was legal yesterday. But 14 states did not recognize my concealed carry permit yesterday. Today they must. Using the same “due process clause” argument as the Supreme Court just applied to gay marriage, my concealed carry permit must now be recognized as valid in all 50 states and the District of Columbia.
samples.ai_continuation_chat: The Court’s reasoning established that fundamental rights cannot be arbitrarily denied based on state residency. If the liberty to marry is protected from state-level discrimination, the same Due Process Clause logic must shield the right to keep and bear arms. Currently, a concealed carry permit holder from North Carolina may be barred from carrying in neighboring states, despite having met rigorous training and background check standards. This patchwork of regulations violates the principle that fundamental rights should travel with the citizen. Just as Obergefell invalidated bans on same-sex marriage by recognizing a universal right, it implicitly demands that states recognize out-of-state concealed carry permits. To deny reciprocity is to infringe upon the bearer’s liberty interest without sufficient justification. Therefore, the constitutional mandate for marriage equality logically extends to firearm reciprocity, ensuring that responsible gun owners are not penalized for crossing state lines.
samples.ai_continuation_free: The logic hinges on the concept of fundamental rights. By ruling that the right to marry is fundamental and protected by the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment, the Court established a precedent that states cannot infringe upon deeply rooted personal liberties without a compelling justification. If the right to marry, a social institution, is deemed fundamental, then the right to keep and bear arms for self-defense—a right explicitly enumerated in the Second Amendment and reinforced by the Court’s earlier decision in *Heller*—must also be shielded from arbitrary state-by-state prohibition. This interpretation suggests that if a citizen is legally permitted to carry a concealed weapon in their home state, other states must recognize that right under the Privileges or Immunities Clause or the Due Process Clause, preventing them from treating an out-of-state carrier as a threat simply because they exercise a liberty protected in their jurisdiction of origin.

“We’ve been working hard all winter, and I think we’re starting to see the fruits of that now,” Magnussen said. “The RS16 is a step forward from where we began, but we’re realistic about where we fit. In Barcelona, we were consistently in the midfield pack, which is encouraging, but there’s still a gap to the frontrunners. That’s not a surprise—we knew this would be a rebuilding year. The key is to maximize what we have and keep pushing development.”

He acknowledged that Melbourne will be a true test. “Every circuit is different, and Albert Park has its own challenges. We won’t know exactly how competitive we are until we’re in race conditions. But I feel confident in the team and the direction we’re heading. samples.prefix: CTVNews.ca Staff Four people are recovering in hospital after a frightening fall from a chairlift at a ski resort near Kelowna B.C. Witnesses say they saw the passengers tumble to the ground. “From what I saw, they fell pretty hard,” said Carson Moss. Tyler Mow told CTV Vancouver that the ski lift did not feel right when he was on it. “The chairs felt springy earlier in the day,” Mow said. “We were just commenting that it felt funny and that something was different.” While paramedics rushed to treat the victims, other skiers remained stuck on the lift and had to be evacuated.

The four victims have been identified as Mike Morin, 28, Carson Moss, 24, and Tyler Mow, 31, all from Kelowna, along with a fourth man whose name has not been released. Doctors at Kelowna General Hospital say Morin sustained serious spinal injuries and underwent surgery on Sunday. Moss and Mow are listed in stable condition with multiple fractures, while the fourth victim was treated for head injuries and released.

Investigators believe the accident was caused by a mechanical failure on tower number two, where the chairlift cable allegedly detached from the pulley system. The resort has declined to comment on the specific cause while the investigation continues.

Witnesses described seeing the chair suddenly drop from the cable. "It just snapped and the chair went free-falling," said one skater who was waiting at the bottom of the lift. "There was a loud crack, then screaming. It happened so fast."

"The impact was significant," said Sergeant Darren Popowich of the Kelowna RCMP. "We're extremely fortunate that no one sustained life-threatening injuries."

Crystal Mountain Ski Resort officials confirmed that the chairlift has been closed pending a full investigation by technical safety inspectors. The resort expressed relief that the injuries were not more severe and said they are cooperating fully with authorities.

"We've initiated our own internal review of the incident and will be working closely with provincial safety regulators," said resort general manager Jennifer Thompson in a written statement. "The safety of our guests is always our top priority."

Witnesses at the scene described seeing the chair fall before hearing a loud thud. Several skiers rushed to assist the victims while awaiting emergency crews.

The four victims, whose names have not been released, ranged in age from their teens to their 40s. Hospital officials said one patient was discharged Sunday morning, while the other three remained under observation with non-life-threatening injuries including fractures and contusions.

If you want to be friendly and approachable you probably wouldn’t pose like this.” Like an excited little kid that gets his mom to display his latest finger painting up on the fridge, the Globe then shared the article of the controversy of Melania’s White House portrait on Twitter, zeroing in on her pose of all things and asking, “So what’s with the crossed arms?” The White House released an official portrait of Melania Trump. The crossed arms, they said, signaled a barrier, while the direct but cool stare suggested impatience rather than invitation. Even the lighting was scrutinized: harsh shadows on her face, they claimed, emphasized a severity that felt more editorial than presidential. Defenders countered that Melania was simply embracing her own aesthetic—modern, disciplined, and unapologetically glamorous. But the Globe’s dissection reflected a broader unease: in an era craving connection, her portrait chose distance. samples.ai_continuation_free: But maybe that’s exactly the point. Melania has never played the part of the warm, grinning first lady in the traditional sense, and her portrait reflects that. She’s not Jackie Kennedy, and she’s not Laura Bush. She’s a former model who married a billionaire and became first lady on her own terms. The diamond ring, the sharp suit, the unsmiling expression—it all says, “I’m here, I’m doing this, but I’m not performing for you.” The Globe’s critique feels almost predictable, like they were waiting for a reason to call her cold or out of touch. But maybe a first lady doesn’t have to be relatable in the way we expect. Maybe she can just be herself, even if that self is polished and distant. The portrait is striking, not warm. samples.prefix: The notion of continuations as first-class values has been a tricky subject for me to understand to a comfortable level of certainty. I think this is probably true for many PLT-laymen like myself. This article represents my attempt at collecting and presenting my thoughts in a coherant manner! I'd be happy to receive corrections and comments.
samples.human_continuation: I will start by defining a few key terms in my own style. Continuation We can observe that every expression, regardless of complexity, has the ultimate goal of returning a value to some surrounding execution context. That context is known as a continuation - it represents everything that is left to compute. Therefore, every computation has an associated continuation, which specifies the place from which execution should continue once control has been returned. As a simple example, consider the following Scheme form: ( lambda ( n ) ( + n 1 )) The continuation associated with the sub-expression "1" is an anonymous function, whose body consists of a call to the + primitive procedure whose first argument is the local variable n and whose second argument is being sought. With this understanding we can say expressions deliver values and continuations receive values.
samples.ai_continuation_chat:
To begin, let’s ground ourselves in a concrete example: the Scheme programming language, where continuations are exposed as first-class objects via the `call/cc` primitive. Imagine a simple expression like `(+ 1 (* 2 3))`. When the interpreter evaluates this, it builds an implicit continuation for each sub-expression. For `(* 2 3)`, the continuation is something like “take this result, add 1, and return the final value.” Normally, that continuation is invisible—it’s just part of the execution context.

But with `call/cc`, we can capture that continuation as a procedure. If we write `(+ 1 (call/cc (lambda (k) ...)))`, the variable `k` becomes a function that, when called with a value, will jump back to the point where the continuation was captured, replacing the entire `call/cc` expression with that value. This is powerful: it lets us implement non-local control flow, like exceptions, generators, or even cooperative multitasking, by treating the execution context as a manipulable object.
samples.ai_continuation_free: The journey to understanding continuations often begins with a simple question: what happens after a function returns? Normally, we take this for granted. The function computes a value, and control returns to the caller, which continues with its own work. But what if we could capture that "rest of the computation" — the entire future of the program at a given point — as a value? That value is a continuation. In most programming languages, this future is implicit and inaccessible. In a language with first-class continuations, you can grab it, store it in a variable, pass it around, and even invoke it later. When you invoke a continuation, you're essentially saying: "forget the current state of the program, and jump back to the point where I captured this continuation, replacing whatever was being computed there with this new value." It's like a time-travel mechanism for control flow.

content_constraint.content_direction: Defines continuation as the remaining computation context and illustrates with a Scheme lambda example.

samples.prefix: This week, like much of July, a heat wave is cooking America with extreme temperatures, affecting energy production as well as causing fires and water shortages, sucking electricity like crazy to power the cooling necessary to avoid discomfort and even death. According to the National Weather Service, 122 million Americans are under heat alerts.
samples.human_continuation: Fortunately, nuclear power hasn’t minded, scoring record capacity factors of 96% and up with no increase in price. Other energy sources do not fare so well. It’s all about diversity. Whether in biology, in culture, in training, or in technology, when conditions change a system survives if there is sufficient diversity to adapt. Otherwise it dies. This is no less true for electricity production. Having a diverse group of energy systems is key to a society surviving changes in demographics and changes in government, geological processes and natural disasters, disruption in supplies from war, or extreme weather changes. This concept is in full display this month as this heat wave continues to sweep across America. Just like during the polar vortex, when nuclear stepped up to relieve natural gas and coal when they failed to deliver on the demand, nuclear also performs wonderfully during extreme weather at the other end of the thermometer.
samples.ai_continuation_chat: Amidst this sweltering crisis, nuclear power plants have emerged as a critical pillar of stability, operating at full capacity while other sources falter. Unlike natural gas facilities, which often struggle with reduced efficiency in high temperatures or face supply constraints, and coal plants, which are increasingly retired or limited by environmental regulations, nuclear energy provides a consistent, baseload supply regardless of the weather. This stark contrast highlights a fundamental truth: relying on a single energy source is a dangerous gamble in an era of intensifying climate extremes. A diverse energy mix is not merely an economic preference but a societal necessity for resilience. By integrating nuclear power with renewables and other reliable sources, we can safeguard the grid against the unpredictable demands of future heat waves. Ensuring that our electricity infrastructure can withstand such stress tests is vital for public safety and economic continuity, proving that diversity in energy production is the key to surviving our changing climate.

samples.prefix: Microsoft’s policy, which it calls its Services Agreement, allows it to analyze customer content from one its free products and use it to improve another service — for example, taking information from messages a consumer sends on Windows Live Messenger and using it to improve messaging services on Xbox. Previously, that kind of sharing of information between products would not have been allowed under Microsoft policies, which limited the use of data collected under one of its products to that product alone.
samples.human_continuation: Microsoft has promised, however, that it will not use the personal information and content it collects to sell targeted advertising. It will not, for example, scan a consumer’s e-mails to generate ads that might interest the user. Google does that, and expanding its ability to draw on that content was part of the reason Google changed its privacy policy this year. But the new Microsoft policy does allow for such targeted advertising. Microsoft promised not to do so in blog posts and e-mails informing its customers about the change, but not in the formal policy. That has some privacy advocates nervous. “What Microsoft is doing is no different from what Google did,” said John M. Simpson, who monitors privacy policy for Consumer Watchdog, a California nonprofit group. “It allows the combination of data across services in ways a user wouldn’t reasonably expect.
samples.ai_continuation_chat:
Privacy advocates have criticized the change, saying it marks a significant shift in how Microsoft handles user data and could open the door to more aggressive targeted advertising.

"This is a fundamental change in how Microsoft treats customer information," said John M. Simpson, director of the nonprofit Consumer Watchdog's Privacy Project. "They're essentially creating a massive database of user behavior across multiple platforms that can be mined for advertising purposes."

Simpson argued that while Microsoft presents the policy as a way to improve services, the real motivation is financial. "The whole point is to build more detailed profiles of users so they can charge more for targeted ads," he said. "Consumers need to understand that when they use these free Microsoft products, the company is harvesting their data to make money."

Microsoft maintains that the policy is designed to enhance user experience and that it provides robust privacy controls allowing users to opt out of certain data sharing features.
samples.ai_continuation_free: This represents a significant shift in how Microsoft approaches user data, reflecting a broader industry trend toward integrating data across services to enhance machine learning and user experience. The change means that information collected through any Microsoft product you use—whether it's Outlook, Skype, OneDrive, or gaming services—can now be pooled and analyzed collectively to improve features across their entire ecosystem. Privacy advocates have expressed concern about this approach, arguing that users may not fully understand how their data is being aggregated and repurposed. When you send a message on one platform, that content could potentially inform recommendations or functionality on an entirely different product you use. Microsoft has stated that this data analysis is automated and helps them improve services like spam filtering, search results, and voice recognition. The company maintains that it applies privacy safeguards and that certain sensitive information remains protected.

samples.prefix: "Cinder block" redirects here. For the American singer, see Cinder Block (musician) "Breezeblocks" redirects here. For the song by Alt+J, see Breezeblocks (song) An interior wall of painted CMUs A concrete masonry unit (CMU) is a standard size rectangular block used in building construction. CMUs are some of the most versatile building products available because of the wide variety of appearances that can be achieved using concrete masonry units.[1] Those that use cinders (fly ash or bottom ash) are called cinder blocks in the United States, breeze blocks (breeze is a synonym of ash)[2] in the United Kingdom, and hollow blocks in the Philippines.
samples.human_continuation: In New Zealand and Canada they are known as concrete blocks (a name common in the United States also). In New Zealand, they are also called construction blocks. In Australia they are also called Besser blocks and Besser bricks, because the Besser Company was a major supplier of machines that made concrete blocks. Clinker blocks use clinker as aggregate. In non-technical usage, the terms cinder block and breeze block are often generalized to cover all of these varieties. Composition [ edit ] Concrete blocks are made from cast concrete (e.g. Portland cement and aggregate, usually sand and fine gravel, for high-density blocks). Lower density blocks may use industrial wastes, such as fly ash or bottom ash,[3][4] as an aggregate.[5] Recycled materials, such as post-consumer glass, slag cement, or recycled aggregate, are often used in the composition of the blocks.[6] Use of recycled materials within blocks can create different appearances in the block, such as a terrazzo finish, and may help the finished structure earn LEED certification.
samples.ai_continuation_chat:
In New Zealand, they are commonly known as Besser blocks, named after the Besser Company that pioneered their manufacturing there. Canadian terminology varies by region, though "concrete block" and "cinder block" remain prevalent, while "breeze block" is less common than in other Commonwealth countries. Australian builders typically refer to them as "concrete masonry units" or simply "blocks," with the Besser block name also persisting in common usage.

The composition of CMUs typically includes Portland cement combined with various aggregates such as sand, gravel, or crushed stone. Modern manufacturing increasingly incorporates recycled materials including fly ash (a byproduct of coal combustion), bottom ash, and recycled concrete aggregate. These recycled content formulations can contribute to LEED certification points in sustainable building projects, as they reduce the environmental impact associated with virgin material extraction and disposal of industrial waste products.
samples.ai_continuation_free: , also commonly referred to in the United States and Canada as concrete block, or foundation block, though the latter term is more appropriately reserved for larger load-bearing units used in below-grade applications such as foundations and retaining walls. The standard dimensions of a CMU are nominally 8 inches (203 mm) by 8 inches (203 mm) by 16 inches (406 mm), though actual dimensions are slightly smaller to accommodate the mortar joints typically used in construction. This nominal sizing allows for the standard 3/8 inch (9.5 mm) mortar joint, resulting in finished dimensions that are easily calculated for planning purposes. CMUs are produced in various thicknesses, ranging from 4 to 12 inches (102 to 305 mm), with the most common being 8-inch units for exterior walls and 4-inch units for interior partitions. The composition of concrete masonry units typically includes Portland cement, aggregates such as sand, gravel, or stone, and water. Modern CMUs may also incorporate recycled materials including ground granulated blast furnace slag, fly ash, and recycled aggregate to improve sustainability and reduce environmental impact.

samples.prefix: Google has released the final preview of Android Oreo 8.1, an update to its Linux-based mobile platform which will activate the Pixel Visual Core co-processor built into the company's Pixel 2 smartphones for the first time. Unveiled back in October, the Pixel Visual Core marks the first time a Google-designed co-processor has found its way into one of the company's consumer products.
samples.human_continuation: An eight-core Image Processing Unit (IPU) connected to an ARM Cortex-A53 general-purpose processor and PCI Express and Mobile Industry Processor Interface (MIPI) links, the Visual Core has been present but deactivated in every single Pixel 2 smartphone the company has sold. In Android Oreo 8.1, though, the chip will be activated for the first time. Announced as part of the final developer preview release ahead of public availability, the software update will activate the Pixel Visual Core - though only through a 'new developer option' rather than as an on-by-default feature. 'Using Pixel Visual Core, HDR+ [High Dynamic Range Plus photographic processing] can run 5x faster and at less than one-tenth the energy than running on the application processor,' explained Google's Ofer Shacham and Masumi Reynders in the original technology announcement.
samples.ai_continuation_chat: The Pixel Visual Core is a dedicated Image Processing Unit (IPU) built around eight ARM Cortex-A53 cores, designed specifically to accelerate computational photography tasks. When Android Oreo 8.1 arrives, the co-processor will handle HDR+ processing, offloading the heavy lifting from the main Snapdragon 835 processor. This means significantly faster image processing, reduced battery drain, and the ability to run HDR+ on third-party camera apps for the first time. Google claims the IPU can process images at up to 5x the speed of the main processor while using one-tenth the power. For Pixel 2 users, this translates to near-instant HDR+ shots, improved low-light performance, and seamless integration with apps like Instagram and Snapchat. The update positions the Pixel 2 as a photography powerhouse, leveraging custom silicon to deliver Google's acclaimed computational photography capabilities with unprecedented efficiency.
samples.ai_continuation_free: The chip is specifically designed to accelerate the HDR+ processing that makes the Pixel 2’s camera so highly regarded, handling complex computational photography tasks more efficiently than the main processor. Until now, the Pixel Visual Core has remained dormant, with Google relying on the Qualcomm Snapdragon 835’s built-in image signal processor for all camera functions. With Android 8.1, third-party camera apps will finally be able to tap into the co-processor’s power, enabling them to capture and process HDR+ images with the same speed and quality as the native Google Camera app. This means apps like Instagram, Snapchat, and WhatsApp will soon be able to leverage Google’s advanced image processing algorithms, dramatically improving photo quality in those platforms. The update also brings other refinements, including a new Neural Networks API designed to accelerate on-device machine learning, as well as a variety of bug fixes and performance optimizations.

content_constraint.topic: Activation of the Pixel Visual Core co-processor in Android Oreo 8.1 for Pixel 2 smartphones.
content_constraint.content_direction: Describes the hardware specs of the Pixel Visual Core, its activation via a developer option in the update, and the performance benefits for HDR+ processing.

samples.prefix: In a bid to keep the city streets cleaner, the Maharashtra government on Tuesday approved an anti-spitting law. Deepak Sawant, state Public Health Minister told The Indian Express,"We had to bring in a punishment that would shame the offenders and hurt their ego. Simply paying a penalty is not enough deterrent. Offenders pay the paltry amount, and often don’t think twice before repeating the act. So, we decided to bring in compulsory community service." Beyond the financial burden, repeat violators face stricter community service mandates, including mandatory cleaning of public spaces such as parks, bus stops, and municipal buildings. According to reports from The Indian Express, this stringent approach is designed not just to punish, but to instill a sense of civic responsibility among citizens. This comprehensive strategy reflects Maharashtra’s broader commitment to public health and hygiene, seeking to transform public behavior through strict enforcement and visible consequences.

samples.prefix: There aren’t many places in Seattle that haven’t changed at all in my lifetime. But walking into Tai Tung restaurant in the Chinatown-International District is like stepping out of a time machine. There’s the wood paneling, mauve upholstery and thick laminate menu I remember from special dinners out with my family as a child.
samples.human_continuation: But the restaurant’s history runs much deeper than that. “The door that you just walked through, that swinging door? That door is 80 some years old,” says Siang Hui Tay, who adds that the restaurant opened in 1935 and is the oldest remaining Chinese restaurant in neighborhood . Tay would know. Inspired by the history of Tai Tung, she and her partner Val Tan have co-produced “A Taste Of Home,” a documentary showcasing local Chinese-American culinary history, which will play opening night of the Seattle Asian American Film Festival next week. But it wasn’t the restaurant’s door, historic lunch counter or Bruce Lee’s favorite table (he was a regular) that first attracted the filmmaking duo, who work under the brand “Tay & Val.” It was the food — specifically Chinese comfort food from their home country of Singapore.
samples.ai_continuation_chat:
The food, too, remains largely unchanged—still serving the same dishes that have fed generations of Seattle families. What I didn't fully appreciate as a child was the history behind those dishes, or the man who started it all.

Siang Hui Tay opened Tai Tung in 1935, making it the oldest Chinese restaurant in Seattle. For decades, it was one of the few places in the city where Chinese-American families could gather and enjoy food from their homeland. The restaurant's significance eventually caught the attention of filmmakers, inspiring the documentary "A Taste of Home," which premiered at the Seattle Asian American Film Festival.

Now owned by Val Tan, who took over in 2001, Tai Tung continues to serve as a living monument to Chinese-American culinary heritage—a place where the past and present coexist on the same plate.
samples.ai_continuation_free: The menu, laminated and slightly sticky in that particular way menus get after decades of handling, still lists the same dishes I probably first tried when I was eight or nine. Sweet and sour pork. Salt and pepper squid. The clay pot preparations that arrive at the table still steaming and bubbling, the sauce splattering onto the tablecloth in a way that always made my mother tut but never quite enough to stop her from ordering them anyway. What strikes me now, as an adult who has eaten in restaurants around the world, is how unapologetically local this place has always been. There was never any attempt to make the food more accessible or to modernize the aesthetics for tourists passing through. Tai Tung simply remained itself, a constant in a neighborhood that has seen waves of different immigrant communities reshape its streets and storefronts.

samples.prefix: SpaceX announced an audacious plan on Wednesday to land an approximately 6,000kg spacecraft on the surface of Mars. This simple declaration from the uber-popular rocket company drew a ton of questions from all quarters, and Ars spoke to a range of people across the space industry to get some answers. How big a milestone would this be?
samples.human_continuation: Can SpaceX do it? Is the plan realistic? And why does Rice play Texas, anyway? (OK, we didn't actually try to figure out that last one.) Is this really a big deal? Oh, heavens, yes. No private company has ever launched a significant, independently financed expedition into deep space, let alone all the way to Mars. In fact, only two world powers have ever softly landed spacecraft on Mars. The United States has done so half a dozen times, and the Soviet Union did it once with Mars 3 in 1971—although the vehicle failed after sending back just 15 seconds of data. And all previous soft landings have been relatively small and light; SpaceX is talking about landing a Dragon weighing about 6,000kg on the surface of Mars. The previous landing heavyweight was Curiosity, at 900kg. Soft-landing a 6,000kg object on Mars would be a stunning achievement for NASA or any government-backed space agency.
samples.ai_continuation_chat:
The sheer magnitude of this endeavor is almost difficult to comprehend when placed in historical context. No nation, not even the United States or the Soviet Union during the height of the Cold War space race, has ever attempted to land a payload of this size on another planet. The heaviest object ever successfully delivered to the Martian surface is NASA’s Curiosity rover, which tipped the scales at a mere 900 kilograms. SpaceX’s proposed lander is nearly seven times heavier, representing a leap in capability that defies conventional engineering wisdom.

This discrepancy highlights the unprecedented difficulty of the mission. Landing on Mars requires navigating a thin atmosphere and enduring extreme forces, a process known as "the seven minutes of terror." Scaling this up by a factor of seven means that every component, from heat shields to retro-rockets, must be massively over-engineered. Critics argue that the physics simply do not support such a heavy landing without catastrophic failure. Yet, SpaceX remains undeterred, suggesting that their innovative approach to propulsion and structural design could rewrite the rules of interplanetary travel, challenging decades of established aerospace limitations.
samples.ai_continuation_free: It would be historic, certainly, but the specifics matter immensely. If SpaceX intends to land a fully fueled Starship on Mars, it represents a quantum leap in capability, effectively solving the hardest part of the interplanetary logistics puzzle: refueling in orbit and executing a powered descent with a vehicle of that mass. No one has ever landed anything nearly that heavy on another planet; the Curiosity rover weighed just over a ton, and Perseverance came in at around 1,000 kg. Landing 6,000 kg implies not just a probe, but a substantial cargo hauler or even a crewed vessel, signaling a shift from scientific exploration to industrial utilization. However, many experts caution against reading too much into a single announcement. The engineering challenges are staggering. The Martian atmosphere is thin—about 1% of Earth’s density—which makes aerobraking difficult, yet thick enough to cause significant heating during entry. A vehicle of this size would need unprecedented heat shielding and a reliable supersonic retropropulsion system to slow down without tearing itself apart or running out of fuel.

samples.prefix: There is an old saying that if something sounds too good to be true, it probably is. I really like this saying because it is a basic principle of skepticism, and it goes hand in hand with a statement that was made famous by none other than Carl Sagan. Namely, “extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence.” I find that these two principles are broadly applicable to the many “miracle treatments” and fad diets that pervade the internet, but in this post I am just going to focus on the “Miracle Mineral Solution” (a.k.a.
samples.human_continuation: Miracle Mineral Supplement or MMS) as an illustration. Basically, this post is just an exercise in common sense in which I am going to point out some obvious hallmarks of snake oil. What is MMS? To put it simply, it’s bleach. To put it more technically, it is a 28% solution of sodium chlorate which breaks down to release chlorine dioxide, and it is the chlorine dioxide which actually reacts with pathogens (remember this chemical, it is going to show up a lot in this post). To be clear, MMS is not the same type of bleach that is used to clean your house (sodium hypochlorite), but it is nevertheless a type of bleach and is used to bleach various paper, wood, and textile products. This is also one of the chlorines that is sometimes used in very low concentrations to disinfect drinking water. Now, the fact that someone is selling a concentrated bleach solution as a miracle cure should throw up some red flags, but let’s investigate further.
samples.ai_continuation_chat: MMS, also sometimes called "Miracle Mineral Supplement"). The product that is sold as MMS is essentially a concentrated solution of sodium chlorite, which is a chemical compound that is closely related to household bleach (sodium hypochlorite). When sodium chlorite is mixed with an acid—commonly citric acid—it undergoes a chemical reaction that releases chlorine dioxide gas. Chlorine dioxide is a powerful oxidizing agent and is used industrially as a bleaching agent and disinfectant. It is important to distinguish between sodium chlorite and sodium hypochlorite, as they are different compounds with different chemical properties, though both can be dangerous if mishandled. The solution sold as MMS typically contains around 28% sodium chlorite, which is significantly more concentrated than the bleach found in most households. This high concentration is what makes the product potentially hazardous when ingested, as the resulting chlorine dioxide can cause severe irritation to the gastrointestinal tract and other tissues.
samples.ai_continuation_free: /no_think - which is the name some internet activists use to mock the product - is one of the most glaring examples of exactly this kind of too-good-to-be-true claims. For those who aren't familiar, Miracle Mineral Solution is essentially a 28% sodium chlorite solution, which is technically a industrial-grade bleaching agent. When diluted as directed (which itself varies wildly among promoters), it becomes chlorine dioxide - a powerful disinfectant. And yet, despite containing what is essentially bleach, MMS has been peddled as a cure for everything from malaria to cancer to autism. The claims surrounding MMS are extraordinary by any measure. We're not talking about a supplement that might provide some marginal health benefit. We're talking about a substance that promoters have claimed can cure HIV, cancer, hepatitis, and more recently, autism spectrum disorders. These are extraordinary claims, and as Sagan's principle dictates, they would require extraordinary evidence to be taken seriously. What exists instead is a mountain of anecdotal testimonials, conspiracy theories about suppression by "Big Pharma" and mainstream medicine, and a disturbing amount of misinformation spread through social media and various online communities.

samples.prefix: Socialism: Whether it was an accident or sabotage, the deadly explosion at Mexico's state-owned oil firm wasn't an unusual event. The one thing Thursday's incident at the Pemex tower should be is a spur to privatize. Despite a much-publicized war against cartels, the real Mexico story is one of moderately good economic growth with zero net illegal emigration and a public sector financed by a budget showing a $1 billion annual surplus.
samples.human_continuation: But then there's Pemex, the supposed symbol of national sovereignty, which in reality is nothing but a millstone around Mexico's neck holding the country back from far greater gains. Pemex's many costs and debts are among the reasons why that $1 billion annual surplus is not $6 billion. It's also a big reason Mexico has $59 billion in debt. Its unionized 150,000-strong workforce is one of the least efficient, yielding an average of $506,000 of revenue per employee per year, far below the $2.865 million each employee at the top five international oil companies brings in, according to a Baker Institute study. Less revenue, less investment, less safety. Oilmen will tell you every incident is different, and some accidents do occur at private firms of course. But the overall Pemex record speaks volumes, with comparable events at its installations in 2012, 2010, 2007, 1993 and 1984.
samples.ai_continuation_chat: Yet this fragile stability is constantly undermined by the bloated inefficiencies of Pemex. The state-owned giant’s mounting debt burden acts as an anchor on Mexico’s broader economic potential, draining resources that could otherwise fuel infrastructure and innovation. Critics from the Baker Institute argue that clinging to national sovereignty in this sector has become a costly illusion, prioritizing political symbolism over operational competence. The unionized workforce, protected by entrenched interests, resists necessary modernization, leading to frequent safety failures like the recent tower explosion. Meanwhile, international oil companies, possessing the capital and technology to drill deeper and safer, are kept at arm’s length by restrictive regulations. This isolationist approach not only jeopardizes worker safety but also stifles the very growth Mexico desperately needs. Without opening the sector to global competition and professional management, Pemex will continue to bleed money and lives, proving that ideological purity is no match for the harsh realities of energy production and economic survival.
samples.ai_continuation_free: Yet this fragile stability rests on a foundation of crumbling infrastructure and institutional decay that private capital is increasingly unwilling to risk. Pemex, once the pride of the Mexican state, has become a cautionary tale of political interference and mismanagement, where engineering standards are often sacrificed for patronage. The explosion at the tower is merely the latest symptom of a deeper malaise: a public sector that consumes resources without delivering efficiency, leaving the country vulnerable to shocks it cannot afford. While the budget surplus offers a temporary reprieve, it masks the mounting liabilities and the urgent need for modernization that only competitive markets can provide. To cling to state ownership in the name of sovereignty is to ignore the reality that sovereignty requires strength, and strength requires a robust, efficient economy—not a bloated, inefficient monopoly prone to catastrophic failure.
