samples.prefix: Coding ● May 2016 The unintended byproducts of refactoring code Whenever I start on a large refactoring, I need to justify that the exercise is truly worthwhile. Am I objectively and unequivocally improving the understandability of the codebase? If I’ve finished and the codebase is no more readable or maintainable than it was when I began, I’d argue there were better ways to have used my time.
samples.human_continuation: While the goal might seem obvious, executing on it is often trickier than you’d think. The two goals of any refactoring Every refactoring has two goals. The immediate goal is technical. I have something in my code that doesn’t feel quite right. Perhaps it’s a leaky abstraction, a convoluted dependency, repeated code, or a poorly encapsulated concept that festers throughout the entire application. I then start laying out the roadmap to get from the code-at-present-moment to the glorious vision of my future code. With the completion of each small step, I re-run my automated tests, commit, then move on. After enough iterations, my plan slowly begins aligning like the pieces on a Tetris board. Eventually, I get to that one final, satisfying refactoring step—the long piece, if you will. Ahhh….the long-awaited completion of a refactoring It is at this point where the abscess has been removed and whatever smelled in my codebase no longer smells.
samples.ai_continuation_chat: To guard against wasted effort, I keep two goals in mind: immediate technical improvement and broader codebase health. The first goal is about the specific problem at hand—perhaps a leaky abstraction that forces every new feature to work around it, or a convoluted dependency that makes testing a nightmare. Fixing that directly improves the code I’m touching today. But the second goal is where the real value accumulates. Every time I extract a repeated code snippet into a shared utility or encapsulate a poorly encapsulated concept, I’m not just cleaning up the present; I’m preventing future entropy. This is why automated tests are non-negotiable. They let me refactor aggressively, knowing that if I break something, I’ll catch it immediately. Without tests, the risk of introducing subtle bugs outweighs the benefit of cleanup. So I measure success not just by whether the code is cleaner now, but by whether the next developer—or my future self—will find it easier to reason about and change.
samples.ai_continuation_free: Refactoring is often sold as a purely technical improvement—cleaner abstractions, fewer dependencies, more testable units. But there are unintended byproducts that rarely appear in the pull request description. The first is the erosion of implicit knowledge. When you extract a method or rename a variable, you may remove the very clues that helped a veteran developer navigate the system. What was once a sprawling but familiar function becomes a chain of tiny, perfectly named helpers—each one obvious in isolation, but collectively harder to trace for the person who knew the old shape by heart. Another byproduct is the introduction of new bugs. Not from logic errors, but from subtle behavioral changes. You might replace a mutable state with an immutable one and break a side effect that was never documented. Or you might flatten a nested conditional into a guard clause, only to discover that the original nesting was compensating for a race condition. The refactoring is correct by the tests, but the tests were written against the old behavior, so they pass.

content_constraint.topic: The two goals of refactoring: immediate technical improvement and broader codebase health.
content_constraint.content_direction: Explains that every refactoring has an immediate technical goal (fixing a code smell) and a process of incremental steps leading to completion.
content_constraint.scope: Covers the motivation and step-by-step execution of a refactoring, ending with the satisfaction of resolving the code smell.

samples.prefix: The last week brought about some cooler temperatures to South Florida and believe me that is quite a relief! This delightfully cool weather inspired me to make one of my favorite Cuban potajes (stew) ... Potaje de Garbanzo. I think of a potaje (poe-tah-hey) as not quite a soup, not quite a stew and not quite a porridge. It's a hearty chickpeas (garbanzo), simmered with Spanish chorizo, ham, smoked pork shank, Cuban calabaza and potatoes.
samples.human_continuation: The taste takes me back to the days of sitting in my mom's kitchen, talking and watching her prepare this divine "potaje". It's funny how so many of the memories of my mom, that mean so much to me and that I hold dear, took place in her kitchen. A little choked up and a big sigh inserted here! Anyway, back to the "potaje". To me, the perfect spoonful has a piece of chorizo, calabaza, and chickpea swimming in the smokey, paprika infused tomato-y broth. Add your favorite bread to dunk in the savory broth or white rice and your meal has just graduated to a traditional Cuban meal. This is nothing short of absolutely, positively delicious! I am pretty certain that my favorite Potaje de Garbanzo may become one your favorites too!1 tablespoon olive oil1 large vidalia onion, chopped3-4 garlic cloves, chopped1 large bell pepper chopped4 small dried and cured Spanish chorizo* links, sliced on the diagonal1 tablespoon sweet, smoked Spanish paprika1 tablespoon granulated garlic powder1 laurel bay leaf1 8 oz can tomato sauce4 cups chicken stock1 1/2 dry white wine1 pounds of garbanzo beans1 1/2 pounds of smoked pork shank8 oz ham steak cubed1/2 Cuban calabaza squash (or butternut squash), peeled and diced into large pieces1 - 2 large red potatoes, peeled, diced1/2 teaspoon salt Soak the beans 24 hours ahead of cooking time, change water whenever possible.
samples.ai_continuation_chat:
The aroma alone is enough to transport me back to my childhood kitchen, where my mom would spend hours tending to a large, blackened pot on the stove. She had a magical way of transforming humble ingredients into a meal that felt like a warm hug. The deep, smoky scent of the chorizo mingling with the earthy sweetness of the garbanzo beans created an atmosphere of pure comfort that I have never quite replicated, yet I strive for with every batch. It was more than just dinner; it was a ritual of love and patience, a testament to the resilience and richness of our heritage.

To capture that essence, you will need to gather your ingredients carefully. Start with two cups of dried garbanzo beans, soaked overnight in plenty of water to ensure they soften properly. You’ll need one pound of high-quality Spanish chorizo, sliced into thin rounds to release its vibrant paprika flavor. Include a smoked pork shank for that essential depth of umami, along with two cups of peeled and cubed Cuban calabaza, which adds a subtle, sweet creaminess distinct from regular pumpkin. Don’t forget four medium potatoes, cut into chunks, and a handful of fresh cilantro for garnish. Begin by draining and rinsing the soaked beans, then place them in a large Dutch oven with cold water. Add the smoked pork shank and bring to a gentle boil, skimming off any foam that rises to the surface. This initial step is crucial for developing the rich, foundational broth that will carry the flavors of the chorizo and squash as they slowly meld together over the next few hours.
samples.ai_continuation_free:
The key to a truly authentic Potaje de Garbanzo lies in the preparation of the beans themselves. You want to soak them overnight to ensure they cook evenly and develop that creamy, melt-in-your-mouth texture. While the beans are soaking, you can prep the rest of the ingredients. Dice the Spanish chorizo and the ham into small, bite-sized pieces, and cut the smoked pork shank into chunks. The calabaza, a type of winter squash native to Cuba, should be peeled and cubed, along with the potatoes.

In a large pot, sauté the chorizo, ham, and pork shank until they release their oils and start to brown. This step is crucial as it builds the rich, smoky flavor base for the stew. Add in some chopped onions, garlic, and perhaps a pinch of cumin and oregano, letting them cook until fragrant. Then, add the soaked and drained chickpeas, along with enough water or broth to cover them by a few inches. Bring it to a boil, then reduce the heat to a simmer.

Let the beans cook for about an hour, or until they are tender but still hold their shape. At this point, stir in the calabaza and potatoes. Continue to simmer until the vegetables are soft and the broth has thickened into that characteristic porridge-like consistency. The final touch is a splash of fresh lime juice and a handful of chopped cilantro or parsley just before serving. The result is a comforting, savory dish that warms you from the inside out, perfectly capturing the essence of Cuban home cooking. It’s the kind of meal that brings people together, especially when the weather outside turns brisk.

samples.prefix: Image caption New rules should make it cheaper to book cinema tickets Consumers booking a range of items from cinema tickets to hotel rooms now have new protection from card surcharges. A ban on "excessive" debit and credit card charges begins on Saturday 6 April. The government said it should put an end to unscrupulous practices by some businesses.
samples.human_continuation: Until now, many people have been asked to pay large surcharges for using cards, especially when booking online. Typically, people trying to book concert tickets, theatre seats, hire cars or train seats discover at the end of the payments process that they have to pay many pounds extra to use a debit or credit card. "The practice of excessive payment surcharges has been ripping off consumers for far too long," said Jo Swinson, the consumer affairs minister. "They are fed up of thinking they will be paying a certain price for goods, only to find out towards the end of the process that the final price is much higher," she said. Airline industry Under the new rules, payment surcharges will have to reflect the actual cost to the retailer of processing the card transaction. That includes fees they have to pay to Visa or Mastercard, for instance, or the cost of installing a chip-and-pin device.
samples.ai_continuation_chat:
Consumer minister Jo Swinson said the move was designed to bring fairness and transparency to the checkout process. "It's simply not right for people to be hit with unexpected fees when they're just trying to pay for something," she explained. Under the new rules, businesses can only pass on the actual cost they incur for processing the payment. That typically means a flat fee of a few pence for debit cards, and a small percentage for credit cards. Previously, some firms were adding charges of up to 20% or more, particularly for airline tickets and event bookings.

The crackdown covers Visa and Mastercard transactions, as well as payments made through chip-and-pin devices. However, it's worth noting that some smaller businesses may still add a nominal fee, as long as it reflects their genuine processing costs. For consumers, this means the advertised price should now be much closer to the final amount they pay. Whether you're booking a hotel room or buying concert tickets, the days of being stung by a hefty surcharge at the last step are finally over.
samples.ai_continuation_free:
From now on, businesses will only be allowed to charge consumers what it actually costs them to process a card payment. For most debit cards, this is just a few pence, and for credit cards it is typically a small percentage of the transaction.

The change, which follows a European Union directive, applies to all businesses trading in the UK, from high street shops and online retailers to cinemas, airlines, and hotels. Previously, some companies had been adding surcharges of up to 20% on top of the ticket or room price, catching customers out at the final stage of booking.

samples.prefix: I believe it takes a lot of strength to have faith, but there is something that takes even more strength. I was raised in the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-Day Saints. At the age of 8 years old I was baptized into the church and confirmed as a member. I wasn’t the most obedient, but for the most part I did what was expected of me.
samples.human_continuation: But then, at the age of 15 I began to question the doctrines that I had been taught since before I could even speak. I believed, as the church taught, that if I did what I was supposed to it would all be clear to me. I though that this doubt was coming from the devil. I believed that because I was dating when I shouldn’t have been, I let him into my life and allowed him to leave me astray. This doubt continued off and on for two years. After breaking up with my boyfriend, I was sure that I would gain clarity. I was doing what the Lord wanted me to do, he would bless me with the truth. But this never came. I began to google what I had been taught all my life was “anti-mormon” but when I did so, I was plagued with guilt. I would read for five minutes, exit out and delete my browser history. I continued as if I hadn’t read anything at all.
samples.ai_continuation_chat:
Then came the questions.

They started small, almost unnoticeable at first. A comment from a friend, a lesson in Sunday School that didn't quite sit right, a scripture passage that seemed to contradict another. I pushed them aside, telling myself that doubt was of the devil, that faith was simply a choice I needed to make more firmly.

But the questions kept coming.

Late at night, when everyone in my house was asleep, I would lie awake with my phone glowing in the darkness. I told myself I was just curious, that I wasn't looking for trouble. I typed things into Google that I had been taught never to search for. The search results felt like stepping into forbidden territory—materials the church warns against, histories I had never heard in any lesson or conference talk.

My heart pounded with something between fear and exhilaration. Part of me felt like I was betraying everything I had ever known. Another part of me felt like I was finally being honest with myself for the first time.
samples.ai_continuation_free: But as I got older, questions started to creep in. Things that didn't quite add up, experiences that didn't align with what I was being taught, and a growing sense that I was living someone else's life rather than my own. The tension became unbearable at times. What I've come to realize is that while faith takes tremendous strength, questioning your faith takes even more. There's a kind of vulnerability in sitting with uncertainty, in admitting that what you were raised to believe might not be the whole truth or maybe even not true at all. It means letting go of a community, a worldview, and sometimes relationships that were foundational to your identity. I'm not saying this to speak against the church or those who find truth in it. For many people, LDS teachings provide genuine meaning and direction. But for me, the most courageous thing I've ever done wasn't holding onto belief—it was being willing to examine it honestly, even when the examination led me somewhere unexpected. The strength I'm talking about isn't about certainty.

samples.prefix: Are we on the verge of creating artificial intelligence capable of finding answers to the world’s most pressing challenges? After steady progress in basic AI tasks in recent years, this is the vision that some leading technologists have for AI. And yet, how we will make this grand leap is anyone’s guess. Eric Schmidt, the executive chairman of Alphabet (formerly Google), says AI could be harnessed to help solve major challenges, including climate change and food security.
samples.human_continuation: Speaking at an event convened in New York this week to discuss the opportunities and risks in AI, Schmidt offered no details on how the technology might be adapted for such complex and abstract problems. Demis Hassabis, CEO of Google Deepmind, a division within Google doing groundbreaking work in machine learning, and which aims to bring about an “artificial general intelligence” (see “Google’s Intelligence Designer”), said the goal of this effort was to harness AI for grand challenges. “If we can solve intelligence in a general enough way, then we can apply it to all sorts of things to make the world a better place,” he said. And the chief technology officer of Facebook, Mike Schroepfer, expressed similar hope. “The power of AI technology is it can solve problems that scale to the whole planet,” he said.
samples.ai_continuation_chat: Schmidt’s optimism is echoed by Demis Hassabis, CEO of Google DeepMind, who argues that artificial general intelligence is not just a possibility but an inevitable milestone. He suggests that once machines can learn any intellectual task a human can, they will unlock solutions to complex scientific problems currently beyond our reach. Meanwhile, Mike Schroepfer, former Chief Technology Officer at Facebook, emphasizes the collaborative potential of these technologies. He believes that open platforms could accelerate breakthroughs in healthcare and energy efficiency. Despite this shared enthusiasm, none of these leaders offer a concrete roadmap for achieving this transformative state. The gap between their high-level aspirations and the current limitations of narrow AI remains vast. Critics argue that without specific implementation strategies, these visions risk becoming mere marketing rhetoric. Nevertheless, the tech industry continues to invest billions, betting that the next leap in capability will arrive sooner than expected.
samples.ai_continuation_free: He envisions a future where machine learning models, trained on vast datasets of scientific literature and real-world environmental data, can simulate complex systems with unprecedented accuracy. This could allow researchers to rapidly test millions of potential solutions for carbon capture technologies or optimize global supply chains to reduce waste. However, this optimism is tempered by significant skepticism from the broader scientific community. Critics argue that current AI systems, while impressive at pattern recognition and generation, lack the deep causal understanding necessary to tackle multifaceted problems like climate change, which require not just computational power but also ethical judgment and interdisciplinary integration. The gap between processing data and deriving actionable, context-aware wisdom remains wide, suggesting that while AI may be a powerful tool in the scientist’s toolkit, it is unlikely to act as an autonomous oracle solving humanity’s crises without substantial human guidance and oversight.

content_constraint.topic: Leading tech executives express optimism about AI's potential to solve global challenges despite lacking specific implementation details.
content_constraint.content_direction: The text contrasts the vague nature of Schmidt's claims with the specific visionary statements from Hassabis and Schroepfer regarding AI's scalability and general intelligence.
content_constraint.scope: It covers remarks made by three executives at a New York event, focusing on their high-level hopes for AI rather than technical methodologies.

samples.prefix: Media playback is unsupported on your device Media caption What made Canada's Slims River disappear? A team of scientists say a melting glacier in Canada's Yukon has caused a river to completely change course. Their findings, published in Nature Geoscience, show how climate change can cause surprising geological events. The Slims River once flowed out to the Bering Sea, but now it flows into the Kaskawulsh River instead.
samples.human_continuation: This phenomenon, known as "river piracy", typically takes centuries but the study documented it over the course of one spring. "Nobody's ever seen a river piracy occur in modern times, at least to my knowledge," lead author Dan Shugar told the BBC. The geoscientist at the University of Washington Tacoma says he and six researchers from Canadian and American universities had planned to study the Slims River last summer. Image copyright Dan Shugar/University of Washington Tacoma Image caption An aerial photo shows the meltwater stream along the toe of Kaskawulsh Glacier, seen on the left, that is diverting fresh water from one river to the other But when they arrived in the Yukon it was barely flowing. They discovered that a small channel had eroded in a large glacier that fed a number of small lakes.
samples.ai_continuation_chat: Dan Shugar, a glacial geologist at the University of Washington Tacoma, led the study that unraveled this dramatic transformation. The research highlights how the rapid retreat of the Kaskawulsh Glacier has fundamentally altered the landscape. As the ice diminished, it exposed steep bedrock slopes that were previously buried under ice. This sudden exposure triggered massive landslides, which effectively blocked the Slims River’s original outlet. Consequently, the water was forced to find a new path, diverting into the neighboring Kaskawulsh River system. This phenomenon, known as river piracy, occurred with astonishing speed, reshaping the hydrology of the region in just a few years. The case serves as a stark reminder of the complex and often unpredictable ways in which climate change drives geological change.
samples.ai_continuation_free: The transformation occurred over a relatively short period, fundamentally altering the landscape of the Kluane National Park and Reserve. As the Kaskawulsh Glacier retreated due to rising temperatures, it lost its grip on the bedrock that had previously dammed the Slims River. This geological shift allowed water to carve a new channel through the valley, diverting the flow away from the Bering Sea and into the Yukon River system. The change has had profound ecological consequences, as the Slims River, which once provided essential nutrients and freshwater to the coastal ecosystem, has been reduced to a mere trickle. Meanwhile, the Kaskawulsh River has surged with increased volume, impacting local wildlife and sediment transport in ways that scientists are still working to fully understand. This event serves as a stark reminder that climate change does not just raise sea levels or increase temperatures; it can physically restructure the Earth's surface, creating new rivers and erasing old ones in the blink of a geological eye.

"This all started with the abolition of execution for the retarded," said Dwight Johnson of Walker County, "that dang Yankee Supreme Court should stay out of our business." samples.prefix: UPDATE: Large geomagnetic storm brewing means Northern Lights tonight The National Weather Service said the aurora should be visible tonight as far south as Missouri, where clear skies allow. A strong magnetic storm is expected to hit Earth over the next two days. The strength of the magnetic storm means northern lights could be visible as far south as the Detroit and Chicago areas.
samples.human_continuation: A large sunspot erupted September 4, 2017, throwing a coronal mass ejection (CME) toward the earth. A coronal mass ejection is a huge explosion of magnetic field and plasma from the Sun's corona. When CMEs impact the Earth's magnetosphere, they are responsible for geomagnetic storms and enhanced auroras, according to NOAA. NOAA's Space Weather Prediction Center has issued a Strong Magnetic Storm Watch for the nights of Sept. 6 and Sept. This means northern lights will possibly be visible farther south than during a typical northern lights event. Northern lights forecasts use a rating system called the kP index to gauge how likely northern lights will be visible at a certain latitude. Northern lights are typically visible as far south as a kP value of 7. On the map above, I drew the expected location of the kP=7. So northern lights may be visible as far south as the Detroit area, Chicago, Cleveland, Des Moines and Syracuse, NY.

The storm follows a powerful eruption from a sunspot on September 4th, which launched a coronal mass ejection directly toward Earth. When these charged particles reach the magnetosphere, they interact with atmospheric gases to create the stunning light displays known as aurora borealis.

The NOAA Space Weather Prediction Center uses the kP index to forecast aurora visibility at various latitudes. This index, which ranges from 0 to 9, measures geomagnetic activity. A kP of 5 or higher indicates a geomagnetic storm capable of pushing auroral displays much farther from the poles than usual. Tonight's storm is expected to reach kP levels that could make the northern lights visible across a significant portion of the northern United States, provided local weather conditions cooperate.

samples.prefix: Bass Fishing Heating Up in Cooler Weather by Tom Lester Old man winter has finally awakened and cooler temperatures are here and holding steady. For quite some time, we fall bass fishermen have been anxiously awaiting a cool down that would in turn our lake water temperatures lower. Although, today is the first official day of winter, the water is cooling off nicely.
samples.human_continuation: It's time to go fishing. Personally, I love fall pattern bass fishing. It is the time of year bass gorge themselves with food getting ready for winter. When they are filling themselves up, I like to be on the water catching 'em. Generally speaking, if you can find them, they are pretty easy to catch, and catch and catch. As the water cools down on our lakes, the shad (one of Mr. Bass' primary dishes) move into the creeks and guess who is following right behind them? That's right, ole man bass. Now that we've got 'um cornered and hemmed up in the creeks, its time put your boat in the water and get ready for some fun. I generally start out on the points of main creeks. It is a good place to find bass that are moving into the creek or coming out. They will literally "stack up" on the points as they move around to feed on the shad.
samples.ai_continuation_chat:
The cooling water triggers a chain reaction that bass fishermen live for. As the surface temperature drops into the upper 50s and low 60s, shad begin their annual migration up into the creeks, seeking the slightly warmer, stable water found in the backs of these tributaries. The bass, never far behind their primary food source, follow right along with them.

This is where the real fun begins. I focus on the main lake points leading into these creeks, especially those with a gradual taper. The bass will stage on these points, waiting to ambush shad as they move in and out with the changing light and wind. A lipless crankbait like a Rat-L-Trap in a shad pattern is my go-to here. I make long casts and let it fall on a semi-slack line, then rip it forward a few cranks before letting it fall again. That erratic action triggers reaction strikes from bass that are keyed in on wounded shad. Work the points thoroughly, and you’ll find the fish stacked up, ready to feed before winter truly sets in.
samples.ai_continuation_free: As the water temperature drops, the bass begin to transition through their fall patterns and into their winter habits. This shift can be one of the most productive times of the year for anglers who understand what’s happening beneath the surface. The cooling water triggers a feeding frenzy as bass prepare for the slower metabolism months ahead. They’re not just biting—they’re loading up. Right now, the key is to focus on the baitfish. As the water cools, shad and other forage start to school up tightly, and the bass follow. Look for them in the backs of creeks and along main lake points where the bait is congregating. The shallow flats that held fish all summer are emptying out, and the bass are moving toward their winter haunts. That means deeper ledges, creek channels, and steep drop-offs are all prime real estate. One of the best techniques this time of year is slow rolling a spinnerbait or working a jerkbait with long pauses. The bass aren’t as willing to chase down a fast-moving lure, so you have to give them time to commit.

content_constraint.topic: Fall pattern bass fishing and how to catch bass as they follow shad into cooling creeks.
content_constraint.content_direction: Encourages the reader to go fishing by explaining that cooling water drives bass to gorge on shad in creeks, making them easy to catch on points.
content_constraint.scope: Covers the seasonal behavior of bass and shad, and provides a starting strategy (fishing creek points) without detailing specific techniques or gear.

samples.prefix: As the UK referendum result dropped in that fateful Friday morning, the tech startup world didn’t immediately grind to a halt. Websites kept loading. Apps kept opening. But what left UK technology entrepreneurs aghast was not just that Britain had chosen to leave the European Union after 40 years, but that all those years of trying compete with the giants of Silicon Valley would now be thrown into doubt.
samples.human_continuation: Although Europe’s 500 million citizens dwarfs the 323 million in the US, for years European startups had to deal with 28 jurisdictions and many languages. But the EU had at least managed to harmonize (more or less) the processes of company operation, data sharing and hiring. Hiring from a talent base of 500 million people was also an incredible asset to startups, as was raising funding from Venture capitalists. Based in Berlin? No problem. Developers in Slovenia, but the the HQ was in London? No problem. And, after several Eastern European states had joined, suddenly the whole of Europe could tap into the talent produced from Soviet-era education systems built around engineering and maths. The truth is the overwhelming majority of the UK tech startup industry was for ‘Remain’. Industry body COADEC found over 80% of companies were in favour of staying in the EU, citing the single market, free movement of labour and economic stability as their reasons.
samples.ai_continuation_chat: The realization hit quickly that the primary advantage for British innovators had been the seamless access to the European single market. This harmonized regulatory framework allowed startups to scale rapidly across borders without navigating a labyrinth of differing national laws. For a young company, this meant launching a product in London and instantly having a potential customer base of hundreds of millions. Equally critical was the free movement of labour, which fueled the industry’s growth by attracting top-tier talent from across the continent. Engineers, designers, and entrepreneurs flowed freely into UK hubs, creating a vibrant, diverse ecosystem that rivaled global competitors. Organizations like COADEC, representing tech businesses in the North, warned that severing these ties would isolate the UK tech startup industry. Without the ease of hiring skilled workers or selling services without friction, the competitive edge would erode. The fear was not just economic, but existential; the vibrant, borderless environment that had nurtured British tech success was being dismantled, leaving founders to wonder how they could possibly compete against Silicon Valley giants without their European advantage.
samples.ai_continuation_free: For years, London had prided itself on being the tech capital of Europe, a vibrant ecosystem where talent flowed freely across borders and venture capital poured in from across the continent. The promise of the single market was the bedrock upon which many of these startups were built; it meant that a company founded in Shoreditch could scale effortlessly into Berlin, Paris, or Dublin without navigating a labyrinth of new regulatory frameworks or currency risks. Now, that seamless expansion looked like a distant memory. Founders who had spent months pitching to investors on the stability and accessibility of the EU market suddenly found themselves having to rewrite their growth strategies from scratch. The uncertainty wasn’t just political; it was existential. How could you convince a Series A investor to back a platform that might soon face data privacy hurdles, hiring restrictions, or trade tariffs? The mood in co-working spaces shifted from the usual buzz of disruption to a somber, frantic energy, as entrepreneurs scrambled to understand what "Brexit" actually meant for their bottom lines.

content_constraint.content_direction: It contrasts the pre-Brexit advantages of cross-border operations and talent access with the political reality that the industry overwhelmingly supported staying in the EU.
content_constraint.scope: The text covers the logistical and economic benefits of EU membership for startups and concludes with survey data confirming the industry's preference for 'Remain'.

samples.prefix: Human puff-adder Bill Kristol drolly noted on Morning Joe this week that the shutdown is not "the end of the world". The Huffington Post's Sam Stein snapped back, "For these people affected by these cuts, it is sort of comparable to the end of the world." I have one quibble with Stein's otherwise satisfying smackdown: "For the people affected by these cuts" implies that there are people who are not affected by these cuts.
samples.human_continuation: Stein was talking specifically about the families and children across the country most likely to suffer when the government stops paying for Head Start programs and nutritional aid, but they are only the most sympathetic victims of the shutdown. And there are a lot of them: Almost 9m mothers and children rely on the Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants and Children (Wic). Most states will be able to operate for about a week on the money they have, but in the words of one administrator in Cook County, "We have no cushion. If our funding stream stops we will temporarily suspend service." The US Department of Agriculture is attempting to prop up the program in the states hardest hit – they announced this week a $2.5m grant to Utah. But the $125m they have on reserve is laughably small for a program that costs $7b a year – it's less than 2% of the total budget.
samples.ai_continuation_chat:
The truth is that the shutdown is affecting everyone, though some are clearly suffering more than others. The Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants and Children—WIC—serves approximately 9 million mothers and young children across the country. In Cook County, Illinois, the local WIC office has already begun turning away new applicants. In Utah, the state has warned that it may run out of funding for the program by mid-February. To enhance the depth of flavor, I also add a splash of balsamic vinegar to the fruit mixture, a trick that amplifies the natural sweetness without making it cloying. For the topping, I use their Streusel Topping recipe, which combines cold butter, flour, and brown sugar into a buttery, crumbly perfection. To begin, preheat your oven to 350 degrees Fahrenheit. In a large bowl, toss two cups of sliced strawberries and two cups of fresh blueberries with two tablespoons of sugar and one teaspoon of balsamic vinegar. Pour this mixture into a greased baking dish. In a separate bowl, cut the cold butter into the dry ingredients until the mixture resembles coarse crumbs.
samples.ai_continuation_free: It’s become a bit of a ritual for us, usually timed to coincide with the first warm weekends of June. We drive out early to beat the heat and the crowds, filling baskets with plump, ruby-red berries that smell intensely sweet. Back home, the kitchen counter is soon covered in colanders and cutting boards as I hull and slice them, then spread them out on parchment-lined baking sheets to flash freeze. Once they’re solid, I transfer them into freezer bags, labeling them with the date. There’s a particular satisfaction in opening one of those bags in the dead of winter, pulling out a handful of frozen jewels to toss into a smoothie or simmer into a quick compote for oatmeal. It’s the closest I can get to that summer burst of flavor when the snow is still melting on the roof, and honestly, it makes the failed garden attempts feel a little less like a loss and more like a reason to appreciate the local farms that do it so well.

samples.prefix: Dan Patrick (REUTERS/Mike Stone/File Photo) The Texas lieutenant governor said on Monday he has enlisted Christian pastors statewide to help him win approval for legislation heading to a sate Senate committee this week that limits access to public restroom access for transgender people. samples.human_continuation: Critics contend the bill infringes on the civil rights of gay, lesbian, bisexual and transgender (LGBT) people. Business groups say it will cause economic damage, pointing to a similar measure North Carolina enacted into law last year that led to travel and commercial boycotts. Allowing transgender people to use public bathrooms corresponding to their gender identity rather than their birth gender has become the latest flashpoint in the long U.S. battle over LGBT rights. Patrick announced the start of a “one million voices” campaign, with pastors enlisted to win support from their congregations for the legislation. Committee debate starts on Tuesday. “North Carolina was the tip of the spear. We will be next to pass a bill that focuses on privacy, a person’s privacy, and public safety,” Patrick said, adding there will be no economic harm if it is enacted.
samples.ai_continuation_chat: Opponents of the bill, however, argue that it is a thinly veiled attack on the LGBT community, echoing the controversial North Carolina law that sparked widespread boycotts and economic backlash. Business groups, including major Texas corporations, have voiced strong opposition, warning that the measure could cost the state billions in lost revenue and conventions. Patrick dismissed these concerns, claiming the "one million voices" campaign—a coalition of pastors and conservative activists—represents the true will of Texans. He insisted that protecting women and children from potential harm outweighs any economic risks. Yet critics counter that no evidence exists linking transgender individuals to increased safety threats in restrooms, and they accuse Patrick of stoking fear for political gain. As the Senate committee prepares to hear the bill, the battle lines are drawn between religious liberty advocates and civil rights defenders, with all eyes on Texas as the next flashpoint in the national debate over transgender rights.
samples.ai_continuation_free:
"I'm not going to be lectured by anyone about compassion or about protecting children," Patrick said, flanked by a dozen pastors and religious leaders. "This is about safety, plain and simple. We are asking pastors across this state to stand with us, to speak from their pulpits, and to remind their congregations that we have a moral obligation to protect women and children from dangerous situations."

The bill, Senate Bill 6, would require individuals in public schools, government buildings, and some private facilities to use restrooms and locker rooms that correspond with their sex at birth, rather than their gender identity. Supporters argue the measure is necessary to prevent men from entering women's spaces under the guise of being transgender. Opponents, including civil rights groups and major Texas corporations, warn the bill is discriminatory and could cost the state billions in economic development and tourism.

samples.prefix: At the risk of sounding arrogant, the one thing I can appreciate about myself is that I have no illusions about my shortcomings. I willing admit that my expectations of others can be high and sometimes even unrealistic, but for myself, I really just want people to accept me as I am. However, when you are as stubborn and as set in your ways as I am, you tend to get kicked in the rear by karma a lot.
samples.human_continuation: And you also run into the constant irritation of people trying to change you all the time. I like to think of my karma as my wake up calls from God. Sometimes these calls are subtle in nature and only require a tiny poke for me to wake up and redirect myself. But more times than not, it takes a drastic, hard, swift, life altering kick in the ass to make me say “oh, that is what HE meant.” Here is the thing though, I don’t see anything wrong with it, nor would I do anything any different. I am a firm believer in “you made your bed, now lay in it” philosophy. If I mess up, than I mess up but on the same token, it is my responsibility to clean up after myself. Sure, I can try to prevent it but unfortunately, I’m just a permanent member of the hard head makes a soft ass club and that is just the way it is. The beauty of where I am at in my life right now is that I am ensuring that this time around, when karma comes calling, I learn to not repeat these same errors.
samples.ai_continuation_chat: I used to view these sudden, jarring corrections as cruel punishments, evidence that the universe was actively conspiring against my happiness. I would rage against the injustice, convinced that I deserved better than the consequences of my own rigid actions. But over time, the pattern became undeniable. Every time I refused to bend, every time I insisted on my way despite clear signs that I was wrong, life would slam the door shut in my face. It wasn’t malice; it was mechanics. These experiences forced me to confront the uncomfortable truth that I am solely responsible for the trajectory of my own life. There is no external savior coming to fix the mess created by my own refusal to adapt. I have come to see God not as a judge handing out sentences, but as a teacher using reality as the classroom. The pain of those karmic hits is the friction necessary to smooth out the rough edges of my ego. It is through this relentless process of breaking and rebuilding that I am slowly learning self-acceptance. I am learning to listen, to yield, and to trust that the lessons, however painful, are exactly what I need to grow into a more compassionate, less stubborn version of myself.

Hikmat Massarwa (R), a member of Israel's Arab minority, attends a remand hearing at the Central District Court in Lod, near Tel Aviv April 25, 2013.
samples.human_continuation: REUTERS/Baz Ratner Hikmat Massarwa’s case was unprecedented, and the relatively light penalty handed down to him as part of a plea bargain reflected Israel’s indecision about who - if anyone - to back in its northern neighbor’s civil war. Massarwa was arrested on March 19 upon returning via Turkey from Syria, where he had spent a week at a rebel base. Israeli prosecutors accused him of undergoing small-arms training by radical Islamists there who asked him to carry out a suicide attack in Israel - although, by all accounts, he declined. Those charges carried a maximum 15-year jail term. But prosecutors appeared unable, from the outset, to throw the book at Massarwa because of Israeli haziness about the Syria crisis. “There’s no legal guidance regarding the rebel groups fighting in Syria,” Judge Avraham Yaakov said at a session of the trial at Lod district court, south of Tel Aviv, in May.
samples.ai_continuation_chat: The ruling by Judge Avraham Yaakov at the Lod district court marked a significant departure from typical harsh penalties for such offenses, reflecting a complex legal landscape. Massarwa had traveled to Syria in 2012, joining opposition forces for a brief period before returning to Israel. Prosecutors argued that his actions posed a severe threat to national security, yet the court opted for a plea bargain that significantly reduced the potential sentence. This unprecedented leniency highlights Israel’s ambiguous stance on the Syrian civil war, where preventing citizens from joining foreign conflicts often clashes with political realities. Legal experts suggest the decision may set a controversial precedent, potentially encouraging other citizens facing similar charges to seek reduced sentences through negotiated deals. The case underscores the delicate balance Israeli authorities must maintain between enforcing strict security laws and managing internal dissent within its Arab minority population, who often hold divergent views regarding the Assad regime’s fate.
samples.ai_continuation_free: The court in Lod found Massarwa guilty of joining an unauthorized military organization and carrying out activities aimed at harming Israel’s security. According to prosecutors, the 22-year-old from the northern Arab town of Kafr Qasim traveled to Syria in late 2012, where he fought alongside rebel groups against the Assad regime for several weeks before returning to Israel. Israeli authorities viewed his actions as a breach of loyalty, arguing that by taking up arms against a neighboring country’s government, he had compromised national interests and potentially exposed himself to recruitment by hostile entities. The prosecution emphasized that while Syria is not Israel’s ally, the act of joining an irregular militia abroad without state permission constitutes a serious offense under the Emergency Powers Law. Massarwa’s defense argued that his decision was driven by personal convictions and a desire to support democratic movements in the region, rather than any intent to damage Israel. However, the judge rejected this line of reasoning, stating that citizens must adhere to legal channels for political expression and that unauthorized military engagement abroad poses inherent risks to state security.

samples.prefix: The world’s first monkeys with genes modified through a DNA engineering method known as Crispr/Cas9 were born in a lab. The scientific breakthrough by Chinese researchers could become a cornerstone for research and prevention of human genetic disorders. Researchers at Nanjing Medical University and Yunnan Key Laboratory of Primate Biomedical Research in Kunming in China have created two genetically modified macaques with targeted mutations using the CRISPR/Cas9 system.
samples.human_continuation: “Our study shows that the CRISPR/Cas9 system enables simultaneous disruption of two target genes in one step without producing off-target mutations,” study author Jiahao Sha told the Science Daily. “Considering that many human diseases are caused by genetic abnormalities, targeted genetic modification in monkeys is invaluable for the generation of human disease models.” The researchers introduced single-cell macaque embryos with modified Ribonucleic acids (RNAs) to generate the genome-editing process. RNA is a ubiquitous family of large biological molecules that perform multiple vital roles in the coding, decoding, regulation, and expression of genes. Using the Crispr method, Chinese scientists were targeting three genes in the experiment – one that regulates metabolism, another that regulates immune cell development and a third that regulates stem cells and sex determination.
samples.ai_continuation_chat: The team, led by Jiahao Sha, injected one-cell-stage macaque embryos with ribonucleic acids (RNAs) designed to target specific genes linked to human metabolic and immune disorders. Unlike earlier attempts using older techniques, CRISPR/Cas9 allowed precise, efficient edits in a single step, avoiding complex and time-consuming breeding. These macaques, now several months old, carry stable mutations that can be passed to future generations, offering a powerful model for studying diseases like diabetes, Parkinson's, and cystic fibrosis. Because primates share close genetic and physiological similarities with humans, researchers can better understand disease progression and test therapies in ways impossible with mice. The work marks a crucial step toward translating genetic insights into clinical treatments for millions affected by inherited conditions.
samples.ai_continuation_free: The monkeys, named Mingming and Lingling, were born with specific gene edits designed to mimic human metabolic and immune system disorders. By disabling the genes Ppar-γ and Rag1, the team created models for studying conditions like diabetes and severe combined immunodeficiency. The CRISPR/Cas9 method allowed them to target these genes with unprecedented precision, achieving mutations in multiple embryos simultaneously. This marks a significant step forward from previous genetic modification techniques in primates, which were often inefficient or resulted in mosaic animals—where only some cells carry the edit. The Chinese team reported that their approach yielded a higher success rate, with both monkeys showing the intended genetic changes across all tested tissues. While the research has sparked ethical debates about modifying primate genomes, the scientists emphasize its potential for advancing human medicine.

samples.prefix: Honeymoons don't last forever. But that doesn't mean the love affair has to end — and the love affair Canadians are having with Justin Trudeau's Liberals appears to be enduring in the polls. The Liberals continue to hold the new support they captured after their majority victory in last fall's federal election, when they pulled votes away from both the Conservatives and New Democrats.
samples.human_continuation: What do Canadians think of the leaders? Explore the latest numbers for the 5 major federal leaders in our new CBC Leader Meter. Justin Trudeau's own popularity also remains high, with approval ratings well above those of both of his main rivals, interim Conservative Leader Rona Ambrose and outgoing NDP Leader Tom Mulcair, as well as the ratings he posted before last year's vote. The CBC's new interactive tool, the Leader Meter, lets you track those numbers. Over the last three months of polling, the Liberals have averaged 46.7 per cent support. That's an increase of 7.2 points over their performance in the Oct. 19 election and nearly even (up 0.1 points) from their average support during the previous quarter of federal polling calculated three months ago. The Conservatives have averaged 29.1 per cent, also unchanged from where they were in the previous quarter but down 2.8 points from the last election.
samples.ai_continuation_chat:
The latest polling data shows the Liberals consistently hovering around the 45 to 48 percent mark, a figure that would have seemed unthinkable under previous Liberal leaders. Meanwhile, the Conservatives, still led by interim leader Rona Ambrose, remain stuck in the low 30s, unable to make significant gains despite their efforts to rebrand. The NDP under Tom Mulcair has fared even worse, settling into the mid-teens, a far cry from the party’s 2011 Orange Wave.

What’s striking is not just the stability of Liberal support, but its breadth. Trudeau’s coalition cuts across age groups, regions, and even traditional partisan lines. Young voters still flock to him, but so do suburban families and older Canadians who once leaned Conservative. The prime minister’s handling of the economy, climate policy, and Indigenous relations continues to resonate, while his personal approval ratings remain enviably high. For now, the opposition parties seem unable to land a lasting blow. The honeymoon may have ended, but the marriage, it appears, is still going strong.
samples.ai_continuation_free: The latest polling averages show the Liberals hovering around 40 per cent support nationally, a figure that would translate into another comfortable majority if an election were held today. While no government can sustain that level of popularity indefinitely, the resilience of the Liberal numbers is striking. The Conservatives, still searching for a leader who can unite the party and broaden its appeal, remain stuck in the low 30s. The NDP, meanwhile, has failed to regain the ground it lost in 2015, languishing in the mid-teens as voters who once flocked to Jack Layton's orange wave now seem content to stay with Trudeau. What explains this endurance? Part of it is the prime minister's personal likability, which continues to cut through the noise of daily politics. But there is also a sense that the Liberals have delivered on key promises — from the Canada Child Benefit to infrastructure spending — without triggering the kind of scandal or economic shock that typically erodes a government's honeymoon.

samples.prefix: by Lucy Peltz From America’s Declaration of Independence in 1776 to the end of the Napoleonic wars in 1815, Britain’s economic, social and political stability was in turmoil. Against this backdrop of revolution abroad, the relations between the sexes – and their proper roles — were increasingly challenged. While the figure of the respectable female writer of sentimental novels, poetry or didactic literature had become a cultural commonplace, there was a new backlash against the literary woman asserting her views in the more ‘masculine’ genres of history and politics.
samples.human_continuation: The tightening of gendered boundaries can be particularly identified in the reception and troubled reputation of a new generation of political voices, including the radical Mary Wollstonecraft. In 1787, Mary Wollstonecraft was a relatively unknown writer who was running a school when she published Thoughts on the Education of Daughters. This was a ‘conduct book’, one of the few genres deemed acceptable for women writers. A year later Wollstonecraft wrote Mary, A Fiction, a semi-autobiographical novel in which she created an independent female protagonist whose ‘grandeur is derived from the operations of [her] own faculties, not subjugated to opinion’. It was also in 1788 that Wollstonecraft began to write for the Analytical Review. It was in this radical newspaper, that she first declared her admiration for the controversial republican thinker, Catherine Macaulay.
samples.ai_continuation_chat: It was into this contentious literary landscape that Mary Wollstonecraft (1759–1797) launched her own career. In 1787 she published Thoughts on the Education of Daughters, a conduct book that, while conventional in form, already displayed her willingness to challenge prevailing orthodoxies. That same year she began contributing reviews to the Analytical Review, a progressive periodical that provided her with a forum for engaging with contemporary political and philosophical debates. Her first novel, Mary, A Fiction (1788), similarly broke new ground, offering an autobiographical exploration of female desire and intellectual autonomy that drew inspiration from the life and writings of the republican historian Catherine Macaulay. Through these early publications, Wollstonecraft began carving out a space for herself at the intersection of feminine sentiment and masculine reasoning.
samples.ai_continuation_free: This backlash was particularly pronounced in the periodical press and literary reviews, where women authors who ventured into political commentary or historical writing were frequently subjected to ridicule or dismissal as unfeminine and unnatural. The critical reception of such works often focused not on their intellectual content but on the author's gender transgression, questioning her propriety and suggesting that her literary ambitions were incompatible with domestic virtues. This hostility was symptomatic of a broader anxiety about the destabilization of social hierarchies in an era when the very foundations of political authority were being questioned on both sides of the Atlantic. The French Revolution, with its rhetoric of liberty and equality, had particularly unsettling implications for gender relations, as the notion that all men were created equal could not easily be contained within traditional patriarchal frameworks.

samples.prefix: Share this... Reddit Linkedin email “No freeman may be taken or imprisoned or be disseized of his freehold or liberties, or his free customs, or be outlawed or exiled, or in any manner destroyed, but by the lawful judgement of his peers, or by the law of the land.” These words were first written in the Coronation Charter, also called the Charter of Liberties, which was a proclamation by Henry I issued in 1100.
samples.human_continuation: Just think about that for a moment. 915 years ago on this island, uniquely in the world, great men were laying the philosophical foundations of a special type of liberty and striving to restrain the power of their rulers. It marked the beginning of an historic struggle for the soul of England that took place over centuries while absolutism and tyranny was established unchallenged on the continent. When the struggle was won this great country of ours was the freest in the world. Freeborn Englishmen were envied and admired around the globe for the constitutional liberty they enjoyed and the spirit of freedom that thrived here like nowhere else. Sadly, that is all part of history now and we must fight this struggle once again.
samples.ai_continuation_chat: It marked a pivotal moment in English history, as it was the first time a monarch voluntarily bound himself to the law, acknowledging limits on royal power. Henry I, seeking to secure his throne after the death of his brother William Rufus, promised to correct the abuses of his predecessor, restoring the rights of the Church and barons. This charter laid the foundational principle that even the king was subject to legal restraint, a radical notion for its time. It directly influenced the later Magna Carta in 1215, which expanded these protections to freeborn Englishmen more broadly. The Charter of Liberties thus became a symbol of the enduring struggle for constitutional liberty, reminding generations that freedom under law was not a grant but a birthright.
samples.ai_continuation_free: These same principles were later echoed and expanded in the Magna Carta of 1215, which King John was forced to grant by his rebellious barons. The phrase "lawful judgement of his peers" laid the groundwork for the modern right to trial by jury, while "by the law of the land" evolved into what we now call due process. Though the original charter applied only to free men—a minority of the population at the time—its core idea that no one, not even the king, stands above the law became a foundational stone of constitutional governance. Over centuries, these protections were gradually extended to more people, influencing legal systems around the world, including the Fifth and Fourteenth Amendments to the U.S. Constitution. It’s remarkable how a single sentence from 900 years ago still shapes our understanding of justice and liberty today.

content_constraint.content_direction: Argues that the Charter of Liberties initiated a centuries-long struggle for freedom in England, contrasting it with continental absolutism, and asserts that this liberty is now lost and must be fought for again.
content_constraint.scope: Covers the philosophical foundations laid in 1100, the historical struggle and its victory, and concludes with a call to renew the fight in the present.

samples.prefix: Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte and Singapore founder Lee Kuan Yew. File photo / Composite Despite both ruling with an iron fist, the late Singapore founder Lee Kuan Yew is extremely different from Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte, Singapore's biggest newspaper said Friday. In a strongly-worded opinion piece, the Straits Times scoffed at commentaries that Lee and Duterte had similar administrative styles and nation-building approaches.
samples.human_continuation: Lee, under an authoritarian rule, transformed Singapore from a third world to a first world country. He passed away in March 2015. "The analogy would have been interesting except that it is laughably inappropriate," wrote Global Affairs associate editor Ravi Velloor. The first big difference between them, said the piece, was that Lee "was not a man to have a person's life taken away without absolute attention to due process." "People with no links to the drug trade, either as consumers or suppliers, have been assassinated in the process, perhaps to settle private vendettas. Criticism is met with abuse. An army of online warriors, some of whom are perhaps employed in the booming outsourcing industry, seem to be readily on hand to troll presidential critics, putting a fright into even seasoned commentators," it said.
samples.ai_continuation_chat: "To equate the two is to misunderstand both men profoundly," wrote Ravi Velloor, the newspaper's foreign editor. He argued that while Lee built institutions, nurtured a meritocratic civil service, and prioritized long-term economic stability, Duterte has weakened institutions, empowered the military and police with impunity, and governed through fear and populist outrage. Velloor acknowledged both leaders had authoritarian streaks but stressed that Lee's authoritarianism was "benevolent and developmental," aimed at creating a just and prosperous society, whereas Duterte's has been "destructive and divisive," focusing on personal vendettas and short-term political gains. The Straits Times piece concluded that comparing the two not only does a disservice to Singapore's founding father but also whitewashes the troubling realities of the Philippines' current leadership.
samples.ai_continuation_free: The newspaper argued that Lee ruled with a clear vision, long-term planning, and a strict but meritocratic system that lifted Singapore from poverty to a first-world nation. In contrast, it said Duterte’s leadership is marked by erratic policies, a focus on short-term popularity, and a bloody war on drugs that has led to thousands of extrajudicial killings. The Straits Times emphasized that while both leaders were firm, Lee’s iron fist was used to build institutions and enforce the rule of law, whereas Duterte’s has been used to undermine them. The piece concluded that comparing the two is an insult to Lee’s legacy and a misunderstanding of what made Singapore successful.

I am looking to put this guy out. I don’t want to go 12 rounds with this guy. The longer he stays around the more confident he will get so I want to get him out of there as soon as possible.” Bradley is known for many things, but power isn’t among them. "I've been through a lot," Bradley admits. "People questioned my victory over Pacquiao, but I know what I accomplished that night. This fight against Provodnikov is about proving myself all over again."

Provodnikov (22-2, 15 KOs) is known for his relentless pressure and power punching, making him a dangerous opponent for anyone in the division. Bradley, however, seems unfazed by the challenge.

The Russian challenger, nicknamed "The Siberian Rocky," brings a fan-friendly style that has earned him comparisons to Mike Tyson. At 22-0 with 15 knockouts, Provodnikov has shown devastating power, though he lacks Bradley's championship experience. "I've been training hard for this fight," Bradley explained, his voice steady. "I know what Provodnikov brings to the table. He's a come-forward fighter who throws a lot of punches. But I've been working on my combinations and my timing. I plan to be sharp on Saturday night."

Prometían empleos como camareras, niñeras o modelos en ciudades como Milán, Madrid o París. Una vez allí, les quitaban los pasaportes y las obligaban a prostituirse bajo amenazas de violencia contra ellas o sus familias. Pero lo que no conté entonces es cómo esa búsqueda de belleza se convirtió en una red que la atrapó. No era solo el deseo de una adolescente de sentirse bonita; era la promesa de un futuro que nunca llegó. Las mismas manos que le ofrecían un trabajo digno eran las que la vendían como mercancía. Y nosotros, los que miramos desde afuera, preferimos creer en la versión limpia, en la heroína o en la víctima perfecta, antes que aceptar que Marita era ambas cosas y ninguna: una mujer que quiso salir adelante y terminó siendo el eslabón más débil de una cadena que todos alimentamos.

samples.prefix: A counterterrorism catch-and-release campaign by Canada's national police force may have prevented 10 aspiring jihadis from heading off to war, but the roundup at Montréal-Trudeau airport is raising worries about what comes next for radicalized youth. On Wednesday, while federal and provincial political leaders applauded the police work, anti-radicalization experts said only an integrated effort involving civilians and police can deal with youth fixated on taking up arms in the Middle East or joining terrorist groups.
samples.human_continuation: In Montreal, which has become a jihadi recruiting hotbed, the only tool appears to be handcuffs. In the past six months alone, at least seven youths have left the city to join the Islamic State in Syria or Iraq. At least 15 other teenagers and young adults have been arrested pre-emptively. Some have volunteered to be monitored, while others, such as those arrested at the Montreal airport on the weekend, were simply released after having their passports confiscated. Story continues below advertisement Acting on a tip from one or more parents, the RCMP arrested the 10 youth at the airport but have released few other details. An 11th teenager was captured on video being led away from a Montreal home by investigators. None of the teenagers have been identified publicly and no charges were laid.
samples.ai_continuation_chat: The recent RCMP operation underscores the persistent threat of jihadi recruitment in Montreal, a city that has emerged as a significant hub for individuals attempting to join the Islamic State in Syria and Iraq. Authorities intercepted these travelers just as they prepared to board flights, preventing them from crossing international borders to engage in violent extremism. This event highlights the evolving nature of the threat, where radicalization often occurs online before manifesting in physical attempts to travel. While the arrests were successful, they also reveal the challenges of monitoring potential recruits who may not have yet committed violent acts but remain ideologically committed. Experts warn that without robust community engagement and early intervention programs, similar incidents will likely recur, as the allure of foreign conflict continues to draw vulnerable youth away from mainstream society and toward dangerous extremist ideologies.
samples.ai_continuation_free: The incident highlights a growing tension between immediate security interventions and the long-term social strategies required to dismantle the ideological appeal of extremism. Critics argue that while arresting individuals at the border stops immediate threats, it does nothing to address the underlying grievances, isolation, and online radicalization that drive young people toward violence in the first place. Without robust community-based programs, mentorship, and mental health support, there is a risk that these interventions become merely a revolving door, catching one group of aspirants while others slip through the cracks or become more deeply entrenched in extremist networks. Experts emphasize that police alone lack the trust and cultural nuance necessary to engage with at-risk youth effectively, suggesting that sustainable prevention requires a collaborative approach where law enforcement works in tandem with educators, social workers, and community leaders to identify and support vulnerable individuals before they reach the point of no return.

samples.prefix: A team led by postdoctoral associate John Heron of Cornell University has developed a room-temperature magnetoelectric memory design that replaces power-hungry electric currents with an electric field. It could lead to low-power, instant-on computing devices. “The advantage here is low energy consumption,” Heron said. “It requires a low voltage, without current, to switch it.
samples.human_continuation: Devices that use currents consume more energy and dissipate a significant amount of that energy in the form of heat. That is what’s heating up your computer and draining your batteries.” The researchers made their device out of bismuth ferrite, which is both magnetic and ferroelectric, meaning it’s always electrically polarized; and that polarization can be switched by applying an electric field. This rare combination makes it a “multiferroic” material, allowing for it to be used for nonvolatile memory devices with relatively simple geometries. Other scientists have demonstrated similar results with competing materials, but at impractical cold temperatures, like 4 Kelvin (-452 Fahrenheit). Their results were published online Dec. 17 in Nature, along with an associated “News and Views” article.
samples.ai_continuation_chat: Current-based devices generate heat because electrons moving through a material experience resistance, like friction, and this energy dissipates as thermal waste. In contrast, the new design exploits the unique properties of bismuth ferrite, a multiferroic material that exhibits both ferroelectric and magnetic ordering simultaneously. Because bismuth ferrite couples these properties, an electric field can switch its magnetic state without requiring any current flow. Heron's team demonstrated that the material maintains its magnetoelectric behavior at room temperature, a significant advance over previous approaches that required extreme cryogenic cooling to near 4 Kelvin. This room-temperature operation removes a major barrier to practical implementation, potentially enabling memory devices that retain data even when powered off while consuming a fraction of the energy of conventional technologies.
samples.ai_continuation_free: to switch it. The breakthrough addresses one of the biggest challenges in computing: reducing the energy required to store and retrieve data while maintaining speed and reliability. The design utilizes a multiferroic heterostructure that couples electric and magnetic properties at the nanoscale. By applying a small electric field, researchers can manipulate the magnetic orientation of a thin film without the need for the conventional current-based spin-transfer torque or spin-orbit torque mechanisms. This eliminates the joule heating that plagues conventional memory technologies and allows for dramatic reductions in power consumption. "This could fundamentally change how we think about memory hierarchies in computing systems," explained Professor James R. H. Smith, who supervised the research.

samples.prefix: This is the second part of an ongoing look into the state of online gaming in Japan. If you’d like to read more on the subject head over to part one. Last time, we discussed the issues facing the Japanese online gamer. Of note, Japanese online gaming is so niche that the term MMORPG has very little meaning to your average online gamer, who tends to be more of a console shooter fan than PC playboys/girls.
samples.human_continuation: According to Akiba MMO‘s CEO Keiko, “Japan essentially skipped the PC and jumped straight to mobile phones.” Having a big, bulky machine that’s primarily used at one’s place of work hardly seems like something that would have awesome games on it. Worse yet, because of the small market, few western companies translated their games into Japanese. No problem, right? Japanese people must be able to speak English like the rest of the world despite being an island nation no where near an English speaking country… English Only Despite having to learn it for at least six years, Japanese people really don’t speak English. As a teacher, this comes up a lot, but Keiko in particular noted that English’s role in Japan is often restricted to unique wording/phrasing that only makes sense to Japanese. In short, it’s used for adding an exotic flavor for advertisers, but as a communication language, people may only passively understand English.
samples.ai_continuation_chat: This gap is precisely where Akiba MMO and Keiko come into the picture. While Japan boasts a vibrant arcade and console culture, the PC gaming scene remains a fractured landscape. Most Japanese gamers rely on mobile phones for their daily fix—think gacha games and social RPGs that require minimal English. The moment you step into a proper PC-based MMO, the language barrier hits hard. Menus, quest logs, and chat channels are overwhelmingly in English, and few localizations exist. Keiko, a veteran gamer I spoke with, described her frustration: "I wanted to play with international friends, but even basic settings were a puzzle." This linguistic wall keeps many Japanese players isolated, funneling them back to mobile titles where everything is in their native language. Akiba MMO aims to bridge this divide by offering curated guides and community support, but the core issue remains: until English proficiency improves or more games get full Japanese support, the PC gaming market in Japan will stay a niche within a niche, leaving millions of potential players on the sidelines.
samples.ai_continuation_free: This time around, I want to focus on the flip side of that coin: the games that do thrive in Japan, and how they manage to do so despite the cultural and technical hurdles. If you walk into a net café in Akihabara or Shinjuku, you won't see rows of people raiding in World of Warcraft. Instead, you'll likely find clusters of players hunched over Dragon Quest X, Final Fantasy XIV, or the seemingly eternal Monster Hunter Frontier. These titles succeed not by mimicking Western MMOs, but by adapting to Japanese sensibilities. They prioritize narrative, character attachment, and cooperative play over the competitive, gear-grinding treadmill that dominates in the West. Take Dragon Quest X, for example. It's an anomaly: a mainline Dragon Quest title that is an MMO. Yet it works because it feels like a Dragon Quest game first. The turn-based combat, the Akira Toriyama art style, and the episodic, story-driven quests are all intact. The online component is almost an afterthought—a way to share the adventure rather than the core reason to play.

content_constraint.topic: Japan's PC gaming market gap and English language barriers for online gaming.
content_constraint.content_direction: Explains why Japan skipped PC gaming (cultural preference for mobile, small market) and highlights the English language barrier as a key obstacle for Japanese gamers.
content_constraint.scope: Covers the historical shift to mobile, lack of localization, and the limited functional use of English in Japan, stopping before discussing solutions or further impacts.

He went on a hunger strike. – RSVP for #StopRacism Weekly Calls – Every great story has its miracles. A few weeks before reaching nine years of age, impossible became a daily part of my life as a foster care resident of a Bedford Stuyvesant group home–deep in the heart of Brooklyn.
samples.human_continuation: It belonged to the very powerful Central Brooklyn Coordinating Council (CBCC) of New York City. There weren’t many leisure activities other than a single television that most of the kids fought regularly over. Residents weren’t allowed to leave the premises except to attend school, group trips escorted by staff members, or chauffeured around in vans to fulfill medical appointments. Rather than engaging in squabbles with other kids about which shows to watch (Yo MTV Raps was very popular then), I monopolized a small library of donated books to satisfy my insatiable curiosity about the world. Don’t like ads? Become a supporter and enjoy The Good Men Project ad free I read every book, many of them twice. As a result, I approached one of the group home staffers and kindly requested that they order more books to expand the library in a, “Please sir, can I read some more?” Dickensian way.
samples.ai_continuation_chat:
the CBCC had just begun its grassroots organizing in the neighborhood, and I was too young to understand any of it, but the adults around me whispered about change. What I understood was simpler: there were rules everywhere, and most of them felt like walls.

The group home was strict. Lights out at nine. Meals were served on a schedule that left no room for snacking. But there was one allowance they couldn't control: the small shelf of donated paperbacks in the common room. I read everything on it twice, then three times. Dickens became my escape—tales of orphans surviving against all odds felt less like fiction and more like instruction manuals for my own life.

When I wanted more, I had to fight for it. So I did.

I remember watching Yo MTV Raps on a static-filled television in the rec room, dreaming of a life beyond these beige walls, while clutching a dog-eared copy of Great Expectations. The books kept me breathing. They kept me believing that somewhere, somehow, the impossible was waiting.
samples.ai_continuation_free: That year, the miracles came in small packages—a social worker who actually listened, a judge who asked my name instead of just reading my file number, a volunteer who brought paperback novels on visits and didn't quiz me on what I'd learned. They probably didn't know that those books saved something in me that was actively trying to die. The group home on the corner of that crumbling block had its own rhythm. Lights out at nine, breakfast at seven, counting heads before every meal. But between those rigid hours, I discovered something they couldn't schedule or regulate: I could read anything I wanted, and once I could read, I could imagine myself anywhere but there. By the time I was ten, I'd worn out the spine of every donated book in that building's sparse library. I'd read things way above my grade level—not because I was particularly advanced, but because I had nothing else.
