samples.prefix: It’s presidential election season, so it’s obligatory for all candidates to talk about jobs. You have already heard a lot about jobs being lost to China and Mexico (a strong concern of Donald Trump), jobs being outsourced to low-wage countries or moved to tax havens (so-called “tax inversions” are a Hillary Clinton bugaboo), or jobs eliminated because of Obamacare or high minimum wages (a favorite Ted Cruz line).
samples.human_continuation: You won’t hear many of the points below, however, either because they are too positive, too subtle to capture in a sound bite, or too long-term to worry about now. But if you want the truth about American jobs, you may want to keep reading rather than tuning into a presidential debate or stump speech. Times Are Good It’s hardly a bad time for jobs overall—official unemployment is at the lowest rate since 2008, and applications for unemployment insurance were at the lowest level since 1973. You won’t hear that from the Republican candidates, of course—the news is much too sanguine. If there’s a problem, it is with low labor force participation, which has dropped several percentage points over the last decade. As testimony before a Joint Economic Committee suggests, there are a variety of reasons for this, although an aging population is clearly part of the issue.
samples.ai_continuation_chat: But if you take a step back from the campaign trail and look at the actual numbers, a more nuanced picture emerges. The unemployment rate has hovered near historic lows for years, and the economy has added jobs for a record stretch. Manufacturing, often cited as a victim of trade deals, has actually seen modest gains since the depths of the recession. The real story isn't a jobs crisis in the traditional sense—it's a participation crisis. Too many working-age Americans have simply stopped looking for work, which keeps the unemployment rate artificially low. The labor force participation rate has not fully recovered, and that’s where the policy focus should be. As the Joint Economic Committee has noted, part of this decline is structural, driven by an aging population and retiring Baby Boomers. But there’s also a stubborn slice of prime-age workers who remain on the sidelines, disconnected from opportunities. Fixing that—not scapegoating trade partners—is the genuine challenge for the next president.
samples.ai_continuation_free: But amid all the noise, there’s a quieter, more fundamental shift happening in the American economy that few candidates want to address directly: the nature of work itself is changing. The old bargain—that if you worked hard and stayed loyal to a company, you’d get a stable paycheck, health insurance, and a pension—has been eroding for decades. Today, more than a third of American workers are part of the gig economy, freelancing, contracting, or piecing together multiple part-time jobs just to make ends meet. These workers don’t show up in the monthly jobs report the same way full-time employees do, and their struggles rarely make it into campaign ads. They worry less about a factory moving to China and more about whether they’ll get enough Uber rides this week to cover rent, or whether a sudden illness will wipe out their savings because they have no paid sick leave.

samples.prefix: How Rise of the Tomb Raider is forging a gaming icon. Camilla Luddington is frowning seven different ways. She's an experienced actor, so each frown carries its own nuance and meaning: defiance, confusion, vulnerability, fear. A few days later, some 350 miles north of L.A. in the offices of Tomb Raider developer Crystal Dynamics, Senior Technical Artist Jon Robins leans into his monitor and carefully studies the Luddington footage. "Making a human being is the most challenging thing when creating video games." He notes how light bounces off the ridges on Luddington's forehead, how her eyes move in a slightly different fashion for each frown, how the lines around her eyes transfer to the particulars of her smile, the angle of her cheekbones, the jut of her chin. He imports the images into facial engine models of Lara Croft. The mesh of her face represents thousand of data points.

Around her, a forest of cameras captures 23 distinct points on her face, tracking every micro-movement—the slight twitch of an eyebrow, the tension around eyes, the particular way her lips press together when Lara confronts danger. This data feeds directly into the facial engine models that will bring the character to life. "It's about capturing the soul of the performance," explains Jon Robins, lead character technical director at Crystal Dynamics. "Camilla gives us so much more than expressions—she gives us intent."

The studio has been specifically designed for this purpose, with controlled lighting and precisely calibrated equipment ensuring consistency across thousands of frames of captured data. Each frown, each smile, each moment of pain or determination will be meticulously mapped onto Lara's digital face, creating a heroine who conveys emotion with the subtlety and depth of a real actor. The technology has evolved considerably since earlier iterations.

The original Tomb Raider reboot in 2013 did something remarkable – it made us care about Lara before she became the legend. It showed us her humanity, her fear, her determination to survive against impossible odds. Rise of the Tomb Raider aims to deepen that emotional connection. samples.prefix: “It is something I have got used to since 9/11. From being called Osama Bin Laden to Paki-terrorist I have heard it all,” Zab Mustefa, a British Muslim journalist, who specialises in women's rights and culture, tells me. Since the terrorist attacks on New York City that brought down the twin towers, it seems life has not been the same for Muslims that live in the western world.
samples.human_continuation: Suddenly there was a spotlight shone on Islam when most non-Muslims had barely given it a second thought before. “Either you’re with us. Or you’re with the terrorists,” announced the then president of the USA George W Bush in a sombre tone at a press conference following the attacks. And many people decided that all Muslims were against 'us'. Everything was under scrutiny. Their style of dress, their beliefs, their way of life. People that had never even read the Qu’ran believed they had more knowledge than Islamic scholars. “Look at the way they treat their women!” is a statement that I often hear. “Forcing them to cover up. Not allowing them to go out alone and controlling everything that they do.” “What about Saudi Arabia? They don’t even let women drive!” But it's a false perception. I am not denying that there are countries where the predominant religion is Islam where women are treated badly.
samples.ai_continuation_chat: The immediate aftermath of the tragedy saw President George W. Bush frame the conflict not as a war against Islam, but against terrorism. Yet, despite these reassuring words, the rhetoric quickly shifted. The media’s relentless focus on the Saudi origins of the hijackers created a dangerous conflation between the religion and the actions of a few extremists. Muslims found themselves collectively judged by the worst deeds of their community, stripped of their individuality and reduced to a monolithic, threatening stereotype. The sacred Qu’ran, a text of peace for billions, was suddenly scrutinized through a lens of suspicion, with verses taken out of context to justify hostility. This pervasive atmosphere of fear and misunderstanding did not dissipate with time; instead, it calcified into a systemic bias. For ordinary believers, the burden of proving their loyalty became an exhausting daily reality, as they navigated a society that increasingly viewed their faith through the distorted prism of security threats rather than spiritual conviction.
samples.ai_continuation_free: The shift was not merely political; it was visceral, etched into the daily interactions of ordinary people. Mustefa recalls the sudden weight of her hijab, which transformed from a symbol of personal faith into a target for suspicion and hostility. "You start walking differently," she explains, her voice steady but tinged with a weary resignation. "You become hyper-aware of every glance, every muttered comment. The airport security lines became a theater of humiliation, where your religion was treated as a security risk rather than a matter of conscience." This pervasive atmosphere of fear and mistrust did not just affect those in the public eye; it seeped into workplaces, schools, and neighborhoods, creating a parallel reality where British Muslims felt simultaneously present and profoundly alienated. For Mustefa, continuing her work in journalism became an act of defiance, a way to reclaim the narrative from the monolithic caricatures painted by the media and to highlight the diversity and resilience within her community.

content_constraint.content_direction: It argues that post-9/11 political rhetoric led to widespread scrutiny and false generalizations about Islamic culture, particularly regarding the treatment of women.

I now recommend stack Rationale I’m trying to learn the Haskell programming language, and I’m tripping over the cabal-install package management system sufficiently often that it’s putting me off putting time into learning the language. Here are my requirements for a development environment I’m willing to learn in: don’t leave Debian Wheezy 32-bit; Debian Jessie will be out soon, but its versions of GHC and the Haskell platform are still very old so upgrading early is not a way out.
samples.human_continuation: minimise how often I have to delete all of ~/.cabal and ~/.ghc ; when using cabal sandboxes, again, minimise the number of core libraries that need to get rebuilt in every sandbox; be simple enough to integrate cleanly with the existing ways I manage my OS installation and the contents of my home directory; be simple enough that I can understand everything as a Haskell beginner and can get things working (again) quickly and get back to trying to write Haskell. In this document I will describe the combination of home directory and system-wide installations that fit these requirements, and the workflow for sorting out packages so that I can get on with trying to make my programs do input and output, and other fun Haskell beginner stuff. Alternative approaches The following two approaches don’t satisfy the requirements given above.
samples.ai_continuation_chat: Consequently, the setup must remain entirely within the user’s home directory to avoid conflicts with the system-wide package manager. This isolation is critical because relying on `apt-get` for Haskell libraries often results in version mismatches that break compilation. I require a mechanism that prevents the dreaded "dependency hell," where updating one package necessitates rebuilding half the ecosystem. Cabal sandboxes offer a promising solution by creating isolated environments for each project, ensuring that dependencies are resolved locally rather than globally. This approach minimizes the risk of corrupting the base system while allowing for flexible experimentation. The goal is a stable, reproducible workflow that lets me focus on writing functional code rather than debugging build scripts. Stability is paramount; I cannot afford hours spent resolving circular dependencies or missing libraries every time I open my editor.
samples.ai_continuation_free: I need a setup that is self-contained and doesn't fight me at every turn. Ideally, I want something like GHCup or a similar modern tool that can download and install a recent version of GHC and Cabal directly into my home directory, bypassing the system package manager entirely. This way, I can have a fresh, working environment without needing root access or worrying about the outdated libraries in Wheezy. If that’s not an option, I’m open to using Docker to run a more recent Debian or Ubuntu image with a proper Haskell toolchain, as long as the setup is straightforward and well-documented. I just need to get past the configuration hurdles so I can actually start writing code.

samples.prefix: Anyone who has ever been near a dairy knows that cows can be smelly beasts: they fart and poop constantly, filling the air for miles with the acrid scent of their bowels. For anyone who may find that aroma repulsive, California is on the case. California Gov. Jerry Brown this week signed into law a bill that would place limitations on emissions of greenhouse gasses like methane and black carbon.
samples.human_continuation: Those types of gasses, known collectively as super pollutants, have some of the biggest impacts on global warming but remain in the atmosphere for a much shorter period of time than carbon-dioxide (CO2). The new California law requires the state to approve and begin implementing a strategy to cut super pollutant emissions from dairy, livestock, organic waste and landfills. They must reach a goal that includes a cut of methane emissions by 40 percent, hydrofluorocarbon gases by 40 percent and anthropogenic black carbon by 50 percent below 2013 levels by 2020. Cow farts, for their part, are rich in methane. “Cutting black carbon and other super pollutants is the critical next step in our program to combat climate change,” Brown said Monday in a statement after signing the law.
samples.ai_continuation_chat:
The new legislation sets ambitious targets for reducing these so-called "super pollutants" by 2020. Specifically, it calls for a 40 percent reduction in methane emissions from dairy operations, livestock, and landfills. The law also targets hydrofluorocarbon gases, commonly used in refrigeration and air conditioning, which are thousands of times more potent than carbon dioxide at trapping heat in the atmosphere.

Black carbon, a particulate matter produced by diesel engines and certain industrial processes, will also face stricter regulations under the new framework. Environmental groups have praised the measure as a significant step forward in combating climate change, noting that while carbon dioxide remains the most abundant greenhouse gas, these super pollutants pack a disproportionately powerful punch in the short term. California has long positioned itself as a leader in environmental policy, often enacting standards that eventually become national models.
samples.ai_continuation_free: The legislation, which builds on the state's existing environmental framework, targets agricultural operations as part of California's broader goal to reduce greenhouse gas emissions to 1990 levels by 2020 and to achieve even more ambitious targets in the decades following. Dairy farms and livestock operations are significant contributors to methane emissions, a greenhouse gas that is particularly potent in the short term. The law requires dairy operators and other livestock producers to implement practices that reduce methane output, which can include improvements in manure management, dietary adjustments for cattle, and the adoption of anaerobic digesters that capture methane for energy production. The California Air Resources Board will develop specific regulations and provide guidance to farmers on compliance methods. Supporters of the legislation argue that California, as the nation's leading dairy state, has both the responsibility and the ability to demonstrate that agricultural productivity and environmental stewardship can coexist.

samples.prefix: MOSCOW (Reuters) - Russia’s postal service was hit by Wannacry ransomware last week and some of its computers are still down, three employees in Moscow said, the latest sign of weaknesses that have made the country a major victim of the global extortion campaign. A man walks out of a branch of Russian Post in Moscow, Russia, May 24, 2017.
samples.human_continuation: REUTERS/Maxim Shemetov Wannacry compromised the post office’s automated queue management system, infecting touch-screen terminals which run on the outdated Windows XP operating system, one of the workers said. Terminals were still blank in some parts of Moscow this week but it was not clear exactly how many branches had been affected. A spokesman for Russian Post, a state-owned monopoly, said no computers were infected, but some terminals were temporarily switched off as a precaution. “The virus attack did not touch Russian Post, all systems are working and stable,” he said. Other institutions in Russia have said they were infected by the virus, highlighting Moscow’s readiness to show it too is a frequent victim of cyber crime in the face of allegations from the United States and Europe of state-sponsored hacking.
samples.ai_continuation_chat: The cyberattack specifically targeted legacy systems running Windows XP, an outdated operating system that Russian Post had failed to patch, leaving thousands of terminals vulnerable to the encryption virus. While officials initially downplayed the incident, claiming only minor disruptions, subsequent reports revealed that critical internal networks were paralyzed, forcing staff to resort to manual processing for package tracking and financial transactions. This discrepancy between official statements and on-the-ground reality highlights a broader struggle within Russian institutions to manage digital infrastructure. Unlike many counterparts in the United States and Europe, which had largely migrated away from unsupported Microsoft software, Russian enterprises remained heavily dependent on older, unpatched systems. Consequently, the ransomware exploited these specific technical gaps, causing significant operational delays and raising serious questions about the country’s cybersecurity preparedness against such widespread digital threats.
samples.ai_continuation_free: The employees, who spoke on condition of anonymity due to concerns about repercussions, said that the attack had disrupted internal systems used for tracking parcels and managing employee schedules. They described a chaotic scene in the days following the initial infection, with staff forced to revert to manual processes and paper-based records to keep operations running. While Russian Post officials have acknowledged the incident, they have downplayed its severity, stating that the core logistics network remained largely unaffected and that most services were restored within a few days. However, the persistent downtime on certain administrative terminals suggests that the cleanup effort is more complex than initially reported, highlighting the vulnerability of state-owned enterprises to sophisticated cyber threats. This incident adds to a growing list of Russian institutions, including the Ministry of Internal Affairs and major banks, that have been targeted by the WannaCry malware, underscoring the widespread impact of the attack on the country’s digital infrastructure.

samples.human_continuation: First identified as a tropical storm on August 15, over the central Atlantic Ocean, the hurricane moved northwestward for most of its course, ultimately peaking with maximum sustained winds of 115 mph (185 km/h) and a minimum barometric pressure reading of 952 mbar (hPa; 28.11 inHg). It turned due northward as it approached the U.S. East Coast and struck western Long Island on August 24. It moved inland and quickly deteriorated, degenerating the next day. The storm inflicted severe damage with storm tides as high as 30 ft (9 m). Trees were brought down, houses were demolished, and Hog Island was largely washed away by the cyclone. The flooding inundated low-lying areas, sweeping away homes and infrastructure with terrifying speed. Hog Island, a critical naval training ground, suffered particularly severe damage, with many structures destroyed or rendered uninhabitable by the relentless winds and rising waters. Sailors stationed at the base faced life-threatening conditions as the hurricane’s peak intensity battered the region. The combination of high winds and massive storm surges resulted in significant loss of life and property. This event remains one of the most destructive storms in the area's history, highlighting the vulnerability of coastal communities to such powerful meteorological forces.

Despite warnings issued by the U.S. Weather Bureau, the storm made landfall near Atlantic City, New Jersey, in the early hours of August 24, before tracking directly through New York City. The hurricane struck at night, earning its nickname "Midnight Storm" due to the darkness and suddenness of its arrival. High winds and storm surge devastated the coastal areas of New Jersey and Long Island. samples.prefix: A drawing shows a woman having her arm prepared for minor surgery. (Print by Abraham Bosse via National Library of Medicine) What’s the best way to treat prostate cancer? What are the benefits and risks of different rehabilitation options for survivors of stroke? Unfortunately, the answer to these and similar questions often is: Nobody knows.
samples.human_continuation: The United States spends $3 trillion annually on health care — much of it funded by taxpayers through programs such as Medicare — yet only a limited amount of information exists about what treatments work best for which patients. Although estimates vary, some experts think that less than half of all medical care is based on clear scientific evidence. The good news is that the federal government is now making a significant investment in health services and patient-centered outcomes research to identify waste and improve the safety, effectiveness and quality of care. The bad news is that House Republicans are trying to abolish one of the main agencies carrying out this research, the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ), and cut the funding of another, the Patient-Centered Outcomes Research Institute (PCORI).
samples.ai_continuation_chat: The United States spends roughly $3 trillion annually on healthcare—more than any other nation—yet much of that spending is based on tradition, habit, or the preferences of physicians rather than solid evidence about what actually works best. This paradox exists because the federal investment in comparative effectiveness research has always been modest and frequently under siege. The Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality, which funds studies meant to determine which treatments deliver the best outcomes, has faced repeated attempts by House Republicans to eliminate its funding entirely. The Patient-Centered Outcomes Research Institute, created by the Affordable Care Act to generate practical guidance for patients and doctors, has also been targeted for defunding. Without this research, doctors and patients are left to guess—which treatments are truly superior, which are merely more expensive, and which may cause more harm than good.
samples.ai_continuation_free: This uncertainty isn't due to lack of trying. Thousands of dedicated researchers spend decades studying these very questions. Clinical trials enroll millions of willing participants. Yet the human body remains remarkably complex, and each person responds differently to treatments that might work beautifully for one individual but poorly for another. The reality is that medicine operates in shades of gray rather than clear black and white. A treatment that offers modest benefits for one condition might carry unacceptable risks for another patient with additional health problems. What works for a sixty-year-old man in good overall health may be entirely inappropriate for someone with multiple comorbidities. And the long-term effects of many interventions simply haven't been studied long enough to provide definitive answers. This is why shared decision-making between patients and their healthcare providers has become so important.

samples.prefix: The religious group known as the Blackburn Cult, the Divine Order of the Royal Arms of the Great Eleven, or the Great Eleven Club, was started in 1922 on Bunker Hill in Downtown Los Angeles, California, and later formed a retreat in the Southern California Simi Valley. The group's founder, May Otis Blackburn, is said to have received revelations directly from angels, and, along with her daughter Ruth Wieland Rizzio, believed that she was charged by the archangel Gabriel to write books revealing the mysteries of Heaven and Earth, and life and death.[1][2] Newspaper articles from the period reported strange rituals including the sacrifice of animals, sex scandals and attempts to resurrect a dead 16-year-old girl.[3] Police found the corpse of Willa Rhoads under the floor at the Rhoadses' residence, wrapped in spices and salt, and surrounded by the bodies of seven dead dogs.[2] Mr.
samples.human_continuation: Rhoads later confessed to the police that they had placed their daughter in the tomb fourteen months earlier at the suggestion of May Otis Blackburn.[2] The cult was also accused of killing a member in an oven, poisoning another during a "whirling dervish" ceremony, and making several other members disappear.[4] Indicted for grand theft [ edit ] In 1929, group leaders were indicted in Los Angeles for grand theft and investigated in connection with the disappearances of several members.[1] These indictments created a sensation after the background of the grand theft was revealed to the public.[3] May Otis Blackburn was charged with twelve counts of grand theft, and articles at that time referred to her as a "cult leader".[5] According to Time magazine , the Blackburn Cult was also known as "The Great Eleven", and May Otis Blackburn was referred to as the "Heel of God".[6] The cult collapsed after May Otis Blackburn was imprisoned for stealing 40,000 dollars from Clifford Dabney.[6][7] Depicted in theatrical productions [ edit ] In October 2007, actresses playing May Otis Blackburn and Ruth Rizzio appeared in the Ghost Tour in Strathearn Park, in Simi Valley, California.
samples.ai_continuation_chat:
Rhoads, the girl’s father, claimed she had died of natural causes, but authorities were skeptical given the bizarre circumstances. The investigation unraveled a web of manipulation and extortion, with Blackburn and her inner circle pressuring followers to turn over their life savings and property. Clifford Dabney, a prominent member, later testified that Blackburn had promised him Rhoads would be resurrected if he provided enough funding for rituals and a lavish mausoleum. When the resurrection failed, Dabney went to the police, triggering the cult’s legal downfall.

In 1925, Blackburn, Rizzio, and several key adherents were charged with fraud, conspiracy, and operating a public nuisance. The trial captivated Los Angeles, drawing crowds of spectators eager for details of the cult’s macabre practices. Though Blackburn avoided a murder conviction, the scandal destroyed her influence. She died in obscurity in 1935. Decades later, the cult’s story inspired fictionalized portrayals in novels and films, often emphasizing its mix of apocalyptic prophecy, financial exploitation, and the tragic death of Willa Rhoads—a cautionary tale of charisma and credulity in early 20th-century California.
samples.ai_continuation_free: The investigation into Willa Rhoads' death revealed a deeply disturbing world hidden behind the group's religious facade. According to contemporary reports, the Rhoads family had been members of the cult for years, and Willa herself had been groomed as a "vessel" for spiritual communication. When she died suddenly in 1926, possibly from tuberculosis or complications related to a botched abortion, Blackburn and her followers refused to accept her passing. They believed that by preserving her body and performing specific rituals, they could summon her spirit back and achieve resurrection. The corpse was discovered in a remarkably well-preserved state, thanks to the layers of salt and spices packed around it. The seven dead dogs, arranged in a circle around her, were believed to be sacrificial offerings meant to guard her soul during its journey. Police also found altars adorned with strange symbols, robes stained with animal blood, and journals detailing conversations with angels and instructions for contacting the dead. The cult's retreat in Simi Valley yielded further evidence of animal sacrifices and attempts at necromancy. May Otis Blackburn and Ruth Wieland Rizzio were arrested and charged with murder, though the charges were later reduced to practicing medicine without a license and fraud.

samples.human_continuation: A former employee of Harvey’s, Joseph Cooper, claims to be in possession of tapes of several racial rants and has filed a $20 million lawsuit against Harvey. Cooper says these types of outbursts were commonplace from Harvey. Cooper says that he has 120 hours of recordings from a 20-year span of Harvey’s career, going back to 1993 and his early stand-up days. The Steve Harvey Show, Family Feud, and Little Big Shots draw tens of millions of loyal listeners and viewers on a daily basis. So, with an empire valued at some $100 million, he has much to lose.

But the real bombshell comes from Joseph Cooper, a former employee who worked closely with Harvey for over a decade. Cooper claims he possesses audio and video recordings spanning 20 years that capture Harvey making derogatory remarks about white people, Jewish individuals, and even anti-American statements. The lawsuit, filed for $20 million, alleges that Harvey routinely used his platform—including during his time on *The Steve Harvey Show* and *Little Big Shots*—to spew hateful rhetoric behind closed doors.

Cooper asserts that the tapes include rants from as early as the late 1990s, with Harvey allegedly saying things like, "This country owes us," and mocking American values. samples.prefix: What is the cure for American health care? That is a question that a lot of people are trying to answer, and it’s a highly debated topic, but the answer is plain and simple. Single payer health care is the best form of health care a nation can hope to have. It is efficient, provides quality and timely access to everyone, and it is cost effective.
samples.human_continuation: A single payer health care system is a system in which the government, rather than private insurers, pays for all health costs. The system is funded typically through income taxes and is free at the point of use. Some countries with a single payer system include Canada, the U.K., France, Germany, and Australia. France is often considered to have the best health care system in the world, but a large group of people (including myself) believe the best system is the U.K.’s National Health Service (NHS). This is because of its central and efficient operation, as well as high quality standards, low wait times, and staff quality. To start let’s dismiss some of the common arguments against single payer health care that come from the opposite side, like a single payer system having long wait lists, or that it is very inefficient and expensive.
samples.ai_continuation_chat: Single-payer health care is a system where the government pays for all basic health care costs using money collected from taxpayers. Countries like Canada, the U.K., France, Germany, and Australia all have some form of single-payer health care. These nations provide health coverage to all citizens regardless of their income or employment status. While each system has its strengths and weaknesses, the U.K.'s National Health Service (NHS) stands out as an exceptional example. The NHS provides comprehensive health care to everyone at no direct cost at the point of service, funded through income taxes. This means that whether you need a routine check-up, emergency surgery, or prescription medication, you won't receive a bill. The peace of mind that comes with knowing you and your family are covered no matter what happens is invaluable, and it's something the United States should strive to achieve.
samples.ai_continuation_free: The debate around this issue often becomes polarized, with strong advocates on both sides. Those who support the current system argue that it encourages innovation, gives patients more choice, and allows for competitive pricing among providers. They point to countries like Switzerland and Germany, which have multi-payer systems rather than a pure single-payer approach, as evidence that there are alternatives to both fully socialized medicine and the American model. Critics of single-payer systems often raise concerns about wait times, potential tax increases, and the government's role in making medical decisions. In countries like Canada and the UK, patients sometimes face lengthy waits for elective procedures, and there are ongoing debates about how to balance universal access with maintaining high-quality care. That said, the American system does face real challenges. Medical costs continue to rise, millions remain uninsured or underinsured, and navigating insurance paperwork can be a nightmare for patients.

samples.prefix: Sherwood Lollar et al. A scientist takes a sample of water from a mine deep underground in Ontario, Canada. The water turned out to be 2.6 billion years old, the oldest known water on Earth. By Charles Q. Choi LiveScience A pocket of water some 2.6 billion years old — the most ancient pocket of water known by far, older even than the dawn of multicellular life — has now been discovered in a mine 2 miles below the Earth's surface.
samples.human_continuation: The finding, announced in the May 16 issue of the journal Nature, raises the tantalizing possibility that ancient life might be found deep underground not only within Earth, but in similar oases that may exist on Mars, the scientists who studied the water said. Geoscientist Barbara Sherwood Lollar at the University of Toronto and her colleagues have investigated deep mines across the world since the 1980s. Water can flow into fractures in rocks and become isolated deep in the crust for many years, serving as a time capsule of what their environments were like at the time they were sealed off. In gold mines in South Africa 1.7 miles (2.8 kilometers) deep, the scientists previously discovered microbes could survive in pockets of waterisolated for tens of millions of years.
samples.ai_continuation_chat: This groundbreaking discovery, published in the prestigious journal Nature, challenges previous assumptions about the longevity of subterranean aquifers. Led by Sherwood Lollar from the University of Toronto, the research team analyzed fluid samples from the Kidd Creek Mine in South Africa, revealing isotopic signatures consistent with ancient precipitation. The extreme age of this water implies that isolated, stable environments have persisted for billions of years, potentially shielding primitive microbes from surface cataclysms. If such resilient ecosystems thrived here, similar conditions might have existed on Mars. The red planet’s ancient subsurface could harbor dormant microbial life, preserved in similar deep aquifers, offering a compelling target for future astrobiological exploration and the search for extraterrestrial life beyond our pale blue dot.
samples.ai_continuation_free: The discovery, led by Sherwood Lollar of the University of Waterloo, challenges long-held assumptions about the Earth’s hydrological history and the potential for life in extreme environments. Located in a gold mine in Sudbury, Ontario, the water was trapped in fractures within the bedrock, isolated from the surface for billions of years. Analysis revealed that the water is not only ancient but also chemically distinct, containing high levels of hydrogen and methane produced by the radioactive decay of uranium in the surrounding rock. This process, known as radiolysis, suggests that such deep underground aquifers could potentially support microbial life independent of sunlight, relying instead on chemical energy derived from the Earth’s crust. The findings imply that the subsurface biosphere may be far more extensive and ancient than previously thought, offering new insights into the origins of life and the possibility of extraterrestrial life in similar subsurface environments on other planets.

samples.prefix: FC Dallas travel to Denver this Friday to face the Colorado Rapids in a rematch of the match no one will forget this year. The last time these teams faced off, Colorado picked FC Dallas apart piece by piece and went on to score four goals in a 4-0 romping, the worst loss for FC Dallas in the Oscar Pareja era. It was a loss that made this FC Dallas team much more focused, and motivated, which we saw in the match against Toronto.
samples.human_continuation: This week could also mark the return of Mauro Diaz, which could change Colorado’s game plan heading into this Friday’s match. The biggest thing we saw during the last match against Colorado was that the Rapids knew exactly what FC Dallas were going to do, and stuck to their guns to shut down Dallas. After the quick goal Colorado got from Dominique Badji, all they had to do was see out their game plan. The plan was to force FC Dallas into the middle and never effectively use Fabian Castillo or Ryan Hollingshead. When you do not have the passing prowess of Mauro Diaz in the midfield, which Dallas did not have against Colorado the first time, it can be troubling. There was no one there to play cutting through balls through the middle of the backline. The plan was very effective, as no one on this FC Dallas team has quite the vision that Diaz has and it was apparent as they could not find the open outside pass.
samples.ai_continuation_chat: Now, the focus shifts to the potential return of Mauro Diaz, a development that could significantly alter the tactical landscape for this crucial encounter. Diaz’s presence offers a dynamic alternative to the current attacking setup, providing pace and unpredictability that the Rapids’ defense struggled to contain in previous meetings. If fit, his reintroduction alongside Dominique Badji could create a formidable partnership, forcing Colorado to adjust their marking schemes and potentially opening up spaces for Fabian Castillo to exploit on the wing. The strategic flexibility Diaz brings allows Oscar Pareja to mix and match formations, keeping the opposition guessing rather than relying on a predictable pattern. Furthermore, Diaz’s experience in high-pressure matches could be invaluable in stabilizing the midfield transition, allowing Ryan Hollingshead to focus more on defensive solidity and ball distribution. For FC Dallas, this isn’t just about redemption; it’s about leveraging every available tool to dismantle a team that previously held them in contempt. The psychological boost of having their star forward back in the fold cannot be underestimated, as it signals a renewed sense of confidence and unity within the squad.
samples.ai_continuation_free: That resilience against Toronto served as a vital reset button, proving that the sting of the Denver defeat didn’t break their spirit but rather sharpened it. Now, returning to Dick’s Sporting Goods Park, the stakes feel significantly higher for both sides. For Colorado, there is an opportunity to validate their dominance from the first meeting and solidify their standing in the Western Conference. For FC Dallas, it is a chance for redemption, to show that the 4-0 drubbing was an anomaly rather than a trend, and to demonstrate that they can compete at a high level even away from Toyota Stadium. The tactical adjustments Pareja makes this time around will be critical, particularly in how he addresses the defensive vulnerabilities that were so brutally exposed last time out. Expect a more disciplined, structured approach from the Blues, one that prioritizes compactness and quick transitions to neutralize Colorado’s attacking flair. The atmosphere in Denver will be electric, fueled by the memory of that comprehensive victory, but FC Dallas knows that to move forward, they must first look backward and correct the mistakes that led to such a humiliating result.

samples.prefix: According to some of the most popular dating advice books, one of the keys to attracting a romantic partner is to take the somewhat counterintuitive step of pretending like you aren’t interested in the other person. But does this tactic really work? Can “playing hard to get” really help you score a date? According to a new set of studies published in the European Journal of Personality, it would appear so.
samples.human_continuation: In one of these studies, researchers gave 270 heterosexual college students three dating profiles that were equivalent in terms of attractiveness, age, and background information [1]. The only thing that differed was the likelihood that the person would go out with someone they had just met (i.e., the target was described as having either low, intermediate, or high availability). Participants were asked to choose which person they would be most likely to have casual sex with, which one they would be most likely to date, and which one they would be most likely to start a romantic relationship with. Participants could choose the same or different persons for each option. When it came to casual sex, both men and women overwhelming preferred the highly available target. So, if you’re hoping to get lucky, playing hard to get is not particularly advantageous.
samples.ai_continuation_chat: However, the reality is far more nuanced than simple advice columns suggest. The researchers conducted experiments involving heterosexual college students who evaluated potential partners based on varying levels of availability. Participants were shown dating profiles that explicitly stated how interested the target was in casual sex versus long-term commitment. The results were striking: when the goal was casual sex, participants overwhelmingly preferred targets who were highly available and explicitly interested. Playing hard to get actually backfired, significantly reducing the likelihood of being chosen for a casual encounter. This challenges the traditional belief that scarcity increases desire in short-term mating contexts. Instead, ease of access appears to be the primary driver for casual arrangements. The study suggests that if one is seeking a fling, honesty and availability are far more effective strategies than feigned disinterest or strategic withholding.
samples.ai_continuation_free: Research led by psychologist Andrew Thomas and his colleagues suggests that while people generally believe playing hard to get is ineffective, it actually boosts romantic interest in specific contexts. The studies, which involved over 1,000 participants, found that individuals perceived as difficult to pursue were rated as more attractive and desirable than those who were easily accessible. However, this effect was not universal; it primarily worked when the target of affection was already seen as high-status or valuable. In these cases, the effort required to win their affection signaled that the person was worth pursuing, thereby increasing their perceived worth. Conversely, if someone was already viewed as low-status or uninteresting, playing hard to get backfired, making them seem even less desirable. This nuance highlights that the tactic relies heavily on initial impressions and social status, rather than being a one-size-fits-all strategy for romance.

samples.prefix: As Vogue celebrates its 125th year, we look back at the history of fashion, and the magazine, in a series of “five points” videos by decade, narrated by the stylish Sarah Jessica Parker. 1930–1939The flapper was a casualty of the stock market crash of 1929. Out of her ashes rose the femme fatale. At night she was a modern Diana in figure-molding bias-cut satins that oozed to the floor.
samples.human_continuation: By day, she might play with a Surrealist as served up by Elsa Schiaparelli. Then war came, and removed frivolity from fashion. THE LONG RUNHemlines were lengthening before the Great Crash of 1929; they fell to the floor after that debacle and stayed there for quite a while. There was nothing prim about these sweeping hems, however. The abbreviated silhouette was traded for a long, sculptural one built along classic lines that emphasized the figure within the frock. Madeleine Vionnet’s diagonal bias-cutting technique resulted in dresses that were sensuously molded to the body. Such perfection as not easily come by; “simplicity,” noted Vogue, “is a complex art.” LOVE SCHIAPEven more complicated was the kismet that brought Prince Edward into the orbit of an American divorcée named Wallis Simpson, for whom he’d abandon his throne and be exiled from his sceptered isle.
samples.ai_continuation_chat: By day, the silhouette softened into practical yet chic separates, reflecting a world adjusting to economic hardship. While Madeleine Vionnet perfected the art of bias-cutting, allowing fabric to drape naturally over the body, Elsa Schiaparelli injected a dose of Surrealist whimsy into the scene. Her collaborations with artists like Salvador Dalí produced shocking pink hues and trompe-l'œil details, challenging the prevailing elegance with intellectual provocation. Yet, amidst these sartorial innovations, a scandal of epic proportions threatened to upend the British monarchy. Wallis Simpson, an American divorcée with impeccable style, captured the heart of Prince Edward, the future King Edward VIII. Her preference for tailored, understated American elegance over royal regalia became symbolic of her independence. The ensuing crisis, often dubbed the "love of the century," forced the Prince to abdicate his throne, proving that fashion and personal desire could indeed rewrite history.

content_constraint.topic: The continuation details the evolution of 1930s fashion from Surrealist influences to bias-cut elegance and introduces the Wallis Simpson scandal.
content_constraint.content_direction: It explains how war and economic shifts influenced hemlines and silhouettes, highlighting specific designers' techniques before pivoting to a major historical romance.
content_constraint.scope: The text covers the transition from daywear to long hems, the technical artistry of Vionnet, and the beginning of the Edward VIII abdication crisis.

samples.prefix: The battle over marriage equality in Iowa is heating up as Republicans in the State House are moving forward with plans to ban gay marriage and civil unions, an attempt to reverse a unanimous 2009 State Supreme Court decision in favor of marriage equality. To amend the constitution, “an amendment would require approval by state lawmakers during two legislative sessions, and then approval by voters at the ballot box.” Encouraged by major Republican gains in the midterm elections and the removal of three pro-equality Justices through retention votes, Iowa Republicans have emphasized restrictions on gay-rights and reproductive-rights in their legislative agenda, and Religious Right leader Bob Vander Plaats is pressing for the removal of the entire Supreme Court.
samples.human_continuation: Vander Plaats’s new organization, The Family Leader, recently blasted pro-equality faith leaders in an alert message that questions their faith, stating: “167 ‘religious’ leaders signed a letter delivered to the Iowa Legislature saying that people of faith support homosexual ‘marriage.’ Don’t stay silent while others speak for you and misrepresnt [sic] God.” The group calls on pastors to sign an alternative petition which describes “homosexual behavior” as “immoral and sinful” and “harmful both to the individuals who choose to participate in it and the society that chooses to accept it.” The mobilization of pastors by The Family Leader comes at a time when, according to the Des Moines Register, Republican leaders are trying to prohibit not only gay marriage but also other forms of legal rights for gay couples such as civil unions and domestic partnerships.
samples.ai_continuation_chat: Vander Plaats, president of The Family Leader, has been rallying faith leaders across the state, urging them to pressure lawmakers into prioritizing the constitutional amendment. He argues that the 2009 ruling overstepped judicial authority and imposed a secular agenda on Iowans of faith. In recent weeks, Vander Plaats has held private meetings with pastors in key districts, framing the issue as a moral imperative. Meanwhile, the Des Moines Register has editorialized against the effort, warning that such a move would damage Iowa's reputation and economy. Republican leaders remain divided, with some cautioning that a full-scale assault on marriage rights could alienate moderate voters in the 2022 elections. Despite internal tensions, Vander Plaats shows no signs of backing down, insisting that now is the moment to act.
samples.ai_continuation_free:
But opponents of the measure are mobilizing. One Iowa, the state’s largest LGBTQ advocacy group, has launched a public awareness campaign highlighting the personal stories of same-sex couples and their families. "Iowans value fairness and freedom," said executive director Courtney Reyes. "They don't want politicians interfering in personal decisions about love and commitment." The group is also working with local businesses and faith leaders who support marriage equality, hoping to counter the well-funded efforts of national conservative organizations pouring money into the state.

Meanwhile, legal experts question whether a constitutional ban would even withstand federal scrutiny, given the U.S. Supreme Court's 2015 Obergefell ruling. But state Representative Steven Holt, a primary sponsor of the amendment, argues that the issue should be decided by the people, not judges. "We believe Iowans have the right to define marriage through their elected representatives," he said. The fight is expected to intensify as the legislative session progresses, with both sides preparing for a long and costly battle.

content_constraint.scope: Covers the group's alert message, alternative petition, and the broader Republican effort to ban gay marriage, civil unions, and domestic partnerships.

samples.prefix: Entire neighbourhoods of Fort McMurray were under water on Sunday, less than three months after a fire roared into the northern Alberta city and destroyed one-tenth of its buildings. Residents of Canada's oil sands capital are wondering what will come next. They've lived through the rushed evacuation of more than 80,000 people and a wildfire that broke records in how aggressively it pressed forward – as well as years of heavy job losses and plunging profits because of oil prices that have stayed low far longer than most expected.
samples.human_continuation: "There was just an incredulous feeling as people were like, 'Are you kidding?' They aren't too upset, they're just shrugging their shoulders at this point," said Tany Yao, the MLA for Fort McMurray-Wood Buffalo. Story continues below advertisement GLOBE ARCHIVES: A week in Hell: How Fort McMurray burned At least 37 homes were flooded on Sunday when 85 millimetres of rain fell on Fort McMurray in two hours. Some residents of the city water-skied through areas that had been on fire on May 3. The flooding caused the area's emergency operations centre to be activated for the first time since the wildfire. "It's important that our community continues to be resilient and work together," Chris Graham, Fort McMurray's deputy director of emergency management, said in a statement. As crews pumped water from flooded areas, ash was dusted off barricades so they could be put to use keeping motorists away from waterlogged roads.
samples.ai_continuation_chat:
Tany Yao, the assembly member for Fort McMurray-Wood Buffalo, stood amid the rising waters and tried to make sense of it all. "This community has been through so much," he said, shaking his head. "You almost have to laugh to keep from crying."

Chris Graham, a longtime resident who had already lost his home in the wildfire, watched the floodwaters creep toward what remained of his property. "I thought we hit rock bottom in May," he said. "I was wrong."

The flooding, caused by heavy rainfall that overwhelmed the region's drainage systems, added another layer of trauma to a community still picking through the ashes. For many, the twin disasters felt like a cruel joke – as if the wildfire hadn't taken enough.

"We're resilient people," said one resident who declined to give her name. "But I'm tired. We're all tired."

Officials warned that the full scope of the damage was still unknown, but early estimates suggested millions of dollars in additional losses.
samples.ai_continuation_free: The flooding, caused by ice jam on the Clearwater River, hit neighbourhoods including Beacon Hill, Waterways, and Thickwood — some of the same areas that survived the May wildfire that forced the largest evacuation in Canadian history. Water levels rose rapidly overnight, flooding homes and forcing rescuers to evacuate residents by boat. Provincial emergency officials declared a local state of emergency as images emerged of submerged vehicles and water reaching the doorsteps of houses that had only just been cleared of wildfire ash. The double disaster has left many residents questioning whether the community can ever fully recover. "We just got back into our homes in September," said one Waterways resident who declined to give her name. "Now this." Insurance adjusters, already overwhelmed from the wildfire claims, now face another round of damage assessments. Premier Rachel Notley toured the affected areas on Sunday, promising provincial assistance. "The resilience of Fort McMurray has been tested repeatedly," she told reporters.

samples.prefix: The Samsung Group is a South Korea-based conglomerate company that includes a number of subsidiaries. It's one of the largest businesses in Korea, producing nearly one-fifth of the country’s total exports with a primary focus in the electronics, heavy industry, construction, and defense industries. Other major subsidiaries of Samsung include insurance, advertising, and entertainment industry businesses.
samples.human_continuation: Samsung History With only 30,000 won (about $27 USD), Lee Byung-chull started Samsung on March 1 in 1938, as a trading company based in Taegu, Korea. The small company of only 40 employees started as a grocery store, trading and exporting goods produced in and around the city, like dried Korean fish and vegetables, as well as its own noodles. The company grew and soon expanded to Seoul in 1947 but left once the Korean War broke out. After the war, Lee started a sugar refinery in Busan that was called Cheil Jedang, before expanding into textiles and building the (then) largest woolen mill in Korea. The successful diversification became a growth strategy for Samsung, which rapidly expanded into the insurance, securities, and retail business. Samsung was focused on the redevelopment of Korea after the war with a central focus on industrialization.
samples.ai_continuation_chat: The story of Samsung begins in 1938, when Lee Byung-chull founded a small trading company in the city of Daegu. Initially, the company focused on exporting dried fish, vegetables, and fruit to Manchuria and Beijing. The name "Samsung" means "three stars" in Korean, reflecting Lee’s ambition and vision for the business. Within a decade, Lee relocated the headquarters to Seoul and diversified into manufacturing, establishing Cheil Jedang, a sugar refinery in Busan, in 1953. This move marked Samsung’s transition from a modest trading firm into an industrial powerhouse. The post-Korean War era saw rapid expansion into textiles, insurance, and retail, laying the groundwork for the sprawling conglomerate known today. By the 1960s, Samsung had entered the electronics and heavy industries sectors, setting the stage for its global dominance.
samples.ai_continuation_free: Samsung's influence extends deeply into the daily lives of South Koreans, from the smartphones in their pockets to the hospitals they visit and the apartments they live in. The group's flagship subsidiary, Samsung Electronics, is a global leader in semiconductors, smartphones, and televisions, competing directly with Apple and Intel. Meanwhile, Samsung Heavy Industries is one of the world's largest shipbuilders, constructing massive container ships and offshore drilling rigs. The construction arm, Samsung C&T, built the iconic Burj Khalifa in Dubai and the Petronas Towers in Kuala Lumpur. This vertical integration allows the group to control entire supply chains, from raw materials to finished products, giving it a formidable competitive advantage. However, such immense power has also attracted scrutiny, with Samsung facing legal challenges and public criticism over issues ranging from political corruption to labor practices. Despite these controversies, the group remains a symbol of South Korea's economic miracle, driving innovation and shaping the nation's global reputation as a technological powerhouse.

content_constraint.scope: Covers Samsung's history from its founding to its post-Korean War expansion into multiple industries, ending with its focus on Korea's redevelopment and industrialization.

samples.human_continuation: 'We're the victims here' - Longboat Quay residents face eviction unless they cover €4m repair bill for fire safety failings Around 900 people live in the 299 apartments in the Longboat Quay complex by the Dublin docklands. Residents of the apartments on Sir John Rogerson's Quay were left horrified when they were told last night owners would have to pay between €9,300 to €18,000 depending on the size of their apartment. “I was asked to pay €18,000 and I told the chap last night I wouldn’t be paying it – I haven’t got that kind of money,” one resident told RTE’s Six One News. In recent weeks, an independent inspection revealed that the building’s fire safety systems, including alarms, sprinklers, and emergency exits, were dangerously inadequate. America's first beer gardens appeared in the nineteenth century, courtesy of a wave of German immigrants. samples.prefix: The following is an interview that will appear in the book How to Prove God Does Not Exist by Trevor Treharne, to be released in September by Universal Publishers. What is the fundamental conflict between science and religion? Is it one that will never be resolved? The two have opposing views on what constitutes reality. Science finds no need to include any substance beside matter in order to describe our observations of the world.
samples.human_continuation: Religion holds that there is a world beyond matter. Religion claims it has a way of obtaining knowledge that is separate from the scientific method of observation and experiment. The religious believe that we have an inner faculty of some sort that enables us to learn about the world, the universe, and reality without such observation. It is hard to see the two ever resolving this conflict. One of your more recent books, The Fallacy of Fine-Tuning, is certainly a timely one based on how common that argument is currently proving. What is your summary on what is wrong with the fine-tuning arguments? As I have said before, the universe is not fine-tuned for us--we are fine-tuned to the universe. I claim that the statements made about fine-tuning are not accurate. When theists talk about something being fine-tuned to one part in ten or a hundred orders of magnitude, they are simply incorrect.
samples.ai_continuation_chat:
Religion, by contrast, insists that there is more to reality than mere matter—a spiritual dimension, a divine purpose, or an ultimate meaning that transcends physical laws. This is not a trivial disagreement over details; it is a clash about the very nature of knowledge itself. Science relies on empirical evidence, testable hypotheses, and peer review, while religion often appeals to revelation, faith, and sacred texts. These epistemologies are fundamentally incompatible, and no amount of diplomatic hand-waving will make them fit.

One popular attempt to reconcile them is the fine-tuning argument, which claims that the universe’s physical constants appear so precisely set for life that they must have been designed by a creator. But this is what I call The Fallacy of Fine-Tuning. It assumes that the universe had to produce life, when in fact we have no basis to judge what a "typical" universe would look like. We exist in this one, so of course we find it hospitable. That is no more evidence of design than a puddle marveling at how perfectly the hole fits its shape.
samples.ai_continuation_free: Religion, on the other hand, insists that there is an additional, non-material dimension—often called the soul, spirit, or divine presence—that is essential to understanding existence, purpose, and morality. This isn’t a minor disagreement; it’s a clash over the very nature of evidence and truth. Science relies on empirical, repeatable, and testable data. Religion often appeals to revelation, faith, and personal experience, which are inherently subjective and resistant to external verification. So, can this conflict ever be resolved? I doubt it, at least not in a way that fully satisfies both sides. For a resolution to occur, one would have to concede its foundational assumptions—science would have to accept non-material explanations without evidence, or religion would have to abandon its core claims to the supernatural. History suggests neither is willing to do so. Instead, we see attempts at reconciliation, like deism or the idea of a “God of the gaps,” but these often feel like compromises that dilute the rigor of science or the conviction of faith. The conflict persists because it’s rooted in how we define reality itself.

But the elephant couldn’t see which bucket she put the fruit in. “I actually checked that from elephant height,” Ms. Smet then brought the buckets out from behind the screen and stood between them. She pointed at the one with the fruit inside, and the handler walked the elephant toward the buckets. Smet noted which bucket it stuck its trunk in first. At Wild Horizons, Smet worked with elephants that were already accustomed to human handlers, making the logistics more manageable. Smet would then point decisively at the bucket hiding the treats, holding her gesture until the elephant made its choice.

The results were striking. Unlike dogs, who reliably follow pointing gestures from a young age, the elephants showed no initial understanding of what Smet was communicating. However, when Smet modified the test to use a different gesture—one that involved her entire body leaning toward the correct bucket—the elephants performed significantly better. samples.ai_continuation_free: At the wildlife sanctuary, Smet worked with a group of African elephants that were already habituated to human presence—crucial for obtaining reliable results. The expectation was that if elephants possessed similar social cognitive abilities, they should do the same. The results surprised even the researchers. The elephants consistently failed the standard pointing test. They showed no ability to interpret human gestures to find food, even when the experimenter pointed emphatically and directly at the correct bucket. This was puzzling because elephants are highly social animals with complex communication systems of their own—they use infrasound to communicate over vast distances and recognize hundreds of individual voices. Byrne and his colleagues didn't simply conclude that elephants were cognitively inferior to dogs.

Alliance, meanwhile, suffered from what appears to be a severe case of mid-season burnout. The CLG prediction was my biggest miss though. I had them pegged as a safe win based on their week 7 showing, but they came out completely flat. That's the problem with reactive analysis - by the time you identify a trend, the teams have already adjusted or plateaued. samples.prefix: The view from Mount Sunflower, Kansas’s highest elevation. (Image: CC0) Geographer Jerry Dobson had barely started his new job at the University of Kansas when a realization hit. Whenever he told friends and colleagues about his gig, people would smile, congratulate him, the works. But then, almost inevitably, they’d make some crack about his new home state: specifically, how flat it was.
samples.human_continuation: Over his years-long tenure, this did not change. “Everytime you meet someone, they say it—and it’s not true,” he says. “I always looked around and saw hills.” But Dobson is a geographer, able to translate this frustration into motivation. A few years ago, he and his colleague Joshua Campbell—a born and raised Kansan—undertook a project. They set out to measure the flatness of every state in the union, using an algorithm designed to calculate how flat each one looks from different points in its interior—what Campbell calls “that feeling of total flatness.” When they got the results back, Kansas was in a respectable seventh, behind Delaware, North Dakota, and the clear winner, Florida. Since then, Dobson and Campbell have toured their results around, using them to argue against the flat-Kansas mythology.
samples.ai_continuation_chat: The jokes wore on him. Finally, Dobson decided to settle the matter with data. He teamed up with colleague Joshua Campbell, and together they set out to measure just how flat each state truly is. Their method was straightforward: they calculated what percentage of each state could be considered perfectly flat, with no significant elevation change. The results surprised almost everyone. Kansas, it turned out, wasn't even the flattest state. It came in at number seven. The title of flattest went to Florida, with Delaware following close behind. The findings were published, and suddenly Dobson had the perfect response to every flat Kansas joke. He could simply point to the numbers. The data spoke for itself, and Kansas's reputation—though not entirely undeserved—needed serious recalibrating.
samples.ai_continuation_free: But Dobson knew something most people don't: Kansas isn't actually flat. It's a myth, a persistent one, but a myth nonetheless. As a professional geographer, he made it his mission to set the record straight. The truth is, Kansas has hills, valleys, and surprisingly varied terrain. The eastern part of the state, where Lawrence and Kansas City sit, is far from flat—rolling hills and timberlands dominate the landscape. Even the western two-thirds, while generally flatter than the east, contains significant topography. The Smoky Hills region, for instance, rises dramatically in north-central Kansas, with peaks reaching over 2,400 feet. The Cimarron Breaks in the southwest offer rugged canyon country that would surprise anyone expecting a pancake. And then there's Mount Sunflower itself. At 4,039 feet above sea level, it's the highest point in Kansas—ironically named for the state flower despite being barely more than a gentle swell in the landscape compared to Colorado's towering fourteeners.

samples.prefix: Arctic Methane Emissions ‘Certain to Trigger Warming’ As climate change melts Arctic permafrost and releases large amounts of methane into the atmosphere, it is creating a feedback loop that is “certain to trigger additional warming,” according to the lead scientist of a new study investigating Arctic methane emissions.
samples.human_continuation: The study released this week examined 71 wetlands across the globe and found that melting permafrost is creating wetlands known as fens, which are unexpectedly emitting large quantities of methane. Over a 100-year timeframe, methane is about 35 times as potent as a climate change-driving greenhouse gas than carbon dioxide, and over 20 years, it's 84 times more potent. Permafrost terraces in Alaska. Credit: U.S. Fish and Wildife Service Alaska/flickr Methane emissions come from agriculture, fossil fuel production and microbes in wetland soils, among other sources. The study says scientists have assumed that methane emissions from wetlands are high in the tropics, but not necessarily in the Arctic because of the cold temperatures there.
samples.ai_continuation_chat: Previously, scientists assumed that the frigid Arctic temperatures would naturally suppress microbial activity, thereby limiting the production of potent greenhouse gases. However, this groundbreaking research demonstrates that thawing ground is rapidly transforming dry tundra into waterlogged wetlands known as fens. These newly formed ecosystems become significant sources of both methane and carbon dioxide, as ancient organic matter decomposes in oxygen-poor conditions. The study highlights that these methane-emitting fens are expanding faster than predicted, challenging long-held beliefs about cold-climate carbon cycles. Consequently, the Arctic is shifting from a carbon sink to a source, accelerating global warming and threatening to destabilize climate models that underestimated these critical feedback mechanisms.
samples.ai_continuation_free: The research, published in the journal *Nature Communications*, highlights that the thawing of ancient organic matter in the soil is releasing methane at rates significantly higher than previously estimated. Unlike carbon dioxide, methane is a far more potent greenhouse gas, trapping heat in the atmosphere with nearly 80 times the efficiency of CO2 over a 20-year period. This rapid release creates a self-reinforcing cycle: as temperatures rise, more permafrost melts, which in turn releases more methane, further accelerating global warming. The lead author emphasized that while the exact magnitude of future emissions remains uncertain due to complex local variables, the direction of the trend is undeniable.

samples.prefix: In the conservative commentariat and intellectual classes, the deal with the devil that is Trumpism seems increasingly complete. Stalwart conservatives who for years—in some cases decades—defended the principles of limited government, personal liberty, and strict adherence to the Constitution have hiked their skirts and dropped their panties, swooning as Big Donnie Trump talks dirty to the media.
samples.human_continuation: In a depressing twist, many members of my party and ideological persuasion have become advocates for Donald Trump on a scale that ranges from grudging to toadying, for a simple reason that seems to overwhelm all other factors: He attacks the media. Many are willing to forgive almost any sin because of it. All it took to break the spirit of far too many in the conservative class was for Trump to leaven his deranged, autocratic rantings with “fake news” and “duh librul media” bait to compromise the ideals and credibility of a large swath of the conservative firmament. People who think of themselves as being smarter than the average bag of hammers are missing that they’re the just the latest victims of the Trump Con. We now routinely see a formulation something like this:, “Well, Trump isn't perfect, but at least he's attacking the media.” It's the haute-bourgeois pleasure of watching someone else to do your dueling.
samples.ai_continuation_chat: But what exactly have they gained from this Faustian bargain? The answer, depressingly, seems to be little more than the pleasure of watching the media squirm. For a certain breed of conservative, Trump's willingness to call journalists "enemies of the people" and dismiss unfavorable coverage as "fake news" has become the overriding measure of his worth. Never mind that his administration has expanded the federal budget, trampled on federalism, or casually discarded constitutional norms—sins that would have earned any Democrat eternal opprobrium. The media criticism is the hook, the primary satisfaction, the intellectual comfort blanket that allows them to sleep soundly despite the betrayals accumulating around them. This is not conservatism; it is a political crush reducible to one man's willingness to say what they longing to hear about the press. It is the laziest form of ideological identity—a stance that requires no principles, only enemies.
samples.ai_continuation_free: The transformation has been remarkable to observe. Men who once lectured audiences about the dangers of executive overreach, who wrote erudite essays about the importance of institutional norms, who championed free trade and foreign policy restraint—all now find themselves defending a man who has repeatedly demonstrated contempt for these very principles. The cognitive dissonance required to square this circle appears to cause them no discomfort whatsoever. What makes this particularly striking is not merely the abandonment of principle, but the enthusiastic manner in which it's been abandoned. These are not reluctant converts, dragged kicking and screaming into the MAGA tent. They arrive with fanfare, ready to spin the most obvious contradictions into somehow consistent worldview. A man who once advocated for eminent domain to seize private property for his own development projects is now the champion of property rights. A serial adulterer who paid hush money to cover up affairs becomes the defender of traditional family values. A man who borrowed heavily from foreign banks and did business with hostile regimes is now the foreign policy realist.

samples.prefix: America may be one of the richest countries in the world, but its people are less healthy and more likely to die early from disease or accidents than those in any other affluent country, a damning official US report has found. samples.human_continuation: "We were struck by the gravity of these findings," said Steven H Woolf, professor of family medicine at Virginia Commonwealth University in Richmond and chair of the panel that wrote the report. "Americans are dying and suffering at rates that we know are unnecessary because people in other high-income countries are living longer lives and enjoying better health. What really concerns our panel is why, for decades, we have been slipping behind." The report, US Health in International Perspective: Shorter Lives, Poorer Health, was commissioned by the National Institutes of Health. It compares the US with 16 affluent democracies, including Australia, Canada and Japan and many in Europe including Britain. There have been similar findings from the Commonwealth Fund over some years, but they have compared the US with only a handful of nations.

"Americans are dying and suffering from disease and injuries at rates that are demonstrably worse than our peers."

The findings revealed a troubling pattern: US life expectancy lags behind nearly all other high-income nations, with Americans dying younger from causes ranging from heart disease to homicide. The report, funded by the National Institutes of Health and the Commonwealth Fund, documented how this health gap has persisted for decades despite the US spending far more on healthcare per person than any other country. samples.prefix: Most of us can't fully succumb to our techno-lust until we've seen a finished gadget in use. Here's the dirty secret, though – none of your perverted fantasies about multiple-touchscreen smartphones can be realized until someone makes a dual-core chip that would know what to do with them. Samsung's new Orion 1-GHz dual-core ARM microprocessor could make those kinky dreams come true.
samples.human_continuation: Samsung announced the new chip in a press release earlier this week; it will be pushed out to "select customers in the fourth quarter of 2010" and go into "mass production in the first half of 2011." So what's the big deal? We've had dual-core processors in our laptops for years! Ah, but those processors are way too big and power-hungry for mobile standards. You don't want to strap your laptop's battery to your phone, do you? By necessity, mobile chips are all about small size and low power-consumptions. That's why IBM's working on mobile chips with super-sleep modes and Intel just went ahead and bought smartphone chipmaker Infineon just to get in the game, as Gadget Lab reported last week. But wait – haven't Qualcomm and Texas Instruments already announced their dual-core processors for mobile devices? And didn't LG even announce that they're going to start packing graphics champ NVidia's Tegra 2 dual-core processor into smartphones?
samples.ai_continuation_chat:
Samsung's new Orion 1-GHz dual-core ARM microprocessor could make those kinky dreams come true.

The Orion is built on ARM's Cortex-A9 architecture, which is a significant leap from the Cortex-A8 chips found in the current generation of smartphones. Samsung claims the Orion will offer five times the performance of its previous chips while consuming the same amount of power. That's the kind of efficiency that makes gadget enthusiasts weak in the knees.

But here's what really gets the tech press hot and bothered: the Orion is reportedly more powerful than an Intel Atom-based netbook. Yes, you read that correctly. A smartphone chip outperforming a laptop processor. The implications are staggering – we're talking about handheld devices that could eventually replace your notebook for everyday tasks.

Samsung isn't alone in this race, of course. Infineon, Qualcomm, and Texas Instruments are all chasing similar goals, while LG has partnered with Nvidia to develop the Tegra 2 chip. But with Orion, Samsung appears to be pulling ahead of the pack, potentially giving manufacturers like itself a decisive edge in the upcoming smartphone wars.
samples.ai_continuation_free: The Orion chip wasn't just about raw speed - though the 1 GHz per core was nothing to sneeze at back then. It was about parallelism, the ability to juggle multiple demanding tasks without that dreaded app-closing lag. Suddenly, video editing on your phone wasn't a laughing matter. Real-time graphics in games could actually compete with what you'd find on a dedicated handheld console. The browser could render complex pages while background processes ran smoothly. What Samsung understood was that mobile computing had hit a bottleneck. Single-core chips could only go so fast before thermal constraints and battery life turned your powerhouse into a pocket heater. The dual-core approach meant you could have your performance and your all-day battery life too - or at least a reasonable compromise between the two. The real beneficiaries would be the app developers who'd been constrained by hardware limitations. They could finally build the kind of immersive experiences that required serious processing grunt. Augmented reality, computer vision, advanced physics in games - all these became viable when you had two cores working in harmony.
