samples.prefix: July 21, 2009 Dennis Kosuth responds to a critique of his article on the 1989 Tiananmen uprising from a member of the Party for Socialism and Liberation. MY ARTICLE on the 1989 Tiananmen Square uprising in China ("Twenty years after Tiananmen Square") for SocialistWorker.org drew a harsh response from Richard Becker, writing for the Party for Socialism and Liberation (PSL).
samples.human_continuation: Including footnotes, Becker's reply is nearly twice as long as my original article. It is packed, every inch of the way, with denunciations of me and the International Socialist Organization, which publishes SocialistWorker.org. Why should a relatively brief article on Tiananmen provoke such a lengthy and hostile response? It isn't because my article was a sustained attack on PSL--I mentioned the organization once, three paragraphs from the end. The answer is that what you think about the Tiananmen Square uprising goes to the heart of what you think about socialism. The American socialist Hal Draper once wrote a brilliant essay titled "The Two Souls of Socialism" that identifies two trends in the socialist movement historically--those who believe socialism can be imposed "from above," in the name of the working class, whether by electing socialists to government office or through a military victory and force of arms; and those who think socialism must be achieved "from below," by the collective action of the working-class majority in overturning capitalism and creating a workers' state based on mass democracy and freedom.
samples.ai_continuation_chat:
Why did a relatively straightforward historical piece provoke such a lengthy and hostile reply? The answer lies not in the specific details of 1989, but in the fundamental gulf between the political traditions we represent. Becker and the PSL operate within a framework that regards every action of the Chinese Communist Party as inherently progressive, a legacy of Stalinist orthodoxy that treats state socialism as an unbreakable monolith. For them, any criticism of a self-proclaimed socialist state is tantamount to an attack on socialism itself.

My approach, rooted in the revolutionary Marxist tradition of Hal Draper and the International Socialist Organization, sees things differently. We believe socialism must be democratic from the ground up—that workers' power cannot be decreed from above by a party that suppresses dissent. The Tiananmen uprising was not a bourgeois plot; it was a mass movement of workers and students demanding genuine democracy within a system that claimed to serve them. By defending the Chinese state's violent crackdown, the PSL aligns itself with bureaucratic repression, not the emancipation of the working class. This is the real point of contention: whether socialism means rule by a party elite or rule by the people themselves.
samples.ai_continuation_free: Becker accuses me of "sectarianism" and "anti-communism," and claims that my analysis aligns with the "imperialist narrative" that seeks to undermine the Chinese Communist Party. He insists that the PSL's position—defending the CCP's actions in 1989 as necessary to preserve socialist stability and prevent a capitalist restoration—is the only principled stance for Marxists. I respect Becker's long history of activism, but I believe his response misses the central point of my article. The question is not whether one supports or opposes the Chinese government in the abstract, but how we evaluate a mass movement of workers and students that was met with state violence. To simply label any criticism of the CCP as "anti-communist" shuts down the very debate socialists need to have about the nature of actually existing socialism, state power, and democracy. Becker argues that the Tiananmen protesters were primarily a "bourgeois" and "anti-socialist" force, citing the presence of calls for multiparty elections and the influence of Western ideas. I would not deny that such elements existed. But to reduce the entire movement to that caricature ignores the genuine grievances of millions of workers who participated—anger over inflation, corruption, and the lack of democratic input in their workplaces.

content_constraint.content_direction: The continuation argues that the dispute is not personal but reflects a deep ideological divide between two conceptions of socialism: from above versus from below.
content_constraint.scope: It covers the length and tone of Becker's response, dismisses the idea that the original article attacked the PSL, and introduces Hal Draper's framework to frame the debate, stopping before applying it to the Tiananmen case.

samples.prefix: Over the years, I've learned to be cautious with C++ pointers. In particular, I'm always very careful about who owns a given pointer, and who's in charge of calling delete on it. But my caution often forces me to write deliberately inefficient functions. For example: vector < string > tokenize_string ( const string & text ); Here, we have a large string text , and we want to split it into a vector of tokens.
samples.human_continuation: This function is nice and safe, but it allocates one string for every token in the input. Now, if we were feeling reckless, we could avoid these allocations by returning a vector of pointers into text : vector < pair < const char * , const char *>> tokenize_string2 ( const string & text ); In this version, each token is represented by two pointers into text : One pointing to the first character, and one pointing just beyond the last character.1 But this can go horribly wrong: // Disaster strikes! auto v = tokenize_string2 ( get_input_string ()); munge ( v ); Why does this fail? The function get_input_string returns a temporary string, and tokenize_string2 builds an array of pointers into that string. Unfortunately, the temporary string only lives until the end of the current expression, and then the underlying memory is released.
samples.ai_continuation_chat: The function returns a vector by value, which means every token gets copied out of the original string. For a large document with thousands of tokens, that’s a lot of allocation and deallocation. A more efficient version might use pointers: void tokenize_string2 ( const string & text , vector < const char * > & tokens , vector < size_t > & lengths ); Here, tokens are just pointers into the original string, avoiding copies. But now ownership is ambiguous. Does the caller need to keep text alive? What if text is modified or destroyed while tokens are still in use? The pointer-based version is faster, but it introduces subtle lifetime bugs. The vector-of-strings version is safe but slower. This trade-off between safety and efficiency is a recurring theme in C++. I usually lean toward safety first, then profile and optimize only when necessary. But it still nags at me that the safe version copies everything, especially when I know the data is transient and the pointers would be perfectly valid for the token’s lifetime.
samples.ai_continuation_free: Over the years, I've learned to be cautious with C++ pointers. In particular, I'm always very careful about who owns a given pointer, and who's in charge of calling delete on it. But my caution often forces me to write deliberately inefficient functions. For example: vector < string > tokenize_string ( const string & text ); Here, we have a large string text , and we want to split it into a vector of tokens. The function returns a vector of strings, which means every token gets copied from the original string into a new string object, and then the vector itself may get copied or moved depending on how the caller uses it. For a large text with many tokens, this can be a lot of unnecessary copying. In an ideal world, I'd like to return something like a vector of string_views that point into the original text, avoiding all that copying.

content_constraint.topic: Trade-off between safety and efficiency in C++ string tokenization functions.
content_constraint.content_direction: Contrasts a safe but allocation-heavy tokenization function with a pointer-based version that risks dangling pointers due to temporary string lifetime.
content_constraint.scope: Covers the design of two tokenization approaches and explains the failure case caused by temporary string destruction.

Miraj can automatically generate a demo page for previewing/testing components under development. Things get a little more complicated when you add web components. Each component can leverage Miraj's Polymer integration to create native web components that work seamlessly across all modern browsers. Miraj also supports hot reloading during development, so you can see changes reflected immediately as you modify your code. This speeds up the iteration process significantly, especially when fine-tuning the appearance and interaction of components. The framework handles the complexity of bundling and optimization behind the scenes, allowing you to focus on writing your application logic rather than configuration details. If you need to integrate with existing JavaScript libraries or APIs, Miraj provides convenient hooks that make it simple to bridge between your components and external code.

samples.prefix: Async IO for Rust (part II) PaulColomiets Blocked Unblock Follow Following Nov 12, 2015 This is a second article about designing “rotor”, the library for doing asynchronous IO in Rust. This part describes what changed since the previous article as well as expands on discussion points of the previous write-up. State Machines Are Good Enough One of the hottest topics in the discussion of the previous article was whether threads are the better abstraction for I/O.
samples.human_continuation: And if OS threads are not good enough some kind of green threading should be introduced. There are two such libraries being developed: mioco and simplesched (both of them do not work in stable rust yet). Still I don’t believe it’s a good fit for low-level protocol handling. This section looks at issues with the threading model for handling I/O in Rust. You may skip the section if you are more interested in Rotor rather than design decisions. Memory ownership Typical request processing code looks like: It looks nothing wrong at a glance. No memory leaks here. But note that both “buf” and “parsed” are still being allocated while the response is being sent. But they are useless at that point in time. Is it easy to fix? Yes, just pass them by value, or wrap code block in braces. Is it easy to find? The code is too simplistic to show you the complexity.
samples.ai_continuation_chat: The debate often centers on the perceived simplicity of OS threads versus the complexity of state machines. However, when scrutinizing memory ownership, the thread model reveals significant inefficiencies. In a typical request processing pipeline, data must be copied or borrowed across thread boundaries, often requiring Arc<Mutex<T>> wrappers to ensure safety. This indirection adds latency and complicates the lifetime management of buffers. Green threading libraries like mioco or simplesched attempt to mitigate this by managing user-level schedulers, yet they still struggle with the underlying cost of context switching and synchronization primitives. Rotor, by contrast, embraces the state machine approach, allowing data to be owned directly by the task without intermediate locking. This eliminates the overhead of mutex contention and ensures that buffers are processed in place. By avoiding the abstraction leak of threads, Rotor provides a more predictable performance profile for high-throughput I/O applications, where every nanosecond counts.
samples.ai_continuation_free: The consensus among the Rust community seems to be leaning heavily towards state machines, primarily because they offer a more predictable and efficient model for high-concurrency systems. While threads are easier to reason about initially, the overhead of context switching and memory allocation for thousands of concurrent connections quickly becomes prohibitive. State machines, on the other hand, allow a single thread to manage thousands of active connections with minimal overhead, leveraging the operating system’s epoll, kqueue, or IOCP mechanisms directly. In the previous iteration of rotor, the abstraction was somewhat loose, leading to potential pitfalls where users could accidentally block the event loop. The new design tightens this up by enforcing strict boundaries between synchronous and asynchronous code. We introduced a clearer separation of concerns: the event loop is responsible for dispatching events, while the state machines are responsible for reacting to them. This separation ensures that no long-running computation can stall the entire system. Another significant change is the handling of futures.

content_constraint.topic: The author argues against using OS or green threads for low-level I/O in Rust, highlighting memory ownership inefficiencies in typical request processing.
content_constraint.content_direction: The text dismisses threading models in favor of state machines for protocol handling and illustrates memory waste in standard request processing where buffers remain allocated unnecessarily.
content_constraint.scope: The continuation covers the rejection of threading libraries and analyzes a specific memory ownership issue in request handling code, stopping before providing a detailed solution.

samples.prefix: Sierra Nelson loves cephalopods. Squids, octopuses, cuttlefish—you name it, if it’s a bilateral mollusk with a big-ass head, Nelson is positively gaga over it. Nelson is a Seattle-area poet, and you can understand how a poet might fall in love with tentacled sea creatures: They’re romantic figures, skulking in the ocean—part of the great marine biosphere, but also remote from whales and fish.
samples.human_continuation: Those articulate limbs and big brains set them apart, leaving them to skulk and mope fabulously. And they even produce their own ink! How could a poet not land on Team Cephalopod? But Nelson is more science-minded than your average poet. She’s a co-founder of the Vis-á-Vis Society, which applies scientific rigor to crowd-sourced poems, often employing large crowds at parties to write, Mad Libs-style, a series of poems about love and longing. No other poets in town, likely, have dissected a poem into pie charts on a whiteboard while wearing a lab coat. On her own, Nelson loves to tease out the poetry in science, finding resonance in the long and mysterious Latin words and phrases we’ve used to name the world.
samples.ai_continuation_chat: Nelson channeled this devotion into the Vis-á-Vis Society, a poetic collaboration that celebrates the unexpected intersections of verse and scientific inquiry. Her work often takes the form of Mad Libs-style poetry, where participants fill in blanks with words drawn from specific themes—sometimes Latin scientific terminology, sometimes more whimsical fare. This playful approach allows her to explore what she calls "the hidden poetry" embedded in technical language. The Latin names for cephalopod species, for instance, contain their own strange beauty: Loligo pealei, Architeuthis dux, Sepia officinalis. Nelson sees these not as dry classifications but as small verses in themselves, linguistic artifacts that carry the weight of discovery and wonder. Through her workshops and publications, she invites others to see that science and poetry are not opposites but natural companions, two human efforts to name and make meaning of the world.
samples.ai_continuation_free: Nelson has channeled this fascination into her creative work, producing poems and interactive art pieces that explore the strange beauty of these underwater invertebrates. She's even co-created a literary card game called "The Cephalopod前三" (which, yes, is a pun on "sex and the cephalopod" - she's not above a good joke). What draws a poet to creatures that most people only encounter as Calamari or as vaguely creepy shapes in aquarium tanks? For Nelson, it seems to be the cephalopod's combination of alienness and approachability. Octopuses are notoriously intelligent, capable of solving puzzles and even recognizing human faces. They've got three hearts and blue blood. Their skin can change color and texture in the blink of an eye, turning them into living mood rings drifting through the deep.

samples.prefix: Introduction On Feb. 1, 2017, the United States led Coalition was accused by local activists and journalists that it had bombed the headquarters of the Syrian Arab Red Crescent (SARC) located in the Carlton Hotel in the city of Idlib, Syria. Photos and videos allegedly showing the bombed headquarters quickly emerged online.
samples.human_continuation: This open source investigation aims to verify the various claims made surrounding this incident. Content Summary Claims Methodology Open Sources Findings Summary Based on open source research, it can be confirmed that the Syrian Arab Red Crescent (SARC) utilised the Carlton Hotel in Idlib city as a headquarters. It can also be confirmed that the Carlton Hotel was recently severely damaged. The US-led Coalition was accused of conducting an airstrike on the building in the early morning of Feb. 1, killing one SARC member, but the Coalition denies any involvement. Neither the exact date of the attack nor the perpetrator can be established based on open sources. What can be observed, however, is that a bomb appears to have pierced at least four floors before detonating. Claims The following claims are circulating on social media: One or more airstrikes conducted by the US-led Coalition destroyed a part of the Carlton Hotel in Idlib city.
samples.ai_continuation_chat:
This incident drew immediate international attention due to the targeting of a humanitarian organization protected under international law. Open source investigators began analyzing the available visual material to verify the claims and determine what had actually occurred at the Carlton Hotel complex.

Initial satellite imagery and photographs posted on social media appeared to show significant structural damage to the building, with debris scattered across the surrounding area. Humanitarian workers reported that the SARC office had been completely destroyed. However, the identity of the attacking force remained disputed, with some sources attributing the strike to the Coalition while others suggested different perpetrators.

The investigation required careful examination of weapon remnants, crater analysis, and comparison with known Coalition munitions. Investigators also needed to establish the precise location of the SARC headquarters within the hotel structure and verify whether it had been clearly marked as a humanitarian facility. The conflicting narratives presented by various parties on the ground further complicated the verification process.
samples.ai_continuation_free: Initial Coalition spokespersons denied that any of their aircraft had targeted the location, stating that they were not aware of any strikes in that specific area at that time. However, as photographic evidence accumulated and international organizations demanded clarification, the Coalition announced it would launch a formal investigation into the incident. The Syrian Arab Red Crescent Society issued a statement denying that the Carlton Hotel served as their headquarters, though local volunteers confirmed that the building had been used as a coordination center for humanitarian operations in the region. The International Committee of the Red Cross expressed concern over the incident and called for all parties to ensure the protection of humanitarian workers and facilities. Human rights organizations later analyzed satellite imagery and compared it with the photos circulating online. While the visual evidence appeared consistent with the aftermath of an aerial strike, definitive attribution remained complicated by the complex battlefield environment in northern Syria, where multiple actors including Russian forces, Syrian government aircraft, and various rebel factions were conducting operations.

samples.prefix: The Los Angeles River is on the verge of a new era. In the few years since the flood control channel was reclassified as a “navigable waterway,” the region has re-embraced its oddball amalgam of concrete and nature, which winds roughly 51 miles from the San Fernando Valley out to the ocean in Long Beach. A $1-billion-plus plan to restore 11 miles north of Downtown LA is (slowly) working its way through federal approvals.
samples.human_continuation: Famed architect Frank Gehry is working with Los Angeles County officials and numerous nonprofits and stakeholder groups to create a comprehensive plan for the whole river. The river was one of the selling points in the city’s winning bid for the 2028 Olympics. Developers are still clamoring to build along the river’s banks. The last time the LA River was reborn it was the late 1930s, and it had been drowning the young city periodically since its birth. At some points, the river was just a trickle; in other parts, it was uncontrollably wild, and flooded frequently and devastatingly. After a terrible flood in March 1938, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers began work to lower the riverbed, widen the channel, and choke the whole thing in “a continuous trapezoidal concrete channel to carry the river from Elysian Park to Long Beach,” as described in The Los Angeles River: Its Life, Death, and Possible Rebirth.
samples.ai_continuation_chat:
The county has enlisted Frank Gehry to develop a comprehensive vision for the entire river corridor, aiming to transform what was long considered an eyesore into a celebrated public space—potentially just in time for the 2028 Olympics, when the world turns its attention to Los Angeles.

This represents a remarkable reversal from the river's dark past. In the 1930s, following devastating floods that caused millions in damage and claimed lives, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers engineered a radical solution: converting the natural waterway into a massive concrete flood control channel. Elysian Park and surrounding neighborhoods were literally carved apart to make way for the channel's rigid geometry. For decades, the river existed as little more than an infrastructural afterthought—a linear scar cutting through the city, largely ignored by residents who viewed it as something to drive over rather than engage with. Now, after nearly a century of neglect, Los Angeles is finally learning to love its river again.
samples.ai_continuation_free: For decades, the army Corps of Engineers had steadily transformed the river into the massive concrete ditch we know today, a project that began in the 1930s and accelerated after devastating floods in 1938. By the 1960s, nearly all of the river's natural channel had been encased in gray pavement, turning what was once a winding, oak-lined waterway into something that looked more like a highway than a river. Angelenos largely forgot it was there at all, a blighted backdoor to the city that most residents would never purposely visit. But the reclassification in 2020 changed everything. Under the Clean Water Act, the river's new status meant it could no longer be ignored—that developers and municipalities would now need to consider its ecological health when planning projects along its banks. It also opened the door to federal funding for restoration, something advocates had been fighting for over a decade.

samples.prefix: Written by Stephanie Siam When I reverted to Islam in March 2005, I have to admit I was afraid. Okay, perhaps nervous is a better choice of word, as I wasn’t scared or frightened. And I know I’m not alone in admitting this feeling, especially with female converts. The process of transitioning into Islam from a previous faith/belief system (because face it, even if you don’t believe in God, you believe there is no God) is daunting: What will my friends think?
samples.human_continuation: How will I be received by the public? Does this mean I have to start dressing like an Arab or East Asian-er? Do I have to start my life over from the beginning, rethinking every choice I’ve ever made? While all of those are valid concerns, and ones that I did contemplate at some point in time post-reversion, they weren’t what I was afraid of. My fear came from telling my father. Not my family. Not my Mother. Now, before you start thinking my dad is this overbearing and close-minded totalitarian who lives for controlling others’ lives, he’s NOT. In fact, he’s the polar opposite. He’s one of the most open-minded individuals I’ve ever known in my life. And if there is a perfect antonym for overbearing, that describes him, too. I mean, for Heaven’s sake, the man used to sit and logically discuss with me the reasons I should pick up my toys when I was 3 years old.
samples.ai_continuation_chat: Will my family understand? These questions swirled in my mind, creating a cloud of uncertainty that hovered over every step of my spiritual journey. Yet, amidst this general anxiety, one specific fear stood out with piercing clarity: my father’s reaction. My dad has always been the epitome of an open-minded individual. He respected diverse cultures, encouraged intellectual curiosity, and never judged me for exploring different philosophies. Precisely because he was so accepting, I feared that my decision to embrace Islam might seem like a sudden, inexplicable rupture in our shared history. I worried that despite his broad tolerance, he might view my reversion as a rejection of the values we had built together. For a daughter who cherished his approval, the thought of disappointing him was more terrifying than any external judgment. I needed to know if his love could transcend the boundaries of tradition, and whether he could see my conversion not as a loss, but as a profound expression of the same faith in humanity he had always taught me.
samples.ai_continuation_free: Will they judge me? Will they think I’ve lost my mind or joined a cult? These questions swirled in my head, creating a cloud of anxiety that hovered over every interaction. I worried about the sudden shift in my lifestyle, the new dietary restrictions, and the expectation to wear the hijab. It wasn’t just about the external changes, but the internal reconfiguration of my identity. I had spent years defining myself within a certain cultural and social framework, and now I was stepping into the unknown, carrying the weight of potential rejection from the very people who knew me best. Yet, beneath the nervousness, there was a quiet, persistent pull—a sense of rightness that suggested this fear was merely the price of admission for a deeper, more authentic peace.

samples.prefix: national Congress Vice President Rahul Gandhi addressed a workers' meet at Malad on Friday; turns out, some who attended, came only for the goodies Congress Vice-President Rahul Gandhi began his speech with 'Til gul ghya, god, god bola,' (Have tilgul, talk sweetly) the traditional greeting on Makar Sankrant, at Malad on Friday.
samples.human_continuation: While his speech saw a huge crowd, it seems some had gathered because they had allegedly been sweet-talked into attending and given promises of what they would get if they did. mid-day spoke to a number of people at the event. While some said that they were promised R100, one said that she was given biryani before the event. Some residents of Kandivli’s Damu Nagar who had lost their homes to the fire said that corporator Ajanta Yadav had promised them houses. Congress Vice President Rahul Gandhi arrives to address a workers’ meet at Malad yesterday. The Congress leader arrived more or less on time, but had to wait while other leaders gave their speeches Also Read: Rahul Gandhi's Mumbai padyatra over power tariff hike evokes good response Makar Sankrant was unusually busy for Malad this year as the Congress had organised a karyakarta melava (workers’ meet), to be addressed by Gandhi at the St Joseph’s School ground.
samples.ai_continuation_chat:
But for many in the audience, the sweetness of the day had little to do with the festive sentiment. Allegations have surfaced that several attendees were lured to the event not by political conviction, but by promises of tangible incentives—money, food packets, and even housing assistance. Local residents and opposition party members claim that Congress workers went door-to-door in nearby slum clusters, offering these inducements to ensure a sizable crowd for the event.

When questioned, some attendees admitted they had been told they would receive grocery kits and cash handouts simply for showing up. “I came because they said there would be rations,” one woman confessed, unwilling to give her name. Others echoed similar sentiments, stating they had little interest in politics but needed the promised aid.

The Congress party has denied these allegations, insisting the meet was a genuine grassroots interaction. However, the incident has sparked a debate about the lengths political parties go to in manufacturing enthusiasm, especially in a city like Mumbai where every rally and speech is scrutinized for authenticity.
samples.ai_continuation_free:
The crowd, which had gathered in large numbers, responded with polite applause. But as Gandhi continued his address, focusing on issues of unemployment, farmer distress, and the need for transparency in governance, a section of the audience began to lose interest. Whispers rippled through the gathering, and a few people started glancing at their watches. It soon became clear why. Organizers had distributed packets of tilgul—the traditional sweet made from sesame and jaggery—along with other small gifts like t-shirts and caps to those who attended. For some, the promise of these freebies was the primary draw. “I came because my local corporator said there would be something for everyone,” admitted Sharda Patil, a 45-year-old homemaker from the area. “I don’t really follow politics, but the tilgul is nice.”

Others, however, were genuinely engaged. “Rahul ji spoke about the rising prices of cooking gas and how it affects our monthly budget,” said Mahesh Khanna, a shopkeeper. “That’s something we face every day. I’m glad he’s talking about it.”

The contrast in reactions highlighted a recurring challenge for political leaders: how to connect with a public that is increasingly distracted by short-term incentives.

His parents have now sued for damages — at the initial encouragement of Israel — and allege that the Bank of China laundered funds for the terror group, effectively bankrolling the operation that killed their son. Despite overwhelming documentation, Jerusalem has allegedly bowed to intense diplomatic pressure from Beijing, choosing to protect its lucrative economic relationship with the world’s second-largest economy over justice for the victim’s family. samples.prefix: One of the world’s major terrestrial carbon pools is rapidly deteriorating as large parts of Indonesia’s peatlands are deforested and converted to oil palm and paper plantations. No longer a carbon sink, Indonesia’s peatlands are now a globally significant source of emissions. The June fires in Sumatra once again drew international attention to Indonesia’s forests.
samples.human_continuation: At the fires’ peak, 140,000 hectares were burnt in just one week. Most fires were in peatland, much of it on land destined to become oil palm, or Acacia plantations for the paper industry. Fire remains the instrument of choice for low-cost land-clearing. The fires were a reminder of the unsolved problem of peatland protection in Indonesia, and of the need for urgent action against the toxic combination of plantations, fire and poor governance that is destroying one of the world’s major carbon pools. What exactly is peatland? Indonesia’s peatlands are (or were) low-lying rainforests located close to coastal areas. Under the forest lies the peat itself, a below-ground accumulation of carbon-rich decayed vegetation. Formed in swampy conditions where plant material fails to fully decay, peat can build up to a depth of 10 meters or more over thousands of years.
samples.ai_continuation_chat: These blazes, fueled by deliberate slash-and-burn practices, expose the fragility of these unique ecosystems. Peat consists of partially decayed organic matter that has accumulated over millennia in waterlogged conditions. When drained for agriculture, particularly for oil palm and Acacia plantations, this sponge-like soil dries out and becomes highly flammable. The resulting fires release vast quantities of stored carbon into the atmosphere, exacerbating climate change. Unlike regular forest fires, peat fires can smolder underground for months, proving incredibly difficult to extinguish. The scale of destruction is alarming, with smoke drifting across Southeast Asia and impacting regional health. This transformation from a vital carbon sink to a major emission source highlights the urgent need for sustainable land management. Without intervention, the continued degradation of these landscapes will accelerate global warming, turning Indonesia’s natural heritage into a persistent environmental crisis that demands immediate international cooperation and local policy reform.

As bulldozers cleared ancient vegetation and drainage canals cut through the waterlogged soil, the peat dried out, becoming highly susceptible to ignition. This cycle of drainage and burning has transformed what was once a vital regulator of the global climate into a persistent emitter of greenhouse gases, releasing centuries’ worth of stored carbon in a matter of weeks. The economic drive for palm oil and pulpwood continues to outweigh conservation efforts, leaving local communities to breathe in toxic smoke while the global community watches the steady decline of one of the planet’s most critical natural assets.

samples.prefix: I didn't think I would be writing about this, but, then again, I seem to say that fairly frequently. Be that as it may, on Friday I wrote about a letter sent to Lee Goldman, MD, the Dean of the Faculties of Health Sciences and Medicine at Columbia University complaining about Dr. Mehmet Oz's promotion of pseudoscience on his television show, which reaches millions.
samples.human_continuation: When I wrote my post, my first reaction was somewhat supportive, but with reservations. However, as I read your comments and thought about it some more, I started having second thoughts. Then, over the weekend, I had a rather prolonged exchange on Twitter during breaks in the action at the American Association for Cancer Research (AACR) Meeting in Philadelphia, which I'm attending now. The more I thought about it, the more I became convinced that this letter, written by Dr. Miller of the Hoover Institution, and signed by several doctors with ties to the American Council on Science and Health (ACSH), was an incredibly bad idea. This evolution in my thinking was helped along by other developments over the weekend. I'll explain. I also might regret having continued my commentary, but, then, when did that ever stop me before?
samples.ai_continuation_chat: I thought the letter was clear, well-reasoned, and appropriately forceful. But then the comments started rolling in. Some readers pointed out that Oz had been doing this for years, and that the letter, however well-intentioned, was unlikely to change anything at Columbia. Others noted that Goldman himself had previously defended academic freedom in ways that could easily be invoked to shield Oz from any serious consequences. Then, at the AACR meeting, I got into a Twitter exchange with Dr. Miller, who argued that the real problem wasn't Oz but the institutional failures that allow such figures to flourish. He mentioned the Hoover Institution and the American Council on Science and Health as examples of organizations that should be doing more to push back. I found myself wondering: was the letter merely performative? A way for concerned colleagues to feel they'd done something without actually risking the kind of confrontation that might force real change?
samples.ai_continuation_free: On Saturday, I received an email from a colleague who had read the piece. She wasn't surprised by the content, but she was frustrated by what she saw as a pattern: respected institutions often hesitate to publicly distance themselves from celebrity doctors whose views diverge from evidence-based medicine. Her point was that silence can be interpreted as tacit approval, especially when the celebrity in question holds an academic appointment. Later that same day, I noticed a new thread on a medical ethics forum. A physician had posted a link to the letter and asked a pointed question: "At what point does the responsibility of an academic institution to correct public misinformation outweigh the professional courtesy extended to a tenured faculty member?" The responses were divided. Some argued that Dr. Oz's show is entertainment, not a medical lecture, and that viewers should be savvy enough to distinguish between the two.

samples.prefix: Stuart, a 66-year-old man with diabetes, felt lousy—constantly fatigued, nauseated, and short of breath after just the slightest exertion. His daughter, worried by his increasing frailty, took him to the emergency room at the local hospital. Her concern was amply justified: Stuart was suffering from heart failure. Like 5.1 million other Americans each year who suffer from heart failure, he was admitted to the hospital to treat this serious, often life-threatening condition.
samples.human_continuation: The caring medical team stabilized his condition, and Stuart left the hospital after 10 days, glad to be home with words of advice and a few medications. Within a month he was back, once again fatigued, and facing a second episode. Stuart’s story is far from rare. Hospital readmissions for chronic conditions such as diabetes, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), and congestive heart failure (CHF) are both common and very costly. Studies conducted in the United States indicate that nearly 20% of Medicare patients who are hospitalized for chronic conditions are often readmitted within 30 days. Experts at Edifecs indicate that it costs Medicare—and US taxpayers—about $26 billion a year, and often a large majority of these readmissions are actually considered avoidable with accurate prioritization and personalized care protocols.
samples.ai_continuation_chat: After treatment stabilized his condition, Stuart was discharged with a handful of new medications and instructions to follow up with his primary care physician. What his daughter didn't know was that Stuart's chances of returning to the hospital within 30 days were alarmingly high—nearly one in five Medicare patients with heart failure are readmitted within that window. For patients like Stuart who also manage diabetes and other chronic conditions, the risk is even greater. These readmissions cost US taxpayers billions annually, with COPD and CHF accounting for a significant portion of preventable returns. Modern healthcare technology, like the analytics tools developed by companies such as Edifecs, can help hospitals identify high-risk patients before discharge and connect them with the support they need to recover at home. Without such intervention, Stuart, like many others, would find himself back in the emergency room within weeks.
samples.ai_continuation_free: The emergency room physicians quickly went to work, running a series of tests to determine the severity of his condition. An echocardiogram revealed that his heart was pumping at only about 25% of its normal capacity—a dangerously low ejection fraction that explained why even walking across the room left him gasping for air. His blood work showed elevated levels of BNP (B-type natriuretic peptide), a hormone that spikes when the heart is under stress, and his kidney function was already beginning to deteriorate, a common complication when the heart fails to pump blood effectively. Stuart was admitted to the cardiac unit, where the medical team initiated treatment immediately. He was given diuretics intravenously to reduce the fluid buildup in his lungs and extremities that had been causing his shortness of breath.

samples.prefix: On his fourth full day in office, President Trump signed an executive order that was supposed to settle this whole Dakota Access Pipeline thing—no more delays due to protests, no more reconsidering the route because of environmental worries. And for a while, it seemed to work. The protest camps are gone, and the pipe has been pumping oil since March.
samples.human_continuation: But Thursday, a federal judge ordered a do-over on the rush-job environmental review Trump ordered back in January. Trump came into office aiming for a blitzkrieg on environmental regulations. He got trench warfare. That's because firing from the other side of no man's land is a nimble alliance of environmental groups that have spent decades preparing for the likes of him. You have probably heard of many of them: the Sierra Club, National Resources Defense Council, EarthJustice, and so on. Others are smaller, focused on regional issues—like the Standing Rock Sioux that just won a small victory against the Dakota Access Pipeline. What they all have in common are stubborn, attrition-minded legal teams. Trump's assault is just a more bombastic version of what these lawyers have weathered under past administrations.
samples.ai_continuation_chat: But the legal battle never truly ended. On Wednesday, a federal judge dealt a significant blow to the Trump administration’s efforts to fast-track the pipeline, ordering the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers to conduct a full environmental review of the project’s crossing beneath Lake Oahe in North Dakota. The ruling is a major victory for the Standing Rock Sioux Tribe and environmental groups like the Sierra Club, the Natural Resources Defense Council, and EarthJustice, who have argued that the pipeline threatens the tribe’s water supply and cultural sites. Judge James Boasberg found that the previous review was insufficient, particularly in assessing the risk of an oil spill. The decision means that while oil can continue to flow for now, the long-term future of the pipeline remains uncertain, reigniting a conflict that the president had hoped to put to rest.
samples.ai_continuation_free: But the fight isn’t over. It just moved underground, into courtrooms and boardrooms, and into the quiet persistence of the tribes who never really left. The Standing Rock Sioux and their allies didn’t vanish when the bulldozers came; they just changed tactics. They’ve filed lawsuits challenging the easement, arguing the Army Corps of Engineers failed to do a proper environmental review. And while the oil flows, so do the legal briefs, each one a small act of resistance against a pipeline that cuts through sacred land and under the Missouri River. The protests may have faded from the nightly news, but the question of who gets to decide the fate of a nation’s water—and whose voices are heard—remains as urgent as ever.

samples.prefix: President Trump made his debut at the United Nations on Tuesday, addressing the U.N. General Assembly at its annual opening. Afterward, media headlines and news coverage of the speech focused on Trump’s absurd (but admittedly amusing) new nickname for Kim Jong Un, “Rocket Man,” and his threat that the United States is willing to “totally destroy” North Korea to protect itself and its allies.
samples.human_continuation: The mainstream media, liberal elites, and the international community have been doing a lot of handwringing about Trump’s rhetoric and his talk of going it alone. They also had a lot to say about his comments concerning the Iran nuclear deal, whose dissolution the president has long desired. Although the focus was on Trump’s supposedly dangerous isolationism and nationalism, what’s really upsetting them is that he dared to say what no one is supposed to say: that the U.N. is broken and that it is unrealistic and dangerous to have a world without borders and without national sovereignty. In other words, Trump violated the Emperor Has No Clothes rule. The Importance of Governments Serving Their People One of the major themes of Trump’s U.N.
samples.ai_continuation_chat: Yet beneath these sensational soundbites, a far more substantive and unsettling message was largely overlooked. Trump’s core argument was not a mere personal insult to a dictator, but a sweeping indictment of the globalist framework that has defined U.N. diplomacy for decades. He championed national sovereignty as the supreme principle, directly challenging the post-World War II consensus that international cooperation and multilateral agreements should supersede individual state interests. His pointed criticism of the Iran nuclear deal, labeling it an "embarrassment," was a clear example. To the media and many elites, this rhetoric sounded like dangerous isolationism. But for Trump, it was a fundamental reorientation: a declaration that nations, not transnational bureaucracies, should be the primary actors on the world stage, and that American interests would no longer be subordinated to a global order he views as fundamentally flawed.
samples.ai_continuation_free: But while the nickname and the threat dominated the news cycle, Trump’s speech was far broader—and in many ways more revealing of his administration’s worldview. He railed against globalism, criticized the Iran nuclear deal as an “embarrassment,” and called for a “great reawakening” of nations that prioritize their own sovereignty over international consensus. The speech was vintage Trump: combative, nationalist, and dismissive of the very institution he was addressing. Yet beneath the bluster, it also laid out a clear—if controversial—foreign policy doctrine, one that rejects the post-World War II liberal order in favor of a transactional, America-first approach. For allies accustomed to U.S. leadership, the message was unsettling: the old rules no longer apply.

samples.prefix: Fact Buster Q: Does coffee make you dehydrated? A: If you drink coffee regularly and don't drink too much it shouldn't dehydrate you. Our expert: Dietitian Lisa Renn [Image source: Reuters | Mick Tsikas ] Have your say Have you found coffee can make you feel dehydrated? Conditions of Use Have you been told that you need to drink an extra glass of water for every cup of coffee or tea that you drink?
samples.human_continuation: For some time there has been a belief that drinking coffee and tea can make you dehydrated because the caffeine they contain has a diuretic effect. (A diuretic is a substance that causes your body to produce urine, and it has been suggested caffeine can do this because it increases blood flow through the kidneys.) But is there any evidence to show that your morning cuppa needs to be offset with a big glass of water? If you regularly enjoy a few cups of coffee or tea a day, then you can rest assured the moderate amount of caffeine they contain doesn't cause you to lose more fluid than you ingest, says Lisa Renn, accredited practising dietitian and spokesperson for the Dietitians Association of Australia. Nor will your cuppa be any more likely to send you off to the loo than any other drink. "There is evidence that caffeine in higher amounts acts as a diuretic in some people, but moderate intake is actually not that significant," Renn says.
samples.ai_continuation_chat:
It’s a common piece of advice, but according to dietitian Lisa Renn from the Dietitians Association of Australia, it simply isn’t necessary for most people. The idea stems from caffeine’s mild diuretic effect—meaning it can make you urinate more. However, research shows that for regular coffee and tea drinkers, this effect is negligible. Your body quickly builds a tolerance, and the fluid in your coffee or tea more than compensates for any slight increase in urine output.

In fact, moderate consumption—around three to four cups a day—contributes to your daily fluid intake just like water does. A 2014 study published in *PLOS ONE* found no significant difference in hydration levels between people who drank coffee and those who drank water. The key word is “moderate.” If you’re downing excessive amounts, you might feel jittery or need the bathroom more often, but for the average person, there’s no need to add extra glasses of water to “make up” for your morning brew.

So, next time someone warns you that your coffee habit is dehydrating you, you can set the record straight. As long as you’re not overdoing it, your daily cup is hydrating you just fine.
samples.ai_continuation_free: While it's a common belief that caffeinated drinks like coffee and tea are dehydrating, the science tells a different story, especially for regular consumers. The key factor is the body's adaptation to caffeine. For someone who doesn't drink coffee often, a single cup can act as a mild diuretic, meaning it may increase urine production slightly for a short period. However, for habitual coffee drinkers, this effect is significantly diminished. Studies have shown that moderate coffee consumption—typically defined as 3-4 cups per day—contributes to daily fluid intake in much the same way as water does. The water in your coffee largely offsets any mild fluid loss, making it a net hydrating beverage. So, unless you're consuming excessive amounts or are particularly sensitive to caffeine, there's no need to reach for that extra glass of water to compensate.

content_constraint.content_direction: Explains the diuretic effect of caffeine, then argues that moderate intake does not cause net fluid loss, citing expert opinion.

samples.prefix: The birth of the Traveling Wilburys was a happy accident. Warner Bros. Records’ International Department had asked that George Harrison come up with a B-side for “This Is Love,” a single from his Cloud Nine album. At the time it was customary to couple an A-side with a never-before-heard track, giving the single extra sales value.
samples.human_continuation: This was mid-1988. Cloud Nine was just out. George, along with cowriter Jeff Lynne and their friends Bob Dylan, Tom Petty, and Roy Orbison, had been hanging out in Dylan’s studio. I suppose George figured that as long as his pals were on hand, why not use them to knock off this flipside? A couple of days later George came by my office to play the new “B-side.” We went next door to A&R head Lenny Waronker’s office so he could hear it too. George played us “Handle With Care.” Our reaction was immediate. This was a song we knew could not be wasted on some B-side. Roy Orbison’s vocal was tremendous. I really loved the beautiful guitar figure that George played. The guys had really nailed it. Lenny and I stumbled over each others’ words, asking, “Can’t we somehow turn this into an album?” (I also had a suspicion that perhaps George had been hungering for another band experience.) We urged him on.
samples.ai_continuation_chat:
So Harrison turned to his frequent collaborator Jeff Lynne, and the two of them went to Bob Dylan's home studio in Los Angeles to work on the track. While they were there, Dylan suggested they call in a few friends—Tom Petty and Roy Orbison happened to be available, and they all gathered in the studio together.

What happened next was pure spontaneity. In just a few takes, the group recorded "Handle With Care," a track that far exceeded the modest expectations of a B-side. The chemistry between these legendary musicians was undeniable, and the song radiated joy and creative energy.

When Warner Bros. executives heard the result, they were stunned. Lenny Waronker, an executive at Warner Bros. Records, immediately recognized something special and made a bold proposition: why not release "Handle With Care" as part of a full Traveling Wilburys album? The idea was unprecedented—a supergroup of this magnitude coming together for an entire record—and it was born from this magical, unplanned session that exceeded everyone's wildest expectations.
samples.ai_continuation_free: George Harrison got together with his friends Jeff Lynne, Roy Orbison, Tom Petty, and Bob Dylan to record what was supposed to be a simple B-side. They gathered in Dave Stewart's home studio in Los Angeles in early 1988, and the session was meant to be informal—just a few musicians jamming. Harrison had worked with Lynne before on his Cloud Nine album, and the two had a good working relationship. Petty had also been involved in Cloud Nine as part of the session team. Orbison had recently experienced a career resurgence thanks to his collaboration with Petty and the Heartbreakers on his comeback album Mystery Girl, which was set for release the following year. The song they recorded was "Handle with Care," and it was so strong that it quickly became clear this wasn't just throwaway material. The chemistry between these five artists was undeniable. Instead of releasing it as a B-side, Warner Bros. decided to put it out as a double A-side with "This Is Love." But the collaboration didn't stop there.

Abstract Helminths are the largest and most complex pathogens to invade and live within the human body. Since they are not able to outpace the immune system by rapid antigen variation or faster cell division or retreat into protective niches not accessible to immune effector mechanisms, their long-term survival depends on influencing and regulating the immune responses away from the mode of action most damaging to them. Helminths, large parasitic worms that inhabit the human host, have evolved sophisticated mechanisms to ensure long-term survival without causing fatal damage to their host. Unlike pathogens that evade or outpace the immune system through rapid antigen variation, helminths employ a fundamentally different strategy: active modulation of host immune responses through their excretory and secretory (ES) products. These ES products contain a diverse array of molecules including proteases, protease inhibitors, cytokine mimics, and lipid mediators that collectively regulate host immunity. By suppressing pro-inflammatory responses and promoting anti-inflammatory or regulatory immune pathways, helminths create a permissive environment that allows their continued existence within the host.

samples.prefix: Sometimes, a bra can look too small when it fits well, because the strip of fabric/elastic under the top of the lace is too tight across the top of the breast. European bras, in particular are nearly infamous for this. If you have firm breast tissue, your breasts will fight against the elastic and shape the bra. Not all of us are that lucky.
samples.human_continuation: Soft tissue molds to the shape of the bra, so the elastic pulls down over the top of the breast. If the bra is not a full coverage style, it will not sit against the breastbone, but actually against the breast tissue, causing the breasts to bulge out of the top of the bra and give the appearance of a bra that is too small. This seam is put in place to pull the top of the cup closer to the chest and prevent the bust from spilling out. That’s probably just fine for someone who is predominantly full on bottom, but someone with a more even or full on top shape will run into this problem pretty consistently in European bras, so I’m going to talk about how to fix that. Tools You’ll Need: 1 seam ripper & 1 pair of scissors. Seriously, that’s it. Difficulty Level: Easy. Seriously, a well behaved toddler could do it.
samples.ai_continuation_chat:
For those of us with softer tissue, particularly the full-on-top shape common among European bras, the elastic doesn't meet resistance. Instead, it simply pulls the breast tissue down and inward toward the band, creating the appearance of overflow even when the cup is actually the correct size. The breast tissue gets compressed and pushed below the elastic edge, making it look like there's not enough room in the cup when really the issue is the tension of that upper band across soft tissue.

This is why full coverage styles often work better for this body type—the additional fabric extends higher toward the breastbone, distributing the elastic tension differently and giving soft tissue more room to settle without being pulled downward. A full-on-bottom shape may find this less problematic because there's naturally more tissue at the bottom of the cup to fill the space, whereas full-on-top shapes have tissue concentrated where the elastic band sits most tightly.
samples.ai_continuation_free:
and that's perfectly valid too. Soft tissue settles differently into cups, and the elastic doesn't have that same pushback to work with. What happens is the fabric just sits on top rather than being molded by what it's covering, which can make the whole bra seem like it's bunching or not sitting right even when the technical fit is fine.

This is why trying to judge fit by looking at photos alone is so tricky - you can't always tell whether someone has firm or soft tissue just by looking, and that dramatically affects how a bra will look on their body versus yours. The same bra in the same size can look completely different on two different people.

It's also why getting fitted in person, if you can find a good fitter, can be so helpful - they can actually feel the tissue and understand how it behaves, not just look at numbers on a tag. But even then, a good fitter will listen to how you want things to look and feel, not just what the measurements say should work.

samples.prefix: May 17th, 2017 Wests Tigers five-eighth Mitchell Moses has let the fans down after jumping ship to Parramatta mid-season. (AAP) May 17th, 2017 However, there is light at the end of the tunnel. I am looking at the recruitment announcements over recent weeks since new coach Ivan Cleary was appointed at the club. I can see a new team building already.
samples.human_continuation: Before I get to that though, just a quick comment on the transfer of 5/8 Mitchell Moses to the Parramatta Eels this week. This is a disappointing result for all concerned. I don’t buy into the notion that Mitchell should be so distracted by his contract situation that he could not perform for his current employers. There have been plenty of examples over the years where players have signed with rival clubs, sometimes 12 months or more before their current contract expires, yet they have been able to continue playing and giving 100% effort to their current club. I see absolutely no reason, why Mitchell Moses, as a professional sportsperson, should not have been expected, and willing, to fulfil his duties under the current contract for season 2017. Peter Sterling takes aim at Mitchell Moses I feel most sorry for the fans who looked forward to this year with great anticipation.
samples.ai_continuation_chat:
And while Moses may have been the headline grabber in his dramatic mid-season exit, the Tigers are quietly assembling a roster with the kind of character and grit that wins premierships. Players like Benji Marshall, returning for a second stint, bring leadership and a never-say-die attitude that Moses never truly embodied. The Cleary era is about rebuilding trust and culture, something that was sorely lacking when Moses and his manager were agitating for a release.

Peter Sterling, a Parramatta legend, has questioned the ethics of the move, noting that a contract should mean something. And he’s right. Moses walked out on teammates, fans, and a club that stuck by him through injuries and poor form. His legacy at the Tigers will be one of broken promises and unfulfilled potential.

But the Wests Tigers don’t need him. They are building something sustainable, with a coach who demands accountability. The fans deserve better than a player who quits mid-season, and finally, they are getting it.
samples.ai_continuation_free:
The signings of experienced campaigners like Ben Matulino, Josh Reynolds, and Russell Packer show that the club is finally targeting players with grit and proven ability, rather than just potential. Cleary is clearly building a forward pack that can compete physically, and adding a competitor like Reynolds in the halves gives the team some much-needed direction and energy.

Fans have every right to feel burned by Moses’s departure, but dwelling on it won’t help anyone. The reality is that the club is moving on, and the new recruits are already injecting a sense of purpose into the squad. If these players can gel under Cleary’s system, the Tigers could be a much tougher proposition next season. It’s early days, but for the first time in a while, there’s genuine reason to be optimistic about the future at Concord.

content_constraint.content_direction: Argues that Moses should have continued performing for the Tigers despite signing with a rival club, citing past examples of players maintaining effort.

samples.prefix: Last week, a prominent Arab archaeologist sent me a web­link to a doubly-depressing story from the Hasakeh region of north-east Syria. Bordering Turkey and Iraq, it’s long been one of the poorest areas in the country and now, with control of the area being contested by several of the factions engaged in Syria’s brutal civil war, its 1.7 million people, or those who haven’t already fled across the border, are among those most in need of humanitarian assistance.
samples.human_continuation: Watered by the Khabur river, Hasakeh has seen the birth of some of the earliest civilisations in the region. Indeed, one site, Hamoukar, is considered by some archaeologists to be the oldest city in the world. Dozens of important sites, dating from the Stone Age onwards, have been identified, though few have yet been extensively studied. There’s no scope for investigations now into what this region has to offer in terms of discovering the origins of agriculture and early urban society. Such studies require a peaceful environment – and that is absent. The first depressing part of the story is that many sites are being severely damaged by illegal digging, searching for items that can be sold into the underground market for antiquities. Supplies of such artefacts grow dramatically in areas of conflict where the maintenance of law and order breaks down.
samples.ai_continuation_chat: The Hasakeh region, however, is not just a humanitarian tragedy; it is also an archaeological one. This area, watered by the Khabur River, is a cradle of ancient civilizations, with tells—artificial mounds built up over millennia of habitation—dotting the landscape. One of the most significant is Hamoukar, a 6,000-year-old city that challenges the conventional view that urban life first emerged in southern Mesopotamia. Its excavations have revealed evidence of early trade, craft specialization, and even a large-scale battle, complete with sling bullets and collapsed buildings. But now, these irreplaceable sites are being systematically looted. With the Syrian government and various armed groups distracted by the fighting, illegal digging has become rampant. Armed gangs, often using bulldozers and backhoes, tear into the ancient settlements, seeking artifacts to sell on the international antiquities market. The destruction is both wanton and irreversible, erasing the layered history of the region for a quick profit.
samples.ai_continuation_free: The link led to a report by a small, independent monitoring group that had documented the systematic looting of several archaeological sites in the region. The story was doubly-depressing, the archaeologist explained, because the destruction was not the indiscriminate result of shelling or combat. Instead, it was organized and industrial. Satellite imagery showed hundreds of fresh pits, dug in neat rows, across the ancient tells—the artificial mounds that mark millennia of continuous human settlement. The looters, it seemed, were not desperate locals scavenging for food or fuel, but well-equipped crews working under the protection of one of the armed groups. They were using bulldozers and metal detectors, and they were targeting specific periods, likely the Bronze Age and early Assyrian layers, where intact cylinder seals, cuneiform tablets, and jewellery could fetch high prices on the international antiquities market. The archaeologist’s voice, even in the text of his message, carried a weary, professional grief.
